One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls.
Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child.
Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk.
South Africa is reeling after the discovery of nine women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year.
Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.”
Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet.
The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him.
Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according to News24.
Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct.
“Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.”
When Sibiya appeared before the Madlanga Commission in February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation.
Sibiya also denied that he had received a gift of 20 impalas from Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift.
Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering, declined to comment on the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:
“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.
A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
2,192
That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check
As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.
“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”

Xi Jingping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course.
At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could avoid military conflict between the two competing superpowers.
“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialog, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.
“We should coexist in peace,” he said. “China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”
With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.
His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.
Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was US president.
Trump declared that he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”
He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.

Trump offers Xi state dinner guests first-ever tour of ballroom construction site: ‘Special treat’
The 90,000-square-foot golden ballroom being built in the White House’s East Wing is expected to cost hundreds of millions of dollars

Donald Trump couldn’t help but offer guests at his state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping a first-ever tour of his ballroom construction site.
The president loves to boast to the White House press corps and his Truth Social followers about his passion projects around Washington, D.C., especially the massive White House ballroom being built. Now, in front of an international audience, Trump has offered to share a glimpse of what he called a “clean and sparkly” construction site.
“And if I could go off script just for a second,” Trump said as dinner guests in the East Room of the White House laughed. “But as a special treat in honor of President Xi and Madame [Liyuan] Peng. I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back.”
“It's one year away from completion — the new ballroom that you've heard about, and you will see something that I think you will really love.”
The 90,000-square-foot golden ballroom will fit 650 seats, compared to the 200 seats in the East Room. Trump has said construction will cost about $400 million and that he and other donors would pay for it.
But the project’s contractor told the administration that it would cost $600 million, with at least half expected to be covered by taxpayers, The Washington Post reported in June.
The Trump administration has also been challenged in court over whether it had the authority to tear down the East Wing last October to build the ballroom without Congressional approval. The Supreme Court ruled last month that the president can continue with construction for the time being.
“You'll be the first people to step foot on that, and we'll do that maybe after we're finished with the entertainment tonight. Anybody [who] wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkly, it's our honor to have you do so,” Trump told his dinner guests.
The official delegations from the US and China attended the state dinner. Some notable names on the guest list included first lady Melania Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Trump was photographed next to Melania while waiting to greet Xi and his wife Peng at the White House ahead of the dinner. Makeup was caked on his left hand, which he often uses to cover up bruising.
The Trump administration has said the black and blue on the back of his hands is due to frequent handshaking and aspirin use.
Several of America’s tech leaders, such as SpaceX’s Elon Musk, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, were also in attendance Thursday night amid an AI race with China.
During the legal fight to build his ballroom, Trump argued that it was needed for national security. Underneath the East Wing sits a bunker dating back to 1942, after the U.S. entered World War II. In court filings, the Trump administration noted that bomb shelters, military installations and a medical facility would be added to the bunker during construction.
So when Trump suggested officials from China, an adversary of the U.S., tour the construction site, it raised some eyebrows.
“Of the security bunker? Seems suboptimal,” Reuters journalist Charlie Szymanski wrote on Bluesky.
“Guided tour of the super secure and classified military ballroom for officials of a foreign unfriendly nation. Totally reasonable,” another Bluesky user, Jeff Domingues, posted.
One X user wrote, “Let’s take the leader of China into the ballroom that doubles as a military bunker! Great idea Don!”
Melania led the preparations for the state dinner, which included a menu that the White House said had a “subtle Chinese influence.” For the main course, guests enjoyed sesame-crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy.
Entertainment for the night was headlined by Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at Trump’s second inauguration. Guests were also treated to performances by military ensembles.
“Thank you, Mr. President and Mrs. Trump, for extending to my wife and me your gracious hospitality and thoughtful arrangements,” Xi said at the dinner through an interpreter. “You make us feel truly at home.”
“I would also like to extend my sincere greetings to Americans from all sectors of society who care about China-U.S. relations and support the further growth of our bilateral ties.”

Last month, China delayed the launch of an ambitious robotic mission to the south pole of the Moon, Chang’e 7, until early next year. The country did not provide a detailed explanation for the schedule slip, but it was welcomed by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.
“They are targeting the exact same location on lunar south pole,” Isaacman said Wednesday evening at the Off World conference in Houston. “We may have dodged a bullet with the Chang’e 7 mission a couple of weeks ago because that would have gone to the Shackleton crater.”
Much of the lunar surface is pretty barren, but the south pole, and the Shackleton Crater in particular, offers some of the most coveted real estate there. That’s because the high rims of the crater create permanently shadowed regions known as “cold traps,” where it’s thought that water (in the form of ice, of course) and other useful materials may have accumulated over billions of years.
Limited real estate
In all of NASA’s and China’s plans for long-term settlement on the Moon, relatively few square miles at the south pole of the Moon matter the most. It’s there that both countries believe they can establish an enduring presence that will help them learn techniques for expansion further into the Solar System. Isaacman and other US officials have started to express concerns that China could establish exclusion zones where robotic probes and then human missions go. Chang’e 7 will bring considerable mobility to the Moon.
“It has rovers, it has hopper drones like we now have in development but didn’t eight months ago, and could have potentially denied access to some of the most interesting spots,” Isaacman said. “They want to interact with the water ice, and they want to get really good at the skills for where they’ll want to go next for their Neil Armstrong-like moment. Except it won’t be on the Moon, it’ll be on Mars.”

Meta has a new plan to get people to make games for its Horizon social platform. The company today announced two new development tools that will let you create games with AI prompts: Horizon Create, a mobile app, and Horizon Studio, a browser app that offers more granular controls. The apps will be available in early access, and interested users can sign up for a waitlist.
Meta is going to let you build games with AI right on your phone
The next push for Meta’s Horizon platform involves AI-generated video games.
Horizon has struggled as a platform, but Meta has a plan to give these new Horizon games significantly more reach: It’s going to let published games made with Horizon Create and Horizon Studio get recommended on Facebook and Instagram, where they also will be playable.
“Someone scrolling through Instagram can tap a clip of your game and be in a multiplayer session within seconds, without needing to download an app or being redirected,” Meta says. “Your game lives natively in the feeds where people already discover content and connect with friends.” Games that are “engaging, stable, culturally relevant, and keep players coming back” will get more reach, according to the company.
The company’s announcement comes as Roblox, a similar platform to Horizon that is vastly more popular, is also making a significant push into AI-powered development, including a feature in its mobile app that similarly allows users to generate games with a prompt.
Meta’s news about Horizon, which launched as a VR app, follows a recent pivot to primarily focus on mobile. With Meta stuffing AI into basically everything it can, it’s perhaps no surprise that AI is becoming a big part of Horizon as well.
Giving people the tools to quickly make those could give people more options for things to play. I’m pretty skeptical that a bunch of AI-generated games will be as engaging as a handcrafted experience, but the games made in Create and Studio sound as if they’ll at least have the elements of video games (unlike Google’s Project Genie, which can create brief but empty AI-generated interactive experiences). “Both enable creators to turn any idea into a complete 2D or 3D mobile game, complete with progression systems, balanced difficulty, art direction, multiplayer, and more, then refine every element to their standards,” Meta says in a blog post.
Meta also likely has a very long way to go to reach the scale of Roblox, which has 123 million daily active users. Horizon, by contrast, hasn’t ever really taken off; The Verge reported in early 2022 that it hit 300,000 monthly users.

- Amid U.S. President Donald Trump's many efforts to place his name and image on various sites and items, the claim that Trump or his aides were considering attaching his name to the historic Ford's Theatre — where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in 1865 — circulated online in September 2026.
- The rumor stemmed from an MS NOW article from Sept. 23 that cited "people familiar with the effort" without naming the protected sources.
- As of this writing, we have yet to find publicly available evidence confirming the report. This lack of conclusive information does not make the rumor true or false. Rather, it means that no further information that would allow us to rate the claim currently publicly exists.
- White House spokesperson Davis Ingle criticized MS NOW and told Snopes, "This story is completely false." A spokesperson for the Interior Department added, "This is not true." We also emailed MS NOW for further comment. We will update this article with any potential future developments.
In September 2026, a claim circulated online alleging officials associated with U.S. President Donald Trump, or Trump himself, were considering attaching his name to Washington, D.C.'s historic Ford's Theatre — the site of former President Abraham Lincoln's assassination in 1865.
For example, on Sept. 23, a popular X post (archived) began, "BREAKING: HELL NO! Trump officials are scheming to slap his name on Ford's Theatre — the playhouse where Abraham Lincoln was assassinated by John Wilkes Booth."
(@OccupyDemocrats via X)
Additionally, users shared the rumor on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived) and TikTok (archived).
One Snopes reader emailed us the text from the above-pictured X post and inquired, "Is it true?" Another reader, and some of the users making the posts that we linked above, also cited an MS NOW article from Sept. 23 headlined, "Trump aides explore attaching president's name to Ford's Theatre." That reader asked," Is Trump really thinking about putting his name on Ford's Theatre in Washington, DC?" A third reader asked a similar question, sharing a different article with the headline, "Trump Now Seriously Considering Slapping His Name on Ford's Theater."
In sum, as of Sept. 23, we have yet to find publicly available evidence confirming Trump or his aides are planning to add his name to Ford's Theatre National Historic Site. 
The authors of the article on MS NOW, which first reported the matter, began by saying that "administration officials are circulating a list of government sites that could have his name affixed to them in some way," including Ford's Theatre. In other words, the reporting said a list featured Ford's Theatre as one of a number of sites under consideration for adding Trump's name.
The MS NOW reporters did not name their protected sources, instead citing them as "Trump aides" and "people familiar with the effort." The reporting also said, "It is unclear how seriously the theater is being considered or how the administration would attach Trump's name to it," citing one purported unnamed administration official as telling MS NOW the idea had been discussed but didn't know where it stood.
Laura Barrón-López, one of three people listed as authors for MS NOW's article, said on the MS NOW cable TV channel that the unnamed sources provided the information to her, the other two authors and their colleagues. We emailed MS NOW to request further comment.
The MS NOW story quoted White House spokesperson Davis Ingle as saying, "This story is completely false," as well as an Interior Department spokesperson saying, "This is not true." We independently confirmed both statements. (The National Park Service, a federal government agency under the Interior Department, manages the historic site.)
Over email, t
We emailed Ford's Theatre to ask about the story, including inquiring if officials working at the theater had received any information about Trump's name being added to the site, and will update this story if we receive a response.
Searches of the Ford's Theatre website and social media pages, as well as basic queries of DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo, among other research points, found no further information about this matter.
As MS NOW's article noted, the alleged consideration of adding Trump's name to the theater came to light amid Trump's ongoing pursuit of attaching his name to the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, among other numerous other efforts to add his name and face to U.S. passports, banners on federal buildings and other governmental designations.
We will update this article with any potential future developments.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
- Published
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."
"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"
Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.
The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.
Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.
"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.
"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."
Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.
The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.
His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.
The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.
"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.
"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.
"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."
Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.
Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.
Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.
South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.
The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.
Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.
And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.
It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.
This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.
Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.
"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.
"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."
Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.
It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.
"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."
Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.
President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."
Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.
"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.
"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.
"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."
In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.
"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.
"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."
"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."
Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.
"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.
"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."
"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."

Quick Answer
The iPhone Duo hides several firsts and oddities: horizontal rear cameras, vertical UI elements, top-mounted volume buttons, Apple Pencil support, titanium construction, Smart Take, a circular status bar, unusual USB-C placement, and no Action button or Pro camera controls.
Apple launched many devices at its recent Surprise and Shine event, but there was no doubting the star of the show. It was the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, and the device that many are expecting to do for foldables what the iPhone did for smartphones almost two decades ago. Small wonder then that the past few days have seen everyone and their grandmother discussing the iPhone Duo.
Debates have been raging over its animations, its crease, its cameras, its apps, and of course, its price. Some are hailing it as the coolest thing since sliced bread, while others insist it is a spawn of Satan in smartphone shape. But in all this debate and discussion, some important aspects and features of the Duo have either escaped attention or have not been adequately covered.
Here are ten things you might have missed about Apple’s first foldable.
Table of Contents
The first iPhone with horizontally arranged cameras on the back…selfie cameras on the corners
iPhones have been coming with multiple cameras (two or three) on their backs for a while now. However, they have always been arranged vertically, one below the other, or in the case of some Pro devices, with two cameras one below the other and the third one placed between them but slightly to the side, forming a triangle of sorts. The iPhone Duo thus becomes the first iPhone to have cameras placed next to each other horizontally, in what some would term a very Pixel-like style. The selfie cameras also get new locations – moving to the right corner of the external display and close to the right corner of the internal display (when opened), where it actually lies under the display. Regular iPhone users are sure to notice a change in perspective.
The dock, navigation, and even the Dynamic Island just got radically right, and utterly vertical
The cameras on the iPhone Duo might have gone horizontal, but some elements of the UI have gone vertical! While everyone has been focusing on the crease in the middle of the iPhone Duo and its visibility (it’s not easy to spot, by all accounts). Apple moved many iOS elements to the right side and gave them a vertical orientation. Lock screen controls, navigation buttons, the home screen dock, and even the Dynamic Island are on the right side of the iPhone Duo, and what’s more, are arranged vertically.
The Dynamic Island even slides open vertically to show information and updates. Evidently, this was done because of the width of the iPhone Duo (it is also the widest iPhone ever), which would have made it difficult to reach these elements. They have therefore been placed on the same side as the display unlock/power button, which is also a fingerprint scanner. This is pretty right-wing in UI terms, literally.
Volume buttons on the top
The iPhone Duo comes with a rather different volume button placement from other foldables. While it is conventional for most foldables and indeed, most ‘normal’ phones, to have volume buttons on the right or left side, the iPhone Duo actually has volume buttons on the top, aligned slightly towards the right. This is a volume button placement we have seen on the newer iPad minis but not on any other iPhones or iPads. It is a rather odd location in our opinion, and if opened and rotated clockwise, it would place the buttons on the lower part of the right side, and on the top of the left side if rotated anti-clockwise.
Camera Control? Present! Action button? Er…
While the iPhone Duo comes with a Camera Control button like other recent iPhones, it, rather surprisingly, does not have an Action button, which is generally seen on the left side of most iPhones and can be customized to carry out a number of tasks. It used to toggle Silent mode on and off, before being changed to an action button. Clearly, it was either not good enough to make the cut for the Duo or perhaps there simply was not enough space for it.
Apple Pencil support exists, but only for the Type-C one
The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone to come with Apple Pencil support. What’s more, it supports the Apple Pencil on both its internal as well as external display. But there is a catch – it only supports the basic Apple Pencil (USB-C). This means that while one can scribble and sketch easily, there’s no pressure sensitivity and no support for double taps. One will also need a Type-C cable to charge it, as it cannot charge magnetically. Given the price and potential of the device, it would have been good to have Apple Pencil Pro support on it.
Only new iPhone with Titanium
Remember how Titanium was the coolest thing in premium phones a few years ago. Well, while it still remains a very premium material, it has largely disappeared from the smartphone scene, with even Apple seemingly moving on to other materials, with only the iPhone Air using Titanium last year. This time around, it is the iPhone Duo that carries the Titanium legacy forward. While the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max use “forged aluminum” and ceramic glass, the iPhone Duo comes with a main chassis made with grade 5 Titanium, and 3D-printed titanium is also used for the hinge cover.
The only iPhone camera with Smart Take
Although its cameras might not seem as formidable as those on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the iPhone Duo has a slice of camera magic up its sleeve that no other iPhone has. This is Smart Take, which, with some AI magic, automatically works out when you are perfectly placed for a photograph and takes it without you needing to hit a capture button or prompt the device in any manner. It is supposed to work very well with individual and group selfies, and uses the rear cameras while showing you a preview on the cover display. While the feature is designed mainly for the fold form factor, it would be great to see it on “normal” iPhones too, although one might not be able to see previews!
A Type-C port placed under the cover display
In another case of rather unusual placement, the Type-C port of the iPhone Duo is actually placed on the base of the cover display or the upper panel. In many foldables, the charging port is placed on the lower panel, so that the phone can be opened without moving the charging cable. That is clearly not going to be possible on the iPhone Duo.
The status bar is closed…and is now a circle
The move to a foldable form factor has led to a redesign of some UI elements on the iPhone Duo. Perhaps the most surprising of these is the status bar. Until now seen in the top right corner, and displaying signal strength, Wi-Fi, and battery, it has now been changed to a circle, with the battery life and signal strength being on the circumference and Wi-Fi being at the center. It is not really as intuitive as its predecessor, but we guess users will get the hang of it.
No Pro controls in the camera
The iPhone Duo comes with two 48-megapixel cameras on the back – a new Fusion Main camera, and the same ultrawide that is on the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. But while these pack in a lot of features such as three photographic styles, smart focus tracking, next-generation portraits, macro photography and more, the iPhone Duo’s camera app does not come with the Pro Controls seen on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, which let users play around with shutter speed, white balance, and aperture. This l is a bit of a pity, especially given the vast viewfinder the open Duo can serve up. But well, to be fair, this was never meant to be a camera phone.

Why this break has come at the worst time for De Zerbi & Spurs
- Published
Big spending always means big ambitions, but shelling out so much money on so many players the way Tottenham did this summer produces problems for any manager, and there is no quick fix.
If I was given a bundle of cash and asked to buy an outfit for a wedding, and I spent every penny of it on pink shoes, brown trousers, yellow shirt and orange tie, then I am sure you would all say that just doesn't work.
That is similar to what has happened at Spurs, where the board backed Roberto de Zerbi to the hilt with an outlay on new players of around £400m.
It was an almost unprecedented occurrence from a club that has always been renowned for being careful with investment in their team, and it sent expectations from many Spurs supporters through the roof.
The club had just avoided relegation two seasons running, finishing 17th twice in a row, but suddenly some fans were looking forward to a season competing for trophies and a top-four finish.
Their early results and performances have been disappointing, of course, but fans have to understand all the different factors that affect you when you are building a team - and it is ridiculous to suggest De Zerbi should be under pressure already, especially after he kept them up last season.
Let's give De Zerbi a chance
Finding a way for your club to win takes a manager in lots of different directions but they all involve time - on the grass or with social interaction with the players.
Not only has De Zerbi not been given that early time and opportunity, the majority of his players have now been taken away from him for another three weeks on international duty.
De Zerbi has many other issues to deal with, from Tottenham's poor home form to their inability to recover from conceding the first goal in games.
But his biggest challenge right now will be to fit those players who have just arrived in with the ones already at the club, into a unit that plays as a team and produces results so that the money the club has spent is justified.
All of this will take time, and patience, and all the kinds of little detail that supporters never see.
In my day, we were given time to create a team, and a family. For today's managers, time seems more limited than ever.
We are only five games into the season but there are already some Spurs fans who seem to think De Zerbi is the worst manager in the world, even though he has proved elsewhere how good he is.
I like De Zerbi's passion, and his approach. That will count for nothing if Spurs don't eventually produce, but let's give him a proper chance.
Combinations can take time to click
De Zerbi is a very passionate, straight-talking and ambitious manager who demands total commitment and backing from his board.
He has definitely had that at Spurs, which has left people wondering why he has made such a slow start.
But, before the season started, I thought his biggest challenge with so many different types of players arriving would be to put players together that fit as a team, not as a group of individuals.
I've been in that situation myself, for example in my early days at Stoke, when I signed Gerry Taggart and Michael Duberry to play together, two centre-halves who were complete opposites in relation to how they dealt with space on the pitch.
Gerry always wanted to drop off deeper because he wasn't overly quick, whereas Michael was fast and didn't ever worry about leaving space behind him.
I couldn't make Gerry any quicker, so common sense locked in and I had to convince Michael that he would have to take a step away from his main strengths of pace and power and work along Gerry's lines instead.
We spent a great deal of time on the grass in training until we finally got both working in unison. Both were different, but they understood the importance of working together as a pair for the benefit of the team. Even so, it still took time for it to click.
For any manager trying to build a successful team by developing combinations like that, the main thing you need is time with your players.
It can happen where a lot of new players settle in quickly at the same time and the team starts well - like Sunderland last season, or Brighton pretty much every year when they have lost several key players - but the difference is that while those clubs might also have changed their manager, they have not changed their identity.
Whether it is Sunderland and Brighton, or Brentford and Bournemouth, they all have a set identity so that when they look for a player to fit in a certain position, he has to have certain strengths.
When you don't have that solid base behind you, knowing exactly what is needed for certain positions, then bringing 10 new signings and all in one window like Spurs have just done, is going to create many issues for the coach.
Each player has a different personality and needs different amount of time to settle in, not only to a new environment but also to adjust to the demands of a very single-minded and demanding coach like De Zerbi is.
This settling-in period would have been covered if all the players had had a pre-season together, to get up to speed with their team-mates and what De Zerbi is asking of them, with his front-foot style of play.
That did not happen, and then even after the season started, Spurs were still adding to their squad.
Finding out who understands importance of teamwork
Coaching a team to be a team takes time, patience and a sound idea of the strengths of all your players.
Even when you have got that, trying to knit every player together takes time, and that is still De Zerbi's issue now.
For starters, he was always playing catch-up. Because all of his players were not in place when the season began, he missed the opportunity to assess his squad and impose his own principles on his top group of players.
He is a coach at heart and will want to be out on the training pitch conducting a system of work for the team, in and out of possession, that he believes will bring success to the club. This international break means he cannot do that with all his players.
Another issue De Zerbi has is that he has only been in the job a few months and he is still getting to know the existing players, not just the new ones, on and off the grass.
On it, you need to find out who understands the importance of teamwork and who doesn't, to iron out shortcomings and and see what works and what doesn't.
An example of when you realise something doesn't work was my experience at a club who had just bought a right-back from a top Premier League team, for more than £1m which was big money at the time.
We were struggling at the bottom of the league when I came in and needed a direction on the pitch that would bring better results.
During the defensive work we were doing in training, the full-back kept picking up what were, in my opinion, poor positions while covering from the opposite side to where the ball was.
I must have stopped the session on at least four occasions to remonstrate with him and give my view, but in the end the lad told me that this is not what he believed was right.
I immediately replaced him with a young full-back from the reserves who had been playing for the opposition in the drill, who understood his role was for the team, and not for himself.
Getting to know your players' characters too
Getting things right off the pitch is so important too, and that involves getting to know what your players' characters are like, finding out what they are like as individuals, and understanding their lifestyles.
I had three South American players at West Brom who were fantastic lads but we still had to look after them.
I spoke to my assistant, David Kemp, about taking them and their families out for dinner, and by spending time with them and their children and their wives I believe we won a degree of respect and trust that we would never have had if we had not bothered to meet them all together as a family.
You have to realise that players from different cultures can be used to living a different lifestyle, and this can make a difference to how quickly or how well they fit in.
I had one player in the Premier League whose routine I just could not believe, yet he became such an integral part of keeping a struggling club up.
His 24 hours typically played out like this - training from 8.30am to 1pm, home and bed until 9 or 10pm and then up and out again for dinner and then a casino or whatever, until the early hours.
Then he would be up for training, and he would go again.
It took me a few weeks to get to the bottom of this but, once I confronted him, he was adamant that his routine suited his lifestyle. He certainly knew the best restaurants around town, but his performances were always of the highest quality on the pitch.
Did he heed my advice? I think he did, but he was such a great lad, top player and a great team member that he wasn't a problem anyway.
He had been a bit isolated from the rest of the squad at first, but it just took him some time to integrate.
Again, finding out about him as an individual and making personal contact with him, was important, and it was something I always saw as vital with all my players.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Can Heidi Overton fix the FDA?
Heidi Overton, a soft-spoken physician once described as “bound by her faith,” will answer questions later today in front of the Senate committee that holds the key to her eventual confirmation. She’s likely to be asked about her views on abortion, vaccines, and how to rebuild an agency that DOGE decimated.
Politicians, industry leaders, and public health groups are split on Overton. She is relatively unknown to the pharmaceutical industry and lacks managerial experience. But she has been a key health policy adviser during President Trump’s second term.
It’s been a meteoric rise for Overton, who once told a journalist that her dream was to become a doctor then return to her small hometown of Gallup, New Mexico, off Route 66.
STAT’s Margaret Manto has the scoop on Overton’s prepared remarks and her past, including the former Trump administration official who brought her into the president’s sphere. Read more.
White House shelves controversial NIH executive order
Thousands of researchers collectively unclenched their jaws yesterday after the White House backed off a planned executive order that would have given a commission of political appointees veto power over grant awards.
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), the Appropriations Committee chair, confirmed that the administration appeared to have reversed course. The drama started during a White House meeting last week in which the Office of Management and Budget director sought to assert more control over science funding — the latest in a series of attempts.
Read more from Chelsea Cirruzzo and Anil Oza.
Radiologists rush to embrace AI
Oprah said it best: “You get a scan! You get a scan! You get a scan!”
Americans are getting more medical imaging, and radiologists’ ranks aren’t growing fast enough. It has led the field to full-throatedly embrace AI tools to keep up, perhaps more than any other medical specialty, writes STAT’s Katie Palmer.
Everyone is getting in on the AI feeding frenzy — Silicon Valley, private equity-backed practices, outpatient and teleradiology groups. Startups have aggressively developed and acquired their own tech, deploying it in-house, and marketing their “AI-native” capabilities to radiologist employees and hospital customers.
There’s huge potential for a product that can reduce the administrative and workflow problems that eat up radiologists’ time. But it’s not a given that the strategy will pay off — for patients or their businesses. Katie has the full readout.

In the last several weeks, four unvaccinated people have died from measles in Pennsylvania, according to state officials. But health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has publicly questioned whether the deaths were actually caused by measles, launching a political firestorm. The United States is experiencing its worst year for measles since 1991. Speaking of measles…
…it is one of the most contagious diseases on the planet.
In 1961, there was no measles vaccine. Jewel Murray remembers when one of her siblings caught it. Then another. And then her. Her siblings quickly recovered. But Murray, then a kindergartner, vividly recalls her father carrying her to their station wagon and rushing to the hospital, where she stayed for a month, partly in a coma.
“Since I survived rather than dying, why is my story worth repeating? The answer is simple: Children who die don’t grow up to tell their own stories,” said Murray, an internist and epidemiologist at the Dell Medical School at the University of Texas at Austin. “The current surge in measles cases should worry all of us.”

If Alaska had a customer-care department, James Belmont would have plenty to complain about. A retired Special Forces officer, he heads into the wilderness with Odin, the German Shepherd who served beside him, expecting a little peace. Instead, a medical crisis sends their aircraft down, leaving the pair injured, isolated and with a very long walk between them and civilisation.
That setup sounds like a straightforward survival adventure, but Heart of the Beast has something more intimate at play. James and Odin have both returned from war carrying damage, and their journey gradually becomes a test of how much one can endure for the other. There are bears, wolves, rapids, injuries and the assorted inconveniences of being stranded in the middle of nowhere. Yet the film's emotional centre is remarkably simple: these two refuse to abandon each other.
David Ayer handles the physical danger with confidence, and the brisk 101-minute running time helps. The screenplay, however, occasionally makes things easier for itself. An early conversation explains rather too much, while an opening glimpse of what lies ahead takes some suspense out of the journey. The succession of dangers can also become predictable. Fortunately, the film never loses sight of its central relationship, which keeps the adventure from becoming merely a parade of things going wrong.
Actors’ Performance
Brad Pitt plays James with a quietness that suits a man accustomed to keeping his feelings under wraps. His connection with Odin is particularly convincing because it is built largely through looks, gestures and physical care rather than sentimental speeches. Pitt's casting also gives James an almost reassuring toughness, which helps when the character is battered by one calamity after another.
Odin, played mainly by Uber, is impossible to ignore. The dog's expressive presence gives the film much of its warmth, while J.K. Simmons makes a memorable impression despite limited screen time. Anna Lambe also makes her brief but important appearance count.
Music and Aesthetics
Jared Michael Fry’s score gives the wilderness its own voice, using vocal textures, percussion and sounds that evoke wind and running water. Mauro Fiore’s cinematography makes New Zealand’s South Island a convincing stand-in for the Alaskan wilderness, moving between sweeping vistas and more intimate moments of danger. The wildlife effects are less convincing, but the film’s visual language makes the wilderness feel integral to the story.
FPJ Verdict
Overall, Heart of the Beast is worth watching for its warmth, strong performances and moving bond between man and dog, even if its survival story plays safe.

Joao Felix’s goal from outside the box proved to be the difference as Portugal beat Wales 1-0 in their UEFA Nations League match in Lisbon on Friday.
Portugal’s captain, Cristiano Ronaldo, who is eyeing the 1000-goal milestone, started the match as the lone striker but failed to have the usual impact he has had over the last two decades. He failed to convert from two clear chances in the first half, while his goal in the second half was chalked out as he was found in an off-side position.
Wales, playing Portugal after more than a decade, will be proud to have limited the defending Nations League champion to just one goal, and came close to scoring late in the second half, when Brennan Johnson hit the upright and Lewis Koumas’ shots on the follow-up were eventually saved.
Portugal will face Erling Haaland’s Norway three days later, while Wales travels to Denmark for its next Nations League match on September 27.

As many as 71% of consumers surveyed in Mumbai said chemists never or rarely refused to sell medicines without a doctor’s prescription, compared with 64% nationally, according to a LocalCircles survey published on September 18, 2026. The findings come as the Centre has proposed mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores selling prescription drugs, and the Maharashtra FDA has intensified enforcement against retailers.
The Mumbai survey by LocalCircles, which received more than 20,000 responses across its questions, also found that only 28% of respondents said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 21% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
On prescription checks, 36% of 3,697 Mumbai respondents said chemists never refused to give them medicines without a prescription and another 35% said they did so very rarely. Only 9% said chemists refused such sales most of the time and 5% said they always did so.
The gap was also visible in home deliveries. Of 3,122 respondents, 18% said their chemist never demanded a doctor’s prescription during ordering or delivery and 40% said this happened very rarely. Only 23% said a prescription was sought most of the time or always.
The survey showed that neighbourhood chemists remain the main source of medicines in Mumbai. Of 3,012 respondents, 57% said they visited or sent someone to a local chemist, while 26% ordered from their chemist through phone calls or WhatsApp for home delivery. Only 17% primarily used e-pharmacy apps.
The national survey, published a day earlier on September 17, 2026, showed similar, though somewhat lower, levels of reported non-compliance. Across India, 64% of consumers surveyed said their chemist never or rarely insisted on a doctor’s prescription, while only 15% said chemists did so most of the time or always. Only 31% said they were assisted by a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said the person assisting them was not qualified.
The nationwide survey received more than 106,000 responses from consumers across 327 districts. It also found that 41% said chemists never or rarely sought prescriptions during home delivery, compared with 58% in Mumbai.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated draft amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores supplying medicines sold on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription.
The draft, issued through Gazette notification G.S.R. 791(E) dated September 8, proposes inserting a new sub-rule after Rule 65(2). It states that retail supply of prescription medicines should take place under CCTV surveillance installed and maintained at the premises. The proposal is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs and curbing sales without valid prescriptions. The government has invited objections and suggestions before finalising the amendment.
The proposed rule comes amid a sharper enforcement drive by the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration. Between June and August 2026, the FDA inspected 2,902 drug establishments, including 2,295 sales establishments and 607 manufacturing units, and initiated action against 880 licensees.
Of these, 677 licences were suspended, and 203 were cancelled, with 740 of the 880 actions involving retailers and wholesalers. During the same three-month period, the FDA conducted 104 search-and-seizure operations, seized illegal drugs and cosmetics worth Rs 11.41 crore, registered 20 FIRs and made 21 arrests.
FDA inspectors flagged several of the same issues reflected in the consumer survey, including the sale of medicines without registered pharmacist supervision, dispensing prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, incomplete Schedule H1 records and sales without proper invoices. Other violations included expired medicines being kept in sale stock and inadequate temperature controls for products such as insulin and vaccines.
The Mumbai survey also found billing gaps. While 76% said they generally received a printed GST invoice and 3% received a manually prepared GST bill, 20% effectively did not receive a proper GST bill.
LocalCircles said the Mumbai findings would be shared with the Maharashtra FDA, Union Health Ministry and CDSCO, and called for stricter verification of registered pharmacists, prescription checks for phone and WhatsApp deliveries and better documentation of medicine sales.

Our son's death could have been prevented by FA - Billy Vigar's parents
- Published
"You swing from sadness to anger because you just feel it could have been prevented."
That is the view of Camilla Vigar, whose son Billy, a former Arsenal academy player, died a year ago today from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch.
The 21-year-old striker was playing for Chichester City at Wingate and Finchley FC in north London.
In their first broadcast interview since their son's passing, the Vigar family accuse the Football Association of doing "nothing" after previous similar incidents.
"[Billy] had his whole life ahead of him. He was 21 years old and he lost it playing football when he didn't need to," she told BBC Sport.
"I personally feel that the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings."
They give the example of amateur footballer Ben Hiscox, who died in 2015 after colliding with a clubhouse near Bristol.
After the coroner warned the FA about the risk of future deaths, padding was added to Stoke Gifford United's clubhouse and the run-off between it and the pitch was increased.
The Vigars also point to the life-changing injuries sustained by Alex Fletcher in 2022.
Fletcher fractured his skull when colliding with concrete barriers next to the pitch at Bath City's ground, and was forced to retire in 2024.
The FA conducted a review of clubs after that incident.
"As far as I'm aware, nothing was done with that information and it just sat there. One of the clubs as far as I'm aware that was highlighted as being one of the high-risk clubs was Wingate [and Finchley], where Billy then lost his life," said Camilla Vigar.
When asked by the BBC what was done with the information it had gathered, the FA provided no comment.
Changes needed at 169 clubs
At the time of Vigar's accident, the FA's stadium accreditation criteria, which applies to the National League System in men's football and the Women's National League, said clubs needed to have a "permanent" barrier around the pitch "of sound construction (eg concrete and steel)".
In light of what happened to Vigar, the FA launched a safety review of more than 900 clubs, which was conducted by independent experts.
As a result, the stadium criteria was updated last month and "no longer permits solid brick, breeze block or concrete barriers around pitches".
The BBC has been told 169 clubs in the men's National League System and women's National League were notified they would need to make changes "as soon as is reasonably practicable".
Where walls are structural, they must be "covered with suitable protection", such as padding.
The FA said: "This important work is under way, and we will continue to fully support the clubs involved."
Funding is being provided by the FA and the Premier League.
BBC Sport approached hundreds of affected clubs in an effort to gauge their views on the changes and understand the status of their remedial work.
Bromsgrove Sporting near Birmingham, which has a concrete wall surrounding its pitch, told BBC Sport the changes were "completely understandable and long overdue". It added: "We are fully supportive of this and are grateful for the 100% funding from the FA."
The club said it had been given a deadline of the end of this season but "being high risk it would be good to complete this side of Christmas".
Meanwhile, Sheppey United, in Kent, has a concrete supporting wall around two sides of its 3G pitch, which will be covered in padding.
Asked for their thoughts on the changes, the club said: "There is always an element of risk in all sports and they can't all be mitigated, unfortunately in this instance the remedial works are more a reactive response rather than a proactive one. If the funding wasn't in place I think it would make it difficult for some clubs to fund this."
Bath City, where Fletcher's incident happened, has solid perimeter walls on all sides of its pitch.
The club told BBC Sport: "We welcome the ruling as it seeks to improve player safety and recognises that funding needs to be available to support clubs to implement this fundamental change to the ground grading regulations."
Keith Vigar, Billy's father, said: "I work in the health and safety industry, and the main thing is you don't go to work and expect to get injured, let alone even die at work in the workplace."
The Vigars want the regulations extended above and below the National League.
"It needs to change basically at all levels, not just at the levels that have changed," said Keith Vigar.
That is a view shared by Fletcher, who said the FA had "ignored" his years of campaigning on the issue of pitch perimeter safety.
"It wasn't until Billy's passing that [the FA] came to the table on this issue," he said.
"So for me, that is a complete dereliction of duty on their part, and there should be accountability for that failing."
Fletcher also said he is worried the ban on concrete, breeze block and brick walls does not cover all levels of the game and wants that explored urgently by the authorities.
"There could be still situations where football is being played at some level, to some degree, organised football in this country, with these unsafe pitch perimeters. I would like to see that guidance, or the regulation, extended to consider all of football."
Billy was 'something different'
Compared to many youngsters, Billy Vigar joined the football system late - and yet his talent was still recognised.
He was scouted by Arsenal while playing for local club Hove Rivervale in Sussex, and joined the Premier League side's academy.
"It was just an amazing feeling," said his father.
"Sort of like your son's been chosen. And I'd always promised him a decent pair of football boots if he joined an academy. So yeah, since then it's cost me a fortune.
"He was something different, Billy. I think most, even at Arsenal, they saw something different in him. He was a great athlete, basically. And that started from an early age with his brother, who quickly learned there's not much point trying to challenge him because he wanted to win."
Injuries followed, and Vigar was recuperating from one such setback while playing for Chichester City FC, where he had made an instant impression.
Darin Kilpatrick, the club's first-team manager, said: "He was so coachable, he would run in behind, he would drop in short. His hold-up play was excellent and obviously he had an eye for a goal which all strikers have to have.
"To be fair, the way Bills was playing in his last couple of games that we had him, we would probably have only been able to keep him another six months before we moved him on into the higher levels where he belonged."
Asked what level he was aiming for with Billy, Kilpatrick said: "He would have gone into the National League or [English] Football League, without a doubt."
Watching football again has been difficult for Keith Vigar.
"It did become less important, far less important to start with, the struggle to get back into it," he said. "When we went to see Chichester in that sense, first off, it's hard because you're just thinking, 'Billy should be out there, Billy should be playing' and that sort of thing. That's been hard."
The Vigars said Chichester FC have been "amazing" during the past year, including designing a kit that makes moving but subtle references to their son.
They want accountability and answers. They are awaiting the inquest, which is likely to take place next year.
But today, as they mark the one-year anniversary of their son's tragic accident, they will pour all their focus into climbing Snowdon with their children Phoebe and Ollie, and the family of Billy's girlfriend Lois.
"I think it just gives us something to focus on and gives us a challenge to do," Keith Vigar said. "And I know he'd have liked to do that. I'm sure he will be with us somewhere, looking over us in some way or form, having a laugh at us, no doubt, in the rain."

Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
- Published
When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.
Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.
It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.
"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.
There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.
That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.
It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But it it something that match-going supporters actually want?
What the law says
Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.
It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.
The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.
Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.
The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.
It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.
However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.
It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.
The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.
The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.
The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.
Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".
The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".
It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".
Fans' views differ on drinking in stands
The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.
Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.
"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.
"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.
"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."
The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.
Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.
Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.
The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.
It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.
The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.
Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.
Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine".
"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.
"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.
"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."
For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.
Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it".
"Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said.
"I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere.
"If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."
Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with".
"There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."
But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.
What is it like in other sports and different countries?
Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.
Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.
The restrictions differ around Europe.
There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.
In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.
In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.
In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.
