Turkey will hand over key base in Iraq in a gradual troop withdrawal deal
Turkey has agreed to gradually withdraw forces from a strategic military base in northern Iraq and hand over control to the Iraqi government
ANKARA, Turkey -- Turkey has agreed to gradually withdraw forces from a strategic military base in northern Iraq and hand over its control to the Iraqi government, following a meeting between the two countries’ leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
Iraq, meanwhile, pledged to remove armed groups that Turkey considers security threats from the region of Sinjar, in northwestern Iraq, according to a joint statement issued after the meeting late Wednesday between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.
“In light of the progress Iraq has achieved through security measures, Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zelikan camp to the Iraqi federal government, in accordance with the agreed-upon mechanism and timeline,” according to the joint statement released by Erdogan and al-Zaidi’s offices.
Turkey and Iraq also agreed to “fully extend the authority of the Iraqi state in Sinjar and to end the presence of banned foreign armed elements,” the statement read.
The strategically-located Bashiqa base has long been an issue of contention between Turkey and Iraq, with Turkey failing to fully withdraw forces, despite previous discussions for their removal. Turkey established a military presence there in 2015 to support operations against the Islamic State group and help secure the region.
Although Turkey maintains several bases in northern Iraq for operations against the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK, the Bashiqa camp is Turkey's furthest base from its border.
Turkey, for its part, has long been pressing Iraq to curb groups with links to the PKK and other non-state armed groups from operating in Sinjar.
The Iraqi government announced earlier this month that the Sinjar Resistance Units, a Yazidi militia affiliated with the PKK, had agreed to disarm and eligible fighters would be integrated into the Iraqi security forces. The group played a significant role in the fight against IS, but was seen by Turkey as a threat because of its PKK affiliation.
The agreement came as the U.S. is ending its decades-long military presence in Iraq, with officials saying the hundreds of troops remaining in northern Iraq will be out by a Sept. 30 deadline.
Turkey, meanwhile, is engaged in peace efforts with the PKK aimed at ending a decades-long conflict. The group, whose fighters have launched attacks on Turkish targets from bases in northern Iraq, has agreed to disband and lay down arms as part of the effort.

As Jensen Huang puts it, AI can help fight climate change — but only if it inflicts “an enormous amount of pain and suffering” first.
Jensen Huang talks about AI and climate change like a supervillain
With AI, he says, ‘in order to save you, they’ve got to hurt you first.‘
The Nvidia CEO discussed the future of energy and AI’s impact on our planet in the latest episode of The Ezra Klein Show. But his comments boil down to the same accelerationist spin we’ve seen from a variety of tech leaders as well as President Donald Trump. They promise that AI will be such a gift to humanity that it’s worth the damage caused by data centers currently running on dirty energy.
Huang’s extreme level of privilege is glaring
Huang’s extreme level of privilege is glaring in the interview. He’s right that there will be pain. People are already suffering from fires and floods exacerbated by climate change. People are already dying earlier because of air pollution from fossil fuels. But Huang, with a net worth of around $192.6 billion, will not pay the price of the pollution his company creates through energy-hungry chip factories and data centers.
Huang tells Klein, after complaining that the US hasn’t built out enough fossil fuel plants, that:
It’s kind of like, in order to save you, they’ve got to hurt you first — that’s the nature of surgery. They’ve got to cut you open to save you. They’ve got to inflict an enormous amount of pain and suffering on you so that they can save you. And so I think AI’s kind of like that.
That’s the bit that gives Thanos energy. Resources are too limited and so after disappearing half of humanity, the Marvel supervillain believes, things will be much rosier. (“I will shred this universe down to its last atom, and then create a new one, teeming with life that knows not what it has lost but only what it has been given,” he tells the Avengers.)
Huang goes on to say:
Over the next several years we have to unfortunately use fossil fuels, because we just don’t have enough sustainable energy to make a difference. And then after that, hopefully, we can transition to that.
For context, nearly every country on Earth agreed to limit climate change when they adopted the Paris agreement in 2015. The accord sets a goal of cutting greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030 and reaching net zero around 2050. That can only happen with swift transition to carbon-free energy like renewables and nuclear. Here’s just a short list of terrible things getting worse when we stall that progress to pursue advances in AI:
- Earth is expected to lose 99 percent of its coral reefs. Those reefs support coastal economies, and also serve as a buffer protecting communities from tropical storms, flooding, and coastal erosion.
- One in 10 people around the world, 770 million people, already face “acute risk” from sea level rise.
- Since 2001, peak daily wildfire growth rates have more than doubled in the western US. Wildfires are faster, more frequent, and more intense.
These effects are showing up in Huang’s backyard, even if he’s insulated from them. He mentions in the interview that he doesn’t know what his own address is. However, he reportedly bought a $7.5 million home on Maui in 2004 — before wildfires devastated the island in 2023. That year, an Nvidia spokesperson confirmed with The Verge that the Huangs “have owned the same home in Maui for many years.”
Huang’s property reportedly escaped damage, and the Nvidia spokesperson told me that the Huangs “donated significantly to local relief efforts.” But despite the philanthropy from tech billionaires with residences on Maui, the inferno also inflamed tensions over luxury properties’ hold on Maui’s water supply.
“Billionaires coming to Maui, buying up large swaths of land as their, I don’t know, seventh vacation home, it’s painful for our community,” Maui County Councilmember Keani Rawlins-Fernandez told me at the time. “It underscores the stark disparity between Indigenous people who want to mālama ‘āina, care for our land, and those who see Hawaii as a vacation destination.”
“Billionaires coming to Maui, buying up large swaths of land as their, I don’t know, seventh vacation home, it’s painful for our community.”
While greenhouse gas pollution from fossil fuels makes wildfires more dangerous by exacerbating hot, dry conditions, climate change isn’t entirely to blame for the flames that razed much of Lahaina on Maui. I reported at the time that previous generations of wealthy land grabbers primed the islands to burn. The US annexed the Kingdom of Hawaii in 1898, egged on by American plantation owners who wanted to evade import taxes. They cleared native vegetation for their businesses, allowing invasive grasses to take hold and make the landscape much more flammable than it used to be.
So when I hear Huang make the case now that there will need to be sacrifices in the name of AI progress, it reminds me that we’ve seen this playbook before. An industry that wants to grow at any cost. And nearby communities and their descendants are just supposed to live with the aftermath.
Huang mentions growing community opposition to data centers in the interview with Klein, and scolds other companies for not spreading the good news with residents about how efficient data centers purportedly are before they start construction. “If they don’t want data centers to be built in their town or whatever it is, then so be it. But if you’re going to build in their town, be sure to go there and let them know what’s coming,” he says.
“I am inevitable,” Thanos notoriously said — and apparently, so are AI data centers.
Even so, data centers don’t actually have to be as polluting as they are turning out to be.
In the interview, Huang also (unfairly) attributes record renewable energy purchases to AI. He blames climate action for stalling the construction of energy infrastructure, presumably for fossil fuels.
I think we just have to acknowledge that we got ourselves really gummed up in climate change and sustainable energy, and as a result, we just didn’t plan enough energy production.
Then he proclaims that AI is “the best opportunity we have” to “turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable.” He sees AI accelerating demand for clean energy in the long term. But AI already needs a lot of energy now, and fossil fuels are what we’ve got.
“A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable.”
But renewables were already the fastest-growing sources of new electricity generation before the recent generative AI boom. It’s generally cheaper to generate power from a wind or solar farm than a new gas or coal plant. But Trump, who lined his campaign coffers with money from the fossil fuel industry, is incentivizing the development of gas and coal plants to power data centers.
And now, data centers are in turn spurring the development of far more fossil fuel infrastructure. Air pollution associated with AI could lead to up to 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs by 2028, according to a study from UC Riverside, Caltech, and the Rochester Institute of Technology.
Nevertheless, “A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now,” Marc Boom, a senior director of the Environmental Protection Network, a group made up of EPA alumni, said in a recent press briefing on the growing health risks posed by data centers.
It also depends on the attitudes of industry leaders like Huang. If other people’s pain and suffering is the price you’re willing to pay for so-called progress, that says less about what’s possible and more about your own personal priorities.

Senegal job an 'absolute dream' for new boss Vieira
- Published
Patrick Vieira says it is "an honour" to become Senegal head coach, with the decision to take the job "one from the heart".
The 50-year-old was born in the West African nation but subsequently represented France as a player, winning the 1998 World Cup and the 2000 European Championship with Les Bleus.
The former Arsenal midfielder spoke of his "immense pride" to begin his first international job, following stints with New York City, Nice, Crystal Palace, Strasbourg and Genoa, at his unveiling by the Teranga Lions on Friday.
"Being head coach of the Senegal national team is an absolute dream," he told a news conference in Dakar.
"I was born here, my parents were born here, and it really is a homecoming.
"From the very first meetings I had with the [Senegal football federation] president, I accepted this challenge straight away, because there was also an exceptional generation of players.
"I realise the expectations of the people - all 20 million Senegalese. And I know that with the experience I have, with the determination I have, I'll be able to see this project through."
- Vieira named new Senegal head coach 
  - Published18 August
Taking over after the dismissal of Pape Thiaw, Vieira inherits a Senegal side which exited the 2026 World Cup in dramatic fashion in the last 32, throwing away a 2-0 lead after 85 minutes against Belgium before losing 3-2 following extra time.
Before that the Teranga Lions claimed the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) title with a 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January.
However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be decided by the Court of Arbitration for Sport after a walk-off by some Senegal players and staff protesting against a penalty decision in the final resulted in the trophy being handed to the North African hosts instead in March.
"Today, Senegal is among the major nations in world football," Vieira said.
"Senegal's objectives aren't what they were 10 or 15 years ago. On the back of its recent results, Senegal has moved forward, has reached new levels.
"The demand for results has also stepped up. We need to lay solid foundations."
Vieira plans to build a side with "a very precise structure" which can play with "intensity and aggression".
"What matters to me isn't starting again from scratch," he added.
"It's about respecting what the federation has put in place over the last few years and building the next stage, opening a new chapter.
"A new chapter meaning my job isn't to tear everything down, it isn't to throw everything out of the window.
"It's about keeping this team's strength: its identity, its unity, its ability to suffer together.
"To make this project work, I'll need the whole nation united. I'll work heart and soul to restore the team's pride."
Starting with two away trips
Vieira has been thrust straight into competitive action in qualifiers for the 2027 Afcon with two fixtures in this international window, two more in November and the final two rounds in March 2027.
His stint in charge was due to begin with a home match against Mozambique on Friday, 25 September but the fixture has been reversed as Dakar is in the midst of preparations for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.
"Of course, I'd have preferred to play the first match here in Dakar but unfortunately, with the federation, we all felt the best decision was to postpone the match and go and play in Mozambique," Vieira explained.
"Those are difficulties we're going to accept and deal with."
Senegal will be without several notable names for the trip to Maputo and the subsequent away game against Ethiopia on 29 September.
Long-time number one Edouard Mendy, 34, has retired from Teranga Lions duty and Vieira said talismanic forward Sadio Mane will be absent with "a bit of a physical issue".
Despite previous speculation that Mane, also 34, could follow Mendy into retirement, Vieira said the former Liverpool and Bayern Munich man will "surely" be part of his next selection, fitness permitting.
Right-back Krepin Diatta has been left out because he is currently without a club, while forward Ismaila Sarr, who is yet to feature for Crystal Palace this season because of transfer speculation and a groin injury, is also absent.
'No doubt' about his managerial ability
Vieira's career as a player was trophy-laden but he has found the same kind of success hard to come by as a manager.
He departed Palace in March 2023 with a record of 22 wins from 74 games in all competitions and, after a season at Strasbourg, has been out of work since being sacked by Genoa in November last year with the Italian club bottom of the table.
He had guided them to safety in Serie A in the 2024-25 campaign but was then dismissed after six defeats in nine league games at the start of last season.
"When you talk about my coaching career, or a certain amount of experience, I've always been someone who stays positive," Vieira said.
"That means you learn, and there are always positive things to take from it. I'm a better coach today than I was in my last spell at Genoa, because that experience helped me grow and made me realise certain things.
"Given the experience I have as a manager, I've got no doubt about my ability to meet the expectations of fans."
Vieira was warmly received when he arrived in Dakar on Thursday evening, with video clips posted on social media showing him holding a Senegal flag aloft while shaking hands with a throng of fans gathered at the capital's airport.
"I couldn't have been given a warmer welcome. I saw the supporters' enthusiasm and I thank them for it.
"Taking charge of this national team isn't just a new stage in my career - it's coming back home."

A medical review committee determined that the physician "acted with due care." The Netherlands Public Prosecution Service will determine whether the physician acted within the bounds of the law.
Rumors that a child in the Netherlands was euthanized by medical professionals circulated online in September 2026.
People on social media and YouTube claimed the country had recently allowed physicians to terminate the life of a 2-year-old disabled child. One user posted on X, "My heart hurts for the broken world in which we live that has so abandoned its humanity."
The controversial nature of the claim and the ongoing debate over reproductive rights in the United States led many Snopes readers to reach out via email asking us to verify the story.
Euthanasie of a 2years old baby in the Netherlands: disabled now can be killed and they say it's human not to tet live disabled and kill them without even give thm the possibility to make an own informed decision when they are an adult.: WHAT'S THE DIFFERENCE TO THE NAZIS?!! https://t.co/Wp2eiNlW1g
— KaiTraudvetter (@traudvette8137) September 18, 2026
The claim was true.
A review committee made of four physicians, one lawyer and one ethicist, formed by the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport and the Ministry of Justice and Security, described its duty in the 2025 annual report (translated from Dutch to English by DeepL):
The committee assesses whether a physician acted with due care in cases of late-term abortion or the termination of life in a newborn or a child between the ages of 1 and 12. In 2025, the Commission received three reports of late pregnancy terminations. No reports of end-of-life care for newborns were received in 2025. At the end of 2025, the Commission received its first report of end-of-life care for a child between the ages of 1 and 12. The committee meets every two months and will address this report at its first meeting of 2026.
The committee's judgment for the case in question — available to read on their website — determined the physician who administered the euthanasia "acted with due care."
According to the committee, "due care" is based on the premise that the physician must "arrive at the conviction, on the basis of prevailing medical insight, that euthanasia is the only reasonable solution to alleviate the child's hopeless and unbearable suffering."
Dutch law
According to the government of the Netherlands, "euthanasia (termination of life on request) and assisted suicide are criminal offences" with the only exception being "when the procedure is performed by a physician who has satisfied six statutory due care criteria."
The criteria say the physician must:
- be satisfied that the patient's request is voluntary and well considered.
- be satisfied that the patient's suffering is unbearable, with no prospect of improvement.
- have informed the patient about their situation and their prognosis.
- have come to the conclusion, together with the patient, that there is no reasonable alternative in the patient's situation.
- have consulted at least one other, independent physician, who must see the patient and give a written opinion on whether the due care criteria set out in (1) to (4) have been fulfilled.
- have exercised due medical care and attention in terminating the patient's life or assisting in the patient's suicide.
In October 2024, the euthanasia law was expanded to include children age 1 to 12. The case in question was the first time the expanded law was put into practice.
The government's website about termination of life for children ages 1 to 12 states:
Termination of life is only allowed if a child is terminally ill and is suffering unbearably with no prospect of improvement. This means the child is in constant, severe pain. And that there is no cure, and no reasonable alternative to relieve the child's suffering, even through palliative care.
In this situation, the doctor may decide, together with the parents, to terminate the child's life. This decision is always made in consultation with the parents and, if possible, also with the child.
While the committee found the physician to be acting within the parameters of the stated criteria, the next part of the process requires them to send the details of the case and their review to the Public Prosecution Service, which then determines whether the doctor acted within the bounds of the law.
We reached out to the office of Sophie Hermans, the minister of health, welfare and sport, who first announced the case to the Dutch Parliament in June 2026, for an update on its legal status and will update this article if we get a response.
Details of the case
According to the committee's report on the case in question, the child's condition included being born prematurely at 26 weeks, which caused sepsis.
Over the following months the child suffered extensive brain damage, cerebral visual impairment and severe epilepsy, as well as lack of verbal and cerebral visual development.
The review said that "the child had multiple, very severe disabilities, both mental and physical, and the prognosis was that the child would be dependent on support with all activities of daily living for the rest of their life."
The report continued that because the child was incapable of communicating, "the diagnosis, prognosis and treatment options were discussed extensively with the parents" who ultimately decided to ask the physician to end their child's life.
Other consulted physicians said there were proposed alternatives, such as palliative care, but "the parents were of the opinion that the proposed treatments would only prolong the child's suffering."
In the end, the procedure began "by administering increasing doses of midazolam and morphine through an IV cannula," and then "administered coma-inducing substances (propofol and thiopental), after which the child reached a state of very deep sedation, and died."

Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
- Published
President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim.
China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan.
On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted.
The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January.
Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency.
This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations.
This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions.
The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes.
Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year.
On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China.
The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself.
In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict".
Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing.
Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict.
On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence.
However, Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments.
The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards.
All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans.
But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax".
And, of course, let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes.
There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday.
But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics.
The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal.
Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive.
Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower.
The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever.

Kosovo vs Republic of Ireland; UEFA Nations League Group B3
Kosovo vs Republic of Ireland. UEFA Nations League Group B3.
Prishtina City Stadium.
Kosovo 1-0 Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson's Boys in Green beaten in UEFA Nations League opener
Report from the UEFA Nations League Group B3 match between Kosovo and the Republic of Ireland in Pristina; Heimir Hallgrimsson's Boys in Green slip to deserved defeat courtesy of Vedat Muriqi's late goal
Thursday 24 September 2026 23:33, UK
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.
The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.
Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.
The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.
Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.
Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.
Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.
Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.
Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.
Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.
Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.
Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.
Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.
Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.
Ireland pay price for 'off day'
Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:
"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.
"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."
Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.
"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.
"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."
Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."
He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.
"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

FSSAI proposes nationwide ban on manufacture, sale of non-dairy analogue products as ‘paneer’
The food regulator said the move was undertaken to safeguard consumer interests and ban the practice of marketing analogue products as paneer.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India has moved to ban the manufacturing and sale of any non-dairy “analogue products as paneer”.
The food regulator, in a post on its official social media handle, said it had proposed a ban on “the sale of analogue paneer made from constituents not derived from milk.” It further said the move was undertaken to safeguard consumer interests and ban the practice of marketing analogue products as paneer.
Analogue dairy products are non-dairy alternatives in which some or all milk constituents are replaced with ingredients not derived from milk. Analogue paneer, for instance, can be made using vegetable oils, starches, plant proteins, emulsifiers and other additives instead of milk fat.
What has the FSSAI proposed?
According to a notification released on Thursday, the FSSAI has proposed to amend the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restrictions on Sales) Regulations, 2011.
“The amendment is proposed in the following regulation to restrict manufacturing and sale of analogue product as paneer so as to prevent misleading of consumer's regarding the nature and composition of the product,” the notification stated. It added that the products which have already been registered or licensed under ‘Analogue in Dairy Context’ category would be required to discontinue the use of the term “Paneer” in their nomenclature, labelling or marketing.
The regulator said this was being done as part of the powers conferred to it under sub- section (2) of section 92 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
“Objections or suggestions, if any, may be addressed to the Chief Executive Officer, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, FDA Bhawan, Kotla Road, New Delhi - 110002 or sent on email at regulation@fssai.gov.in,” the FSSAI stated.

The food regulator has also invited objections and suggestions for 60 days from the date the relevant Official Gazette copies are made available to the public. After considering the representations received, FSSAI would proceed with the regulatory process.
Several states ban analogue paneer; Zomato follows suit
The FSSAI move comes even as several states have imposed a ban on the manufacturing and sale of analogue paneer. These include Maharashtra, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Himachal Pradesh.
Food delivery platform Zomato too announced a zero-tolerance policy against the sale of dishes containing analogue dairy products on its platform, saying restaurants that fail to comply could be delisted.
Dishes that restaurant partners declared as containing analogue dairy were removed from the platform, Zomato said in a release earlier this week.

It always creates apprehension because the sight is somewhat gory, but a nosebleed, in general, isn’t a cause for major concern. Occurring mostly in the under 10s and the over 45s, nosebleeds are very common: about 60% of the population is estimated to experience one in their lifetime. They can occur in one or both nostrils, but usually affect one. The medical term for a nosebleed is epistaxis.
How do they occur?
Our noses are lined with a moist, delicate tissue, the nasal mucosa. This lining cleans the air that we breathe in, and also warms and moistens the air. The mucosa is made of many tiny blood vessels, lying to close to the surface. These blood vessels can easily be irritated, injured and broken. When they break, they cause a nosebleed.
There are two types of nosebleeds: anterior and posterior. An anterior nosebleed, which is the most common type, starts at the front of the nose. These types of nosebleeds can mostly be treated at home. A posterior nosebleed takes place place deep at the back the nose, may cause heavier bleeding and could result in blood going down the back of the throat. This type of nosebleed requires medical attention.
Why do they occur?
Common causes include the inside of the nose becoming dry, usually due to a change in temperature, picking the nose, or blowing the nose too hard.
When the air is very dry, it causes the nasal mucosa, which is meant to be moist, to dry out, making it prone to crusting and bleeding. Dry air can occur in hot places with low humidity, areas of high altitude and in air-conditioned or heated spaces. People with upper respiratory infections, sinus infections, allergies or other ailments such as rhinitis may also sneeze, cough or blow their nose frequently, making them more prone to bleeds. The frequent use of medications such as antihistamines, nasal sprays or blood thinners, could also make people vulnerable to nosebleeds, as could breathing in strong fumes.
Nosebleeds can also occur due to injuries to the nose, the insertion of objects into the nose, a deviated septum, recreational drug use as well as less common causes such as having blood disorders, alcohol use, nasal polyps or tumours.
Being pregnant may also increase the chances of nosebleeds.
When to see a doctor
In general, nosebleeds aren’t serious and can be treated at home. In some circumstances, however, it is best to consult a medical professional. You should see a doctor if: the nosebleed has followed an injury or accident; if there is heavy bleeding or the bleeding lasts longer than 30 minutes; blood has been swallowed; if there is a feeling of weakness, dizziness, lightheadedness or if you have breathing difficulties, chest pain or a rapid heart rate. A doctor should also be consulted if the person with the nosebleed has other health issues such as a bleeding disorder, or high blood pressure, or if the person is a child under two years old.
How to stop a nosebleed
To stop a nosebleed, there are some first-aid measures that can be taken:
- Sit upright so the head is above the level of the heart, lean forward slightly
- Breathe through the mouth and gently blow the nose to clear it
- Use the thumb and index finger to pinch the both nostrils shut. Do this for 10 minutes.
- Use an icepack on the bridge of the nose at the same time as the pinching
- Check in 10 minutes, and if the bleeding has not stopped, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes
- Once the bleeding has stopped, lean forward and clean the nose with lukewarm water
- See a doctor immediately if the bleeding does not stop in 30 minutes
Preventing nosebleeds
Using a humidifier in the house especially in dry air conditions, trimming children’s fingernails, managing allergies, using a nasal saline spray or petroleum jelly to keep the inner lining of the nose moist and avoiding smoke exposure can all help prevent nosebleeds.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia.
The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat.
Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India.
“We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife.
The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district.
Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild.
In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia.
Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province.
Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.
The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

British rapper Yung Filly to face rape retrial in Australia next June
- Published
British rapper Yung Filly will face a rape retrial in Australia next June after a jury failed to reach a verdict during an earlier trial.
In July, a jury acquitted the 31-year-old - whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos - of three counts of rape, one of assault and one of strangulation but found him guilty of two assault charges. No decision was reached for three rape charges, which he has denied.
A fan, aged 20 at the time, alleges Barrientos repeatedly raped and assaulted her in his hotel room in Perth, Western Australia, after a 2024 concert.
The court previously heard that Barrientos and the woman had consensual sex before she alleged it turned violent and he refused to stop.
On Friday, Perth's District Court set 15 June as the start date for the retrial which is expected to last eight days.
Barrientos was not required to appear in court and is understood to have returned to the UK after the court granted him permission to leave Australia as part of his bail conditions.
Sentencing for the two assault charges that the jury found Barrientos guilty of in July will take place after the retrial.
Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad.
He has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.

Three infants died after a fire broke out at the Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) ward of Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS) in Telangana’s Adilabad district late on Monday (September 21) night. The incident occurred around 11.40 p.m. As many as 25 other infants being treated in the ward were safely rescued and evacuated in time.
According to Adilabad District Medical and Health Officer (DMHO) Sadhana, the fire was caused after an air-conditioner in the reception area of the SNCU burst into flames.
“The SNCU has two flanks, one with 11 beds, and another with 13 beds, while the Kangaroo Mother Care area located opposite the SNCU has four beds. The sections are enclosed and have glass windows. When the fire broke out, smoke accumulated inside the unit. As soon as the fire was noticed, the attendants of patients broke the glass windows and evacuated the babies from the affected areas,” the DMHO said.
The rescued infants were subsequently shifted to nearby private hospitals for further treatment. The two infants who died, aged five and four days respectively, were preterm babies. One of them died immediately after the incident, while the other succumbed four hours later. The third infant, a two-day-old girl who was born prematurely at 28 weeks and weighed 1.1 kg, was in a critical condition and died while being shifted to a nearby hospital, confirmed Director of Medical Education (DME) N. Vani.
Upon receiving information about the fire, a fire tender was rushed to the hospital and the blaze was brought under control. The exact cause of the fire was is yet to be ascertained. The police have registered a case and launched an investigation into the incident.
Adilabad Superintendent of Police (SP) Akhil Mahajan said the incident occurred at around 11.40 p.m., and police teams reached the hospital within three minutes, by 11.43 p.m. “Although Ganesh immersion processions were under way and a large number of police personnel were deployed, our teams were able to reach the spot within three minutes and assist in evacuating the children,” he said.
CM conveys condolences
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy expressed grief over the incident and conveyed his condolences to the families of the infants. He stated that the death of infants was extremely tragic. The Chief Minister directed officials to ensure better medical treatment for the children undergoing treatment at the hospital and to continuously monitor their health condition.
Mr. Reddy ordered an inquiry into the incident and directed officials to submit a report on the causes of the fire. He further instructed authorities to strengthen fire and other safety measures in hospitals across the State to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Govt. support
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha, who inspected the fire incident site, expressed grief over the deaths and conveyed his condolences to the bereaved families.
The Minister also reviewed the rescue and relief measures undertaken following the incident and the arrangements made to safely shift the infants undergoing treatment in the SNCU to other wards. He also sought updates from doctors on the condition of the infants and other children receiving treatment and directed them to provide the best possible medical care while closely monitoring their health. The Minister later met the families of the affected children and assured them of the government’s support.
“The condition of other children who were in the ward at the time of the incident was stable and none have developed any complications,” said a note from the Minister’s office.
He was accompanied by Adilabad MLA Payal Shanker and Principal Secretary, Health, Medical and Family Welfare, Dr. Christina Z. Chongthu.
A preliminary inquiry indicated that an electrical short circuit in an air-conditioning unit may have triggered the fire, causing plastic components to burn and filling the SNCU with thick smoke, the Minister said. A detailed enquiry by an expert committee would ascertain the exact cause and identify any lapses in safety standards, he added.
The Minister said RIMS staff, district officials, Fire and Police personnel acted swiftly to disconnect the power supply, evacuate the infants and provide emergency medical care.
He said a 150-bed Mother and Child Health (M&CH) Building would be established at RIMS, taking its bed strength from 800 to 950. Plans were also under way to develop the institute into a super-speciality hospital, besides setting up Hematology and Emergency Trauma Care wings.
The Minister said steps were being taken to increase postgraduate medical seats in Paediatrics, Gynaecology, Radiology and other departments and strengthen the out-patient and in-patient services at RIMS.

The proposed 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI payments above ₹2,000 will not result in any additional cost for consumers, news agency PTI reported, citing government sources. The new MDR is scheduled to come into effect from October 15 and will apply only to merchants accepting UPI payments exceeding ₹2,000.
Person-to-person UPI transfers will remain free, irrespective of the transaction value. Responding to criticism from Opposition parties, including the Congress, which have described the move as a tax on consumers, government sources said that not a "single penny" of the money collected through MDR would be transferred to the government.
Instead, the revenue generated from the fee will be distributed among banks and other participants involved in processing UPI payments, the sources said.
Quick answers to key questions
The UPI MDR is proposed to be 0.4% on person-to-merchant UPI transactions exceeding ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 for transactions above ₹75,000.
The revenue from the UPI MDR will be distributed among banks and participants involved in processing UPI payments: 40% to customers' banks, 30% to payment gateways, 20% to UPI apps, and 10% to sponsoring banks.
No, consumers will not bear the cost of the UPI MDR; it is intended to be paid by merchants, and person-to-person UPI transfers will remain free.
The UPI MDR was introduced to create a sustainable revenue model for the digital payments ecosystem, covering costs related to infrastructure, cybersecurity, and customer support.
UPI transactions below ₹2,000, person-to-person transactions, and transactions by small merchants earning up to ₹1 lakh a month will remain exempt from the new MDR charges.
Under the proposed revenue-sharing arrangement, customers' banks will receive 40 per cent of the MDR collected. Payment gateways will get 30 per cent, while 20 per cent will be allocated to the UPI app and the remaining 10 per cent to the bank sponsoring the UPI app.
"MDR levy of 0.4 per cent on UPI transactions above ₹2,000 will not be passed on to the consumers. Banks, as well as the Indian Banks' Association, will address misconceptions related to MDR charges and their impact on users," the sources said.
They also clarified that the MDR should not be viewed as a tax, cess or surcharge.
Government sources further rejected concerns that the introduction of the merchant fee could encourage consumers to return to cash payments. They said such fears were misplaced.
The sources also expressed hope that the GST Council would consider reducing or reviewing the 18 per cent GST applicable to merchant fees on UPI transactions above ₹2,000, citing the decision taken in the case of insurance premiums as an example.
The Indian Banks' Association (IBA) is expected to launch an awareness campaign to address what it described as misconceptions and rumours surrounding the proposed 0.4 per cent MDR.
The proposed fee is intended to establish a more sustainable revenue model for the digital payments ecosystem. MDR refers to the charge paid by merchants to payment service providers for processing digital payments.
From October 15, a 0.4 per cent MDR will apply to person-to-merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000. The charge will be paid by merchants, not consumers, and will be capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 or more. Payments between individuals, as well as the vast majority of everyday merchant payments, will remain free.
Essential services, such as railways, telecom, fuel and insurance, will attract a flat ₹5 fee per transaction above ₹2,000. Capital markets transactions (mutual funds, stockbroking) get a lower 0.02 per cent rate, also capped at ₹300.
Small merchants collecting up to ₹1 lakh a month via UPI QR codes remain fully exempt from any new charge and shield about 96 per cent of all merchant transactions.
The NPCI, which operates the UPI platform, on September 15, issued a circular providing for MDR on certain UPI transactions, with the move aimed at creating a sustainable revenue framework for the digital payments ecosystem.
A dedicated fund for promoting the use of UPI by small merchants will be set up, with a contribution of 5 per cent of total MDR collections. This initiative will expand UPI acceptance, encourage sustained usage, and accelerate the inclusion of small businesses in India's digital payments ecosystem.

Mark Zuckerberg said Meta’s new personal AI agent Muse has become the “centerpiece” of his AI vision, as he unveiled a new handheld AI “charm” device that will feature the interactive assistant.
The Meta chief used the company’s annual Connect event at its Silicon Valley headquarters to announce Muse Charm, a small pendant-like device that fits on a keychain and is activated by a fingerprint sensor.
The device, which features a screen showing the Muse avatar, will also have real-time voice interactivity and is set to be released in December.
“If you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show what’s going on around you,” the chief executive said.
Muse, development of which was first revealed by the FT in May, has helped change the momentum of Zuckerberg’s huge bet on AI, quickly becoming the most downloaded app on both the Apple and Android app stores in the US since its launch two weeks ago.
The easy-to-use app offers consumers a team of autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks, such as ordering groceries, booking travel and organising finances.
Zuckerberg on Wednesday also announced new capabilities for Muse, including the ability to have live conversations with the interactive AI assistant, and insisted that it has “state-of-the-art privacy and security.”
The Meta founder has come under increasing pressure from Wall Street as he pours billions of dollars into AI infrastructure and talent, with Meta’s share price falling by more than a quarter between last September and the beginning of August.
But Meta’s stock has bounced back since the September 8 launch, adding $300 billion to its market capitalisation. The stock was slightly higher in after-hours trading on Wednesday.
The release of a breakout product to Meta’s 3 billion users caps a turbulent two years in which Zuckerberg has repeatedly struggled to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic in developing frontier AI models and features.
Zuckerberg on Wednesday said he believed Muse would “make users money.” As a result, the company would offer a free Muse tier “with the expectation that over time we will profit by taking a small fee from transactions.”

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

White House restores access to media outlets banned by Trump after judge's order
- Published
CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters have been allowed back into the White House after they sought an emergency court hearing to restore their revoked press access.
They accused the White House in a court filing of having "repeatedly violated" a judge's order lifting President Donald Trump's ban on the three media outlets.
But the White House said in a filing that it began reinstating access shortly after 09:00 EDT (13:00 GMT) on Thursday.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico reported they were granted entry hours after some of their staff were turned away. Trump initially said he barred the outlets because of "fake news". The White House later cited national security.
In the early hours, Judge Timothy Kelly had ruled the ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".
The White House in its filing said that the press passes had been restored by 09:07 local time and that confiscated badges were available starting at 09:45.
The standoff limited some TV coverage as Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House ahead of a state dinner.
CNN said some of their journalists were denied entry, including senior White House reporter Betsy Klein. But a producer was allowed to enter, the outlet reported.
Politico said one of its reporters was denied access to the White House and had his press credentials confiscated.
MS NOW reported that its White House reporter Laura Barrón-López and a producer were barred and had their passes taken, but another MS NOW producer was allowed in.
Trump first announced last Friday he was barring CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.
By Saturday morning, each outlet reported that they were denied entry to the White House grounds and that their press badges were confiscated.
All three outlets spoke out against the ban, accusing the Trump administration of violating their constitutional rights.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said they were pursuing legal action to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports".
TV networks including Fox News, NBC, CBS and ABC had suspended their televised coverage of the White House in solidarity.
And more than 50 media organisations across the ideological spectrum filed an amicus brief in support of the lawsuit, including Fox News, the New York Times, the Washington Post and the Wall Street Journal.
There have been previous instances of administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.
The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a specific press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.
But after objections from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was allowed in.

An 11-year-old boy who was shot at a home in northwest of Australia’s Sydney died in hospital on Thursday, police said.
The boy had been in a critical condition since being found with gunshot wounds to his face and neck at a unit in Norwest, a suburb in the Hills District of New South Wales, on Monday.
He died at Westmead Children's Hospital at about 8pm.
Police were called to the unit on Fairway Drive at about 5pm on Monday after reports of a shooting. Paramedics treated the boy at the scene before taking him to hospital.
Five other people who were in the home at the time, including four 18-year-old men and a 44-year-old woman, described as friends or family of the boy, were not injured.
Three men were arrested. Two were taken to the Hills police station but later released pending further inquiries.
The third, Isaac Bechara, was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence. The charge applies when an adult fails to report or conceals information about a major crime.
He appeared on Tuesday at the Blacktown Local Court, where he didn’t apply for bail and was refused it.
In the days after the shooting, police said it was too early to determine what had happened, although initial reports indicated the shots were fired inside the house.
Officers were also trying to locate the firearm used, noting that no gun was registered to the address.
New South Wales police superintendent Naomi Moore said a number of people inside the home at the time were known to police and that investigators were considering their possible links to organised crime, though she said some of those present were not cooperating.
NSW premier Chris Minns described the shooting as an "incredibly distressing situation" and "a very tragic reminder of how dangerous guns are", adding that people who fell victim to gun violence were often innocent people.
Friends and family paid tribute to the boy, who was a member of the Maronite community, a Christian denomination with a significant presence among Sydney’s Lebanese-Australians.
"Rip my baby," his father wrote on social media. "Rest in peace little cuz,” another family member said. “Heart broken."

NATO chief calls for calm as intel agency warns Russia may ramp up hybrid attacks
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte says the alliance is capable of handling sabotage and drone incidents in Europe and has good action plans in place
BRUSSELS -- NATO is capable of handling sabotage and drone incidents in Europe and has good action plans in place to deal with them, the alliance's secretary general said Thursday as a Danish intelligence service warned Russia is expected to increase such attacks.
Secretary-General Mark Rutte said he believes the rising number of hybrid incidents in NATO countries shows that Russian President Vladimir Putin is losing the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, and that the best way to respond is to give more weapons to the Ukrainian armed forces.
“All the response options are there, and we will use whatever we need,” Rutte said, speaking at a ceremony in New York marking the anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.
He said that citizens of the 32 NATO countries can remain calm. “Putin is in a bad place,” Rutte said. “He is not winning the war in Ukraine.”
In a new risk assessment released Thursday, the Danish Defense Intelligence Service said Russia is likely to step up its hybrid campaign — a term for the use of non-conventional hostile acts such as sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and an array of other methods — to pressure adversaries in the West and NATO.
“This could include destructive cyberattacks that cripple critical societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties,” it said.
“Russia has become more willing to take risks,” the agency said.
Hybrid attacks can aim to destabilize a country, test its defenses, strain resources, or influence public opinion — often in a way that makes it hard to identify those responsible.
An Associated Press interactive map tracking the incidents of hybrid attacks shows an escalation, from 59 in March 2025 to more than 200 at this point.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland.
He said Russia will likely pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyze or at least weaken the motivation of NATO countries” to rush to the defense of a member state coming under attack.
The Danish agency said there is “a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia,” but that this “could potentially take place in the coming months.”
The aim would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine and sow division in NATO, the service said. At the same time, it noted there are “no indications that Russia will launch an outright invasion of one or several NATO countries.”
NATO and European Union officials have said that Russia's armed forces are too tied up in Ukraine and that no unusual military activity has been noted near European countries close to Russia.
U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said earlier this week that the number of incidents right now does not indicate a conflict might be imminent.
“I don’t think it’s at a volume that would mean that it’s the beginning,” Whitaker said on Tuesday in Iowa, where he attended a panel about NATO alongside Rutte.
“I don’t think that it’s in anybody’s interest to head towards a conflict,” he said. “I think one of the things that we have to be very careful (about) is overreacting to any sort of hybrid activity.”
“We haven’t reached that threshold,” he said.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision of voters' list, officials said on Wednesday.
The officials made the remarks in the wake of a media report that the two Election Commissioners had objected to the Election Commission's steps 14 times in 10 months amid the SIR.

Officials said the law governing the functioning of the Election Commission and a Supreme Court judgment underline that as much as possible, decisions should be taken unanimously and if need be, majority view should prevail.
The Indian Express reported that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners, Sandhu and Joshi.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Railway Protection Force sets up narcotics cell, plans MoU with NCB
RPF has set up a narcotics cell to curb drug trafficking through trains and will sign an MoU with NCB for information sharing, training and joint operations.
The Railway Protection Force (RPF) has constituted a narcotics cell to curb drug trafficking through trains and is set to sign a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) for capacity building, information sharing and joint operations, the anti-drug agency said on Thursday.
Government's Target Against Drug Trade
The development comes as drug law enforcement agencies in India work towards the Centre’s target of uprooting the drug trade from India by December 31, 2029 — a deadline announced by Union home minister Amit Shah at a conference on Tuesday.
The NCB shared the details after the completion of the two-day conference of anti-narcotics police officers from across the country, chaired by Shah.
Home minister Shah in his address had said that the time has come to move from a seizure-centric approach to targeting trafficking networks and cartels.
According to an NCB statement, replying to a query on drug trafficking through railways at the third National Conference of Anti-Narcotics Task Force (ANTF) Heads of States and Union Territories, NCB director general Anurag Garg said the RPF had already constituted a narcotics cell.
Formalizing Cooperation
“The proposed MoU between the NCB and RPF will institutionalise capacity building, exchange of information and joint operations between the two agencies,” the NCB said in a statement on Thursday.
HT has earlier reported that in line with the three-year targeted crackdown on drugs, every agency is set to start a specialised anti-narcotics force.
The two-day conference, which concluded in New Delhi on Wednesday, brought together ANTF heads from 36 states and Union territories and focused on strengthening coordination among enforcement and intelligence agencies to dismantle drug trafficking networks.
“The fight against drugs is the most difficult of all battles, but it can’t be abandoned and must be won by December 31, 2029,” Shah had said at the conference.
