What is the cost of a life? For the wife and 20-year-old son Chongtham Vikram Singh, it is the lifelong grief and trauma of losing a family member. For Manipur, it is the loss of a homegrown musical talent, who began practicing his craft when he was a child, and made his way from Imphal to the big stages of Delhi. And for the rest of India, it is a reckoning with the systemic racism that has historically exposed Northeasterners living in other parts of the country to racial discrimination, harassment, bullying and violence.
The concerns are not new, nor were solutions entirely out of reach. The Bezbaruah Committee, set up by the Manmohan Singh-led UPA government to address the discrimination faced by people from the Northeast, had made a series of recommendations to the Modi cabinet in 2014. A key component of the proposals was making changes to the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Twelve years on, this is yet to be implemented.
Accused ‘Wanted to Teach a Lesson’ to the Manipuri Guitarist
Singh, a 55-year-old Manipuri guitarist, was allegedly beaten to death by a group of young men outside his home in Kilokari village of Southwest Delhi. On September 6, around 11:30 pm, Singh had objected to the loud noise and commotion being created by the accused outside his apartment.
According to the police complaint, when his son heard him shouting, he opened the door to see the group of men violently attacking Singh. After the altercation, Singh returned home but complained of breathlessness, he was then taken to Holy Family Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries at 6 am on September 7. CCTV footage showed the accused leaving the building. Seven men and a minor have been arrested in the case so far.
A Manipuri music teacher, Chongtham Vikram Singh, living in Delhi’s Ashram area was mob lynched by 8 people following a dispute over alleged noise and nuisance outside his residence.
Police said seven accused have been arrested and a minor detained in connection with the case.… pic.twitter.com/4V0LVeVLiJ
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) September 7, 2026
The autopsy report revealed that Singh died of massive internal bleeding caused by severe physical trauma to his chest and abdomen. The accused allegedly kicked him on the chest and abdomen after he fell to the ground. During questioning, they told the police that they wanted to teach Singh a lesson.
While the police investigation so far has not revealed any racial motive behind the violent attack, his death has brought to the fore larger concerns around hate faced by people from the Northeast in the nation’s capital and beyond. It also brings the Bezbaruah Committee’s recommendations, and the fate of those recommendations, back into focus.
The Bezbaruah Committee and Administrative Inaction
The Bezbaruah Committee was formed in February, 2014, after the killing of Nido Tania, a 20-year-old hailing from Arunachal Pradesh, who was beaten to death with iron rods and sticks by three men after a verbal altercation in Delhi. The accused hurled racial slurs at Tania during the attack. The committee was constituted “to look into the various concerns of persons hailing from the Northeastern states who are living in different parts of the country, especially the Metropolitan areas, and to suggest suitable remedial measures which could be taken by the Government.” It submitted its report to the MHA of the BJP government in July, 2014. It can be read here.
The most crucial among the recommendations, perhaps, was a proposal to amend the provisions of the then IPC by adding Sections 153C and 509A. Section 153C would criminalise words, signs or acts that promote discrimination or violence on grounds of race or place of origin, with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine. Section 509A would criminalise any word, gesture or act intended to insult a member of a racial group, with up to three years and a fine.
On January 2, 2015, then Union home minister Rajnath Singh said that the amendments were accepted and Sections 153C and 509A would be added as recommended by the Committee. However, In 2017, minister of state, home, Kiren Rijiju said in the Rajya Sabha the proposal was still under examination, with states’ views being sought. Later, when the IPC was being officially changed to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in 2024 and discussions were being held from 2023, the recommended amendments were entirely overlooked. The provisions were never enacted.
On September 8, 2026, two days after Singh’s killing, the MHA’s monitoring committee on Northeast issues convened a meeting to discuss the recommendations made more than a decade ago. Joram Maivio, a special invitee to the monitoring committee, MHA, and member of the Bezbaruah Committee, spoke to Alt News.
“We were expecting most of the recommendations of the Bezbaruah Committee to be slowly implemented after we received a confirmation from the MHA in 2015. We deliberated extensively on this with the judicial division of the MHA, after which the recommendation was sent to the law commission and the law ministry. It kept going from one department to another. We were verbally, or in principle, informed that it had been accepted and that it would be included when the comprehensive amendment of the IPC took place,” Maivio said.
“The discussions continued through 2017, 2018 and 2019 as the Supreme Court had ordered the committee to meet at least every three years and in serious instances, meetings can be called at any point. In every meeting we kept discussing the issue of racial discrimination and questioning when the law would be amended so as to criminalise racism against Northeasterners. So when the comprehensive criminal law amendments came in 2023 — the BNS, BSA and BNSS — we were expecting this recommendation to be included. But surprisingly, it did not come up,” he added.
Maivio said that he had flagged this on the two or three MHA monitoring committee meetings and questioned the ministry why the amendments had not taken place, but did not receive any concrete answer.
Meanwhile, Delhi police data accessed by The Indian Express in June 2026 showed that more than half of the accused in cases registered over the past 12 years for crimes against people from the Northeast in Delhi remained “untraced” despite “the creation of a specialised police unit intended to address such cases”. Out of the 2,656 FIRs filed between 2014 and April 30, 2026, in 1,465 (or 55%) cases, the accused were classified as untraced. Only 33 cases resulted in conviction, producing a conviction rate of 1.82 per cent.
Asked about what transpired at the September 8 review meeting, Maivio said, “The committee director and joint secretary said that the amendments would be taken up but we were not given any clear timeline as to when.”
“We will keep following up to ensure justice to people from Northeast as incidents of racial violence are chronic and recurring. There is no quick-fix solution, but by denying the reality, we cannot solve the problem. The Government must continue to act decisively to address it and prevent such incidents,” he asserted.
Maivio noted that some measures were implemented in Delhi, including the creation a Special Police Unit for North East Region (SPUNER) with the helpline number, 1093, two special Delhi Police recruitment drives in the Northeast, and plans for a Northeast Social and Cultural Institute in Dwarka. However, he acknowledged that implementation has largely remained confined to Delhi, with little progress in other states.
Northeasterners Condemn Killing, Speak out Against Discrimination
The North Eastern Students’ Organisation (NESO) condemned Vikram’s killing and demanded an impartial probe. Chairman Samuel B Jyrwa, who in 2024 also demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi “breaks his silence” and visits the crisis-struck Manipur, told the media: “It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home…For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin.”
“It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity…We want justice and we want the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are treated as Indians in Delhi,” said Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, as the former’s mortal remains were brought back to Imphal.
#WATCH | Imphal, Manipur | C Vikram Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, says, “It is a sad moment. Let us see what God has for us. It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity. We want justice. An atmosphere should be created in the capitals of India… pic.twitter.com/QmHjnTkk3W
— ANI (@ANI) September 9, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, the convenor of Delhi-based The Mizo Welfare Association, Thangzamang Henry Simte, condemned the killing and said, “Our organisation was built to create a community and safe space for people from Mizoram and the Northeast living in Delhi, who regularly face racial discrimination and stereotyping in educational institutes, office spaces, or even while taking public transport. The root cause is lack of education in the rest of the country about the Northeast. Some people in Delhi don’t even know which part of India is Mizoram or Nagaland…they do not know the difference between foreigners from other Asian countries and Northeasterns of their country.”
Simte left Nagaland around 26 years ago and moved to Delhi due to ethnic conflicts in his region. He said in 2003, when he was still new to the city, he was routinely referred to as ‘Nepali’ by passerby on the road. “In one particular incident that stayed with me, a man in a suit and tie who was sitting next to me at a bike servicing centre, suddenly yelled ‘Nepali’ at me unprompted. When I retorted sharply, he asked me where I was from. As I replied ‘Mizoram’, he bluntly asked, ‘where is that? Is that in India?”
Alt News spoke to people from the Northeast living in various parts of India, who, like Simte, revealed the daily, oft-normalised patterns of racial stereotyping and harassment they continue to face.
Gopi Kishan Baro (28), who hails from Assam and is currently working as a graphic designer in Gurgaon, alleged that he was systematically discriminated against and bullied by a senior colleague at work. “A few weeks ago, when we were in the lift, he kept mocking me and said something which sounded rather like a warning, ‘Tumahari aankhein choti hai aur hum dikhte nahi, iska ye matlab nahi hum gayab ho gaye hai’ (Your eyes are small, so we are not visible to you but that doesn’t mean we have disappeared). It made me quote uncomfortable but I tried to laugh it off because I did not want to create a scene,” he alleged.
He continued: “Last Wednesday, when I was having tea by myself, he appeared and claimed I stayed aloof most of the time because I came from such a faraway corner. By the end of the conversation when I was leaving, he shouted at me, ‘Waapis chale jaa apne desh’ (Go back to your country). I wrote a formal email to the HR about his racist behaviour. They simply let him off with a warning, while I continue to live in anxiety and disgust, knowing that these insults are directed not just to me, but at my kin, my community, and the entirety of Northeast India as well.”
Heightened Racism During Covid-19
COVID-19 brought this prejudice into sharper focus, as Northeasterners in several places were subjected to racial slurs, harassment and stigma.
Twenty-eight-year-old musician Abhibyanjana, who hails from Sikkim, lived in Pune for her studies and later in Mumbai for work. “When I was studying, as part of my course we were required to visit several slum pockets for a survey in early 2020, during the beginning of the pandemic. I was constantly referred to as ‘Covid’ or ‘Corona’ by locals there. I was jeered at and humiliated but I continued my work regardless, I realised that if I cannot fight back deeply indoctrinated prejudice against people who look like me,” she said.
“I have to move to cities like Mumbai for opportunities because it is scarce in Gangtok. But as a musician working in Mumbai, I am often treated as an ‘outsider’. The discrimination and otherisation against the people of Northeast is pervasive and crimes against our people hardly receive national focus. On the flipside, this has created solidarity within our community, we look out for each other wherever we go,” she added.
A 2022 study, published in the International Social Science Journal, titled ‘‘You people have brought the virus here’: Othering experience of northeastern people amid COVID‐19 in Delhi, India’, focused on how the Covid‐19 pandemic exacerbated discrimination, violence, and othering against Northeasterners living in Delhi, by analysing nineteen qualitative interviews.
The study, conducted to understand their lived experiences in Delhi before and after the pandemic, found that the pandemic disproportionately impacted the Northeastern people living away from their home states. “The Mongoloid features make them ‘non‐belonging’ and outsiders. The experience of othering is an everyday phenomenon for northeasterners… Northeasterners’ experience amid COVID‐19 is dominated by stigmatisation and bullying, as they are being targeted and arbitrarily accused of spreading the virus,” the study highlighted.
An earlier study, commissioned by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) in 2021, further confirms the heightened harassment, abuse, stigmatisation and blatant labelling as ‘coronavirus’ that Northeasterners faced living in other parts of India during the pandemic. Over 60% of the respondents said that their studies, work, and psychological health was impacted by these experience.
“The highest number of incidents were reported from Mumbai (44.7%)…78% of the Northeast people believed that physical appearance was the most important reason for prejudice against them,” the study noted. Mumbai was followed by by Chennai (72%), Pune (67.3%), Delhi (64%), Hyderabad (48.7%) and Bengaluru (43.3%) in racial discrimination comprising offensive and abusive language against Northeasterners.
‘You Look Like a Chinese’
Caroline Devi-Singh (52), who hails from Manipur, moved to Delhi in 1994 to pursue her graduation at Delhi University. She later moved to Chandigarh and subsequently Chhattisgarh. She told Alt News that her experiences living in North India for so many years had been varied, but racial stereotyping was a constant. “In college, we were often called racial slurs, either ‘Chinese’ or ‘Chinki’ or ‘Momo’. As a young girl, I was always taught to be extra cautious, to a point where dressing how we do at home was a threat to my safety,” she said.
“So many years later, my son [now 25-years-old] faces the same racial attacks. He has grown up with the awareness of his rights, but the rest of India still lacks awareness… Nobody thinks twice before resorting to violence against Northeastern. We have been ignored by all the governments and the media has never paid attention to our issues. I stay in a small town now and I see that even educated people cannot differentiate between a person from China and a person from the Northeast… This comes from ignorance and a lack of information. I blame the overall education system and the government for this,” she asserted.
China call us Chinese, mainland Indian call us Chinese, but we call ourselves Indians. 🙂
— Neha Gurung (@nehaGurung1692) November 27, 2025
A former student of Ashoka University, who now lives near the campus in Sonipat, said, requesting anonymity, “I moved here in 2021 from Manipur. In university, I have faced racial slurs regularly. Whenever I have brought it up with the administration, they have simply let the accused go with a warning. Racism is not taken seriously on this campus, or in the NCR region at large.”
“When Northeasterners face racism, people think it is only our responsibility to speak against it… We are always on high alert because what happened to the Manipuri musician could’ve been me. It could’ve been any of us,” he added.
A Violent Pattern Entrenched in History
The cases point to a continuum of discriminatory mindset against the people of Northeast that stretches from racial slurs and stereotyping to intimidation, physical assault and, in the most extreme cases, death. In December 2025, 24-year-old Anjel Chakma, an MBA student from Tripura, died after being allegedly attacked by a group of men in Dehradun. Anjel and his younger brother Michael were reportedly subjected to racial slurs, including being called ‘Chinki’, ‘Chinese’ and ‘Momo’, before the confrontation turned violent.
In July, 2014, 29-year-old Akha Salouni from Manipur was allegedly beaten to death by five youths in Delhi following a road rage incident. Following his death, the deceased’s family and members of the Northeastern community held a candlelight vigil at Jantar Mantar, which also saw the participation of the mother of Nido Tania.
In May 2013, 22-year-old Manipuri girl Reingamphi Awungshi was found dead in her home in Delhi under suspicious circumstances. Delhi police initially said she died by suicide, stating that severe injuries on her face and body were caused by rodents. However, her family and rights groups demanded a deeper investigation, claiming that she was sexually assaulted and murdered, pointing to local stalking complaints and police bias against Northeasterners. After 11 years, in March 2024, the Supreme Court ordered a CBI probe into Awungshi’s case. Two years on, no headway into the investigation has been publicly reported.
More recently, in February 2026, three women from Arunachal Pradesh alleged that their neighbours in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar subjected them to racial and sexist abuse during a dispute over repair work at their rented home. The women said they were called ‘dhandhewali’ and ‘momo’ and that ‘Northeastern people are shit’. In a viral video, the accused woman can be heard asking the Northeastern women, “Rs 500 mei massage parlour mei kaam karne waali dhandhewali (You work at massage parlours as sex workers for Rs 500). Are you sitting here to do business? Have you opened a massage parlour at home?” Delhi police registered an FIR and later arrested the neighbours, a couple, invoking provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
While speaking to Alt News, Maivio admitted that lack of awareness about the Northeast was the primary cause behind cases of racial discrimination. “We had recommended inclusion of the history and culture of the Northeast in school curricula and textbooks throughout the country. In our last meeting, we called the NCERT to find out what had been done so far. They said that they have included some content in Classes 9 and 10 in certain cities and that they would share it with us, which they are trying to implement countrywide. They are also preparing a documentary to be released countrywide, building awareness on the Northeast. But these have largely been verbal assurances, and we will have to see what has actually been included and whether it is sufficient,” he added.

Baljinder Singh, a resident of Sujanpur in Punjab’s Pathankot district, has reportedly been sentenced to death by a court in Saudi Arabia in connection with a drug trafficking case. Singh has reportedly been imprisoned in Saudi Arabia for around three years. His family members have appealed to both the Punjab government and the central government to intervene and provide assistance. They have sought help to understand the legal proceedings and explore possible avenues for relief. The case has drawn attention in Punjab, with the family seeking government support to pursue available legal and diplomatic options to help Singh (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows actor Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and reprimanding the country over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows actor Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and reprimanding the country over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence.
Fact: The video has been digitally altered to depict Shah Rukh Khan criticising Saudi Arabia and speaking about Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. The original footage is from a 2015 event at the University of Edinburgh, where Khan spoke about life lessons. AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya, indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports confirming that actor Shah Rukh Khan criticised or reprimanded Saudi Arabia over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence. Had such a statement been made, it would likely have received significant media coverage; however, no such reports were found.
We also reviewed Shah Rukh Khan’s official social media handles (here, here, and here). Still, we found no reference to the case or any statement regarding Baljinder Singh’s death sentence that could substantiate the claim.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to an extended version of the same video uploaded on the University of Edinburgh’s YouTube channel on 16 October 2015. The background in the original video matches that seen in the viral clip, confirming that both videos are from the same event. In the video, Shah Rukh Khan speaks about various life lessons. At the event, the University of Edinburgh awarded him an honorary doctorate, and he spoke about lessons he learned through his film roles. Combining humour with introspection, Khan discussed the importance of embracing one’s unique identity, facing fears, and maintaining self-confidence in the face of challenges. He also shared anecdotes from his film career and explained how different characters had helped him view life from new perspectives. However, he made no mention of Baljinder Singh or his death sentence in the video.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. This suggests that the viral video has been digitally altered, with the original footage paired with fabricated audio to falsely depict actor Shah Rukh Khan making statements he never made.
To sum up, this viral video of Shah Rukh Khan reprimanding Saudi Arabia over Baljinder Singh’s death sentence is AI-manipulated.

Yemen’s civil war returns and overwhelms hospitals with 'a very dangerous situation'
Hospitals in Yemen are struggling as civil war returns to the Arab world's poorest nation
ADEN, Yemen -- Tarek al-Salami, aged 7, sat in a diaper, looking frail. Normally, the malnutrition and diarrhea that weakened his tiny frame would have been treated within a few days, but nothing is normal in Yemen anymore.
Tarek's father carried him on foot from the southwestern city of Mokha as Iran-backed rebels swept in this month, bringing a return to civil war. The boy reached a hospital two days later in the government-held city of Aden, 270 kilometers (170 miles) away but it said it had no beds. Like others, it was overwhelmed by the wounded. They finally found a therapeutic feeding center.
The boy arrived in “acute crisis” after the delay in care, according to the center's director, Dr. Arwa Atef, and he only began walking again on Wednesday, over a week later.
“I swear to God, when I look at him, my heart breaks,” said his father, Mohammed al-Salami. “He looks almost lifeless.”
This is how the already fragile health system in the Arab world’s poorest nation is collapsing, caught in a new front of the Iran war. The Associated Press spoke with patients, medical workers and aid groups in Yemen and outside as medicines run short and some workers flee. A few facilities have been overtaken by the fighting.
Some health centers are turning pregnant women and others in need away to focus on trauma patients. Vulnerable children are filling incubators and sharing beds. Millions of people are affected by the fighting backed by two of the Middle East’s biggest powers as Iran-backed Houthis advance against government forces supported by Saudi Arabia. Over 130,000 have fled their homes.
The feeding center where Tarek and other children are recovering is struggling to cope with a rise in patients in a country where many already were hungry, Atef said.
“We can’t keep up with the situation,” she said.
Most hospitals and primary health centers affected by the escalation in fighting closed for the first 48 hours before resuming services, the United Nations said. But some are now harder to reach. The Houthis have seized the Red Sea coast, including key ports for aid.
Less than 10% of the affected health centers are fully equipped with the trauma services that wounded people need, the World Health Organization has said. With resources thin, a painful triage is underway.
Fewer facilities are handling the pregnancy-related emergencies that were killing three Yemeni women every day even before the escalation, said Francesco Galtieri with the United Nations Population Fund. That's one of the highest rates in the Arab world.
"Around 2,000 pregnant women are on the move,” with over 200 expected to deliver in the next week or so, he said.
Maternity wards have been converted into emergency rooms in some hospitals close to the fighting, said Hashem Osseiran, an International Committee of the Red Cross spokesperson, adding that many lack enough anesthesia drugs, oxygen supplies and sterile surgical gloves.
At a hospital treating mothers and children in the government-held city of Marib, Dr. Ahmed Modhesh said they are seeing more emergency maternity cases as other city hospitals focus on the wounded.
But his facility, Martyr Mohamed Hayel hospital, lacks intensive care specialists and doesn’t have enough generators to keep all departments running if the power goes out.
A midwife said the number of childbirths the hospital is handling has basically doubled to about 80. One woman with an ectopic pregnancy arrived bleeding heavily, yet the under-resourced staff were still able to perform an emergency procedure to save her life, the midwife said. She spoke on condition of anonymity because she wasn’t authorized to speak with the media.
Even before the escalation, hospitals in Yemen relied on limited government support and citizen donations. Some were not able to fully pay staff.
Now, “we are in a very dangerous situation,” said Fahd al-Nazari, manager of the health office in Taiz province, which has received most of the newly displaced. “Within a day or two, or a week at most, we might have to close down (some facilities). In fact, some hospitals are already closed.”
Three of the province’s 17 hospitals are no longer under government control. Hospitals across Taiz had received around 635 casualties, including 112 bodies, as of Thursday after the Houthis captured Mokha, al-Nazari said. They included civilians and combatants.
“We’re exhausted receiving wounded people under these circumstances,” al-Nazari said.
Medical supplies and fuel are running short after key supply routes between Mokha and Taiz were largely cut off, forcing convoys onto mountainous roads unsuitable for large trucks. Even before the escalation, public hospitals in the province had just one MRI machine available.
At the Yemeni-Swedish Maternity and Children's Hospital in Taiz, incubators were full and two or three children were sharing beds in the emergency room, general manager Sami al-Sharabi said.
“I’m scared that the conflict would reach the hospital,” he said. “Any explosive that could hit us would destroy the hospital, as some parts of the building are already weak.”
Even hospitals in Aden, where Yemen’s government is based, struggle to cope. Doctors Without Borders said more than 60 wounded people had been admitted to Al-Gamhouria hospital in a week. Many needed urgent surgery or blood transfusions.
At a private hospital treating rebels in the Houthi-held city of Sanaa, two medical officials last week said it was overwhelmed with hundreds of wounded. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns.
It was not clear how many Houthi fighters have been killed or wounded overall. Few aid agencies operate in rebel-controlled areas, as the group has detained and harassed dozens of humanitarian workers. Experts say the Houthis have struggled to pay salaries to civil servants, including public sector doctors and diverted most tax revenues to their military wing.
The ICRC, one of the few global agencies still able to operate in Sanaa, last week said it delivered 22 tons of badly needed medical supplies to support “overwhelmed” hospitals.
There is also little information about casualties among government forces, though one government-allied group has said over 1,500 of its fighters were wounded.
Some medical workers have fled the conflict, making it harder to find care.
In Mokha, Doctors Without Borders said its small team was still working “despite the severe shortage of health professionals.” The charity’s deputy coordinator of operations in Yemen, Emmanuel Massart, said three other hospitals there had closed for days before resuming services.
The need for hospital funding and resources in Yemen remains urgent, Massart said, speaking to the AP from Brussels, even as he acknowledged that resupplying remains a major challenge because of closed roads.
“We should not forget about Yemen," he said. It “remains one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world.”
___
Khaled reported from Cairo and Anna from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Abdulnasser Alseddik in Aden and Toqa Ezzidin in Cairo contributed to this report.

Razer's Kiyo V2 Pro webcam can capture 4K video at 60 fps
There are some new AI features, too.
To keep up with new rivals' smaller dedicated video cameras and increasingly capable smartphones, Razer is introducing an upgraded 'pro' version of its Kiyo V2 webcam, with a powerful new imaging sensor, increased dynamic range and some convenient AI tools and features.
The $300 Kiyo V2 Pro's biggest upgrade is 60 fps capture, meaning less blur for your work calls, livestreams and everything else. However, Razer has paired it with a lens that can go as low as f/1.9 aperture, which should improve low-light performance and offer a stronger bokeh blur effect.
AI features include auto-framing, which you might have already seen on recent iPhones' FaceTime calls, with integrated intelligent pan, tilt and zoom to keep users in frame, but... tastefully. Like recent Razer mics, the company is introducing one-click output enhancement, which will automatically handle exposure, white balance and noise depending on your environment.
Razer also says the new cam can capture ultra-high dynamic range to help pull out more detail regardless of your lighting setup. Interestingly, the company chose to reduce the field of view from 93 degrees on the V2 to 86 degrees to maintain image quality at 4K and reduce any fisheye lens effects at the outer edges of the frame.
The Kiyo V2 Pro also supports Razer Synapse for software-based controls to fine-tune ISO, shutter speed and more. Regardless of your PC setup, the Pro webcam includes both a clamp for monitor and laptop edges and a universal mount for separate tripod use. My favorite touch is the slick, integrated privacy shutter that looks like a camera shutter mechanism.

Zidane waited for France - now can he harness their star power?
- Published
France will have a new face on the touchline for the first time in 14 years when they face Turkey on Friday.
Zinedine Zidane replaced Didier Deschamps after France's fourth-place finish at the World Cup, but his appointment had been an open secret long before Les Bleus' third-place play-off loss to England.
Talks between the former Real Madrid manager and the French football authorities kicked off as early as February 2025 - after Zidane's former team-mate Deschamps announced a few weeks earlier he would step down following the 2026 World Cup.
When he was unveiled in Paris, Zidane was keen to highlight the time he had spent waiting on the sidelines and preparing for the job.
"I had several offers in the last four or five years, but I turned them all down," an emotional Zidane said. "The national team is the only thing I wanted."
While his enthusiasm at taking the job was the overarching theme of his first news conference in the French capital, the midfield legend offered few clues to France fans as to how he would approach the role.
Even a question on Kylian Mbappe's captaincy was bypassed: "The most important thing for him now is to rest, we'll have the chance to speak in September."
Mbappe, speaking to Spanish newspaper AS, has since said having the former Real Madrid star as his national team coach was "like a film".
When asked about his preferred style of play, Zidane opted against going into tactical detail.
"I can't explain to you in just a couple of words how we're going win. I have to arrive, meet with the players, and explain my plans to them. After that, it'll be up to me to keep this team winning."
However, Zidane confirmed his intention "to do things differently" and he has called up five uncapped players for this international break.
He went on to signal that there would be a degree of "continuation" from the work of his predecessor, which he made sure to praise.
"I'm going to try do what I know how to, but it won't be a complete break either."
So what will Zidane bring to the France dugout?
Zidane the player
Zidane, who retired in 2006, was one of the most exciting attacking midfielders of his generation.
He won league titles and European trophies with Juventus and Real Madrid, while he helped France to victory at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000.
Zidane started his career at Cannes and then moved to Bordeuax.
He almost joined Premier League side Blackburn Rovers in 1995, but the move broke down with Rovers owner Jack Walker reportedly asking manager Kenny Dalglish: "Why do you want to sign Zidane when we have Tim Sherwood?"
Instead Zidane moved to Juventus, winning six trophies, before he was signed by Real Madrid for a then record £45.8m.
For France he was the hero of the home 1998 World Cup, scoring twice in the final, a 3-0 win over Brazil and was named the best player at Euro 2000.
He retired after the 2006 World Cup, a campaign full of highs, leading France to the final, and one big low, when his playing career ended after he was sent off in the showpiece match for headbutting Italy defender Marco Materazzi.
Zidane the manager
Zidane and Deschamps - two 1998 World Cup winners - do share a few similar traits in their management, not least in their pragmatism, as well as the laissez-faire approach to attacking phases which Deschamps embraced in the recent World Cup.
Given the attacking talent at his disposal, it stands to reason that Zidane would carry on in that vein.
"I was a number 10 as a player," he said, hinting he would retain the role Michael Olise thrived in for much of the summer.
"What motivates me is the game, it's scoring goals," he added.
With the team netting 20 times in North America, Deschamps has arguably laid the foundations for his successor's attacking set-up.
Zidane is finding Les Bleus in immeasurably better shape than his predecessor did at the start of his own tenure, at which point the wounds of the 2010 World Cup fiasco were still fresh.
The appointment does come with a degree of uncertainty, though.
Given that Zidane has spent five years out of management, and the Real Madrid job is the only other senior coaching role of his career, it might seem like a gamble.
The 54-year-old himself has acknowledged leading a national team would be an entirely new proposition: "It's new to me, but I'm not scared. This is what I wanted."
Predictably, the reaction among players and fans to Zidane's arrival has been almost unanimously positive. He was met with a crowd of supporters carrying flares and banners as he left the French Football Federation's headquarters after his unveiling.
"Welcome home," Mbappe wrote on Instagram later in the day.
'A great day for French football'
"It's a great day for French football," his former France and Bordeaux team-mate Bixente Lizarazu told France Info later that day.
"He is more than fit to manage Les Bleus, given what he did at Real Madrid with great players and big egos."
The respect that the former Ballon d'Or winner commands in a dressing room is one of his key strengths.
Even more so than Deschamps, a France legend in his own right, Zidane is a figure who can rival - perhaps even overshadow - his own players in terms of star power.
In this sense, he may be the ideal manager to get the most out of an attack made up of Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele, Desire Doue and Olise.
This international break - lasting four Nations League fixtures over three weeks - will offer the France players a crash-course to the new management style.
After facing Turkey, they have two games against Belgium and one against Italy in Paris.
Given his iconic status within French football and on the wider national stage, Zidane will invariably enjoy an unprecedented degree of goodwill regardless of his initial results.
Whether he uses that leeway to experiment tactically and bring in new faces remains to be seen.
His homecoming at the Stade de France on Friday, 2 October, against the Azzurri no less, is an ideal fixture to begin the new era.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

Police say gunman shouted antisemitic threat before opening fire outside Ontario synagogue
Police say a former Canadian soldier who opened fire on a police officer outside an Ontario synagogue during Yom Kippur shouted “you’re going to die for the Jews” moments before shooting
TORONTO -- A former Canadian soldier who opened fire on a police officer outside an Ontario synagogue during Yom Kippur shouted “you’re going to die for the Jews” moments before shooting, police said Thursday, declaring the attack was motivated by hate.
Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd disclosed the alleged words of 29-year-old Sean Ward as police for the first time publicly identified a motive for Sunday’s attack outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue.
“Make no mistake, this was a targeted attack against the Jewish community,” Rodd said. “The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty.”
Police at a news conference Thursday played audio that they said captured Ward shouting the antisemitic threat before opening fire on Const. Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue.
Rodd said Smith was shot before even getting out of his vehicle but still confronted the attacker, remaining engaged in the gunfight for nearly three minutes despite suffering multiple gunshot wounds to the head and body. A second officer, Const. Michael McCurdy, arrived and joined the exchange of fire.
Rodd said the two officers were the only thing that prevented Ward from entering the synagogue and carrying out what police described as a potential mass killing. He said Ward had multiple weapons, a significant amount of ammunition and gasoline available to him.
About two dozen people were inside the synagogue marking the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar. None was injured.
Ward was critically wounded and died the following day. Smith, a 13-year veteran of the Belleville Police Service, faces multiple surgeries and a lengthy recovery from gunshot wounds, fractures and shrapnel injuries, Rodd said.
The Department of National Defense has said Ward served as an infantry soldier with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry before leaving the Canadian Armed Forces in 2022 at the rank of corporal. He did not deploy during his service.
Documents obtained by The Canadian Press indicate Ward had joined a lawsuit challenging the military’s COVID-19 vaccination mandate, claiming financial losses after he refused vaccination on religious grounds and was released from service.
Investigators are also assessing materials found in Ward’s vehicle, including extra gasoline, to determine how much damage he may have intended to cause, Rodd said.
The province’s police watchdog previously said as many as 30 shots were fired and nearby vehicles and homes were struck.
Synagogue president Norman Weddum said Thursday he believed Ward had the means to kill those inside and possibly destroy the synagogue. He said the congregation plans to reopen soon.
The attack comes amid heightened concern about antisemitism in Canada.
Ontario Solicitor General Michael Kerzner, the province’s public safety minister, said the attack struck him personally as a Jewish Canadian. He praised the community’s response, noting that leaders from a nearby mosque brought flowers to the Sons of Jacob Synagogue to express sorrow and solidarity.
“We will never normalize antisemitism or hate of any kind,” Kerzner said.

Terming it a "broad daylight dacoity" against patients, the Supreme Court on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) expressed shock over the overpricing of essential cancermedicines, noting that one drug carried an MRP of ₹27,000 despite being supplied to retailers for ₹2,700.
"It is very surprising that the authorities who are supposed to take action on this are silent," a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said.
The observations came when the Supreme Court was hearing two petitions that raised drug-related issues, including that of ensuring strict price control over medicines.
The court termed it "absolutely shocking" that the printed MRP of an essential cancer drug was ₹27,000 when the price to retailer (PTR) was ₹2,700.
"The MRP is 10 times the rate at which it is provided to the retailers. If this is not extortion, then what it is? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment," the Bench said.
"This is absolute rampage and carnage. This is broad daylight dacoity with patients," it said.
The Bench questioned how the patients could be cheated like this.
One of the petitioners told the Bench that his plea also raised the issue concerning the prescription of generic medicines by registered medical practitioners. He said fixing MRP of medicines was of critical importance.
Additional Solicitor General K.M. Nataraj, appearing for the Centre in one of the pleas, said the government was not treating it as an adversarial litigation.
The Bench observed that price fixation was a major issue.
It posted the matter for further hearing on September 29, 2026.
Price control
One of the petitions sought a direction to authorities to make drug formulations more cost-effective by preventing alleged unethical overpricing of essential medicines by pharma companies and retailers.
It also sought directions to ensure strict price control under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013, to prevent violations of the price-fixing mechanism in the drug supply chain and disproportionate profit-making by retailers through unfair trade practices.
The other plea has sought disciplinary action against medical practitioners for not prescribing generic medicines to patients.

WASHINGTON — A key Senate committee on Thursday approved the nomination of top federal health official Chris Klomp to be deputy secretary of health and human services, clearing the way for him to be confirmed by the full Senate.
Klomp is currently senior adviser to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He was advanced by the Senate Finance committee in an 15-12 vote. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) joined all Republicans in supporting Klomp.
He will now go to the full Senate for a final vote.
The committee voted 14-13 to advance Ge Bai’s nomination to be HHS assistant secretary for planning and evaluation.
Klomp spent two days last week testifying before Finance and the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committees, where lawmakers highlighted the power Klomp wields at HHS and questioned how he might use that power. Klomp has already helped broker drug pricing deals with pharmaceutical companies, aided in high-profile hires, and acted as a liaison between HHS and the White House.
During his confirmation hearings, Democrats joined by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who chairs the health committee, repeatedly called on Klomp to push back on his boss, Kennedy, and even President Trump, if he continued to undermine vaccine policy. Cassidy, in particular, pressed Klomp to address the CDC’s refusal to report certain measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania.
“People are dying. The American people should know that,” he said. Cassidy had previously threatened to withhold health care nominations if HHS continued its aggressive vaccine overhaul, but Klomp’s nomination was squarely in the hands of the Finance committee, which Cassidy sits on but does not chair.
Klomp, in his statements to the committees last week, acknowledged the outsized role he would play in influencing HHS.
“Part of my responsibility is to enable the smooth operations of the department. I’m responsible for personnel, among other things,” Klomp told Finance last week. “My job is to make sure that we have everything.”
Klomp joined the Trump administration to oversee the Medicare program, before taking on additional duties at HHS. He also advised the first Trump administration on health care matters. Klomp is a health care entrepreneur, and was previously the CEO of health IT company Collective Medical.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

WASHINGTON — Congress is considering the first major overhaul of how Medicare pays doctors in more than a decade, and both Democrats and Republicans appear to agree on the outlines of an approach.
The main policy under consideration would link Medicare’s doctor pay rates to a medical inflation measure, giving doctors guaranteed pay boosts, as hospitals and other parts of the health care system have long received.
In doing so, Congress would be retreating from the notion that Medicare can control how many services physicians provide on a national basis, an idea that has undergirded Medicare’s doctor payments for decades. And it would reduce the government’s push to get clinicians to engage in value-based care, where they get paid more to keep patients healthy.

Indonesia reflags a former Italian warship as its first aircraft carrier
Indonesia’s navy has commissioned its first aircraft carrier after acquiring the former Italian vessel to strengthen its maritime defenses and disaster response
JAKARTA, Indonesia -- Indonesia's navy commissioned its first aircraft carrier Thursday after acquiring the former Italian vessel to strengthen its maritime defenses and disaster response.
The Italian flag on the former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi was replaced with the Indonesian flag on the carrier renamed the KRI Sriwijaya-100 as part of its official transfer at the ceremony held at Tanjung Priok seaport in North Jakarta.
"The ship, which previously served in the Italian Navy, now bears the name KRI Sriwijaya-100, flying the red-and-white flag as a symbol of sovereignty and service to Indonesia,” navy spokesperson Tunggul, who uses one name, said in a statement.
The carrier, which Italy retired in 2024, arrived at the Indonesian seaport last week after a 25-day journey passing through the Suez Canal, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
It has the capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters. Unlike major naval powers, Indonesia will use the vessel as a mobile command and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across the archipelago.
President Prabowo Subianto earlier said the ship would help fight forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of Southeast Asia with hazardous haze.
Italy agreed in March to give the carrier to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defense engagement with the Southeast Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship.
Indonesia is the second country in Southeast Asia with an aircraft carrier. Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain.

SC orders safeguards against Pocso Act misuse in marital disputes
Supreme Court directs police and courts to vet Pocso complaints in matrimonial disputes and seek a child psychiatrist’s assessment before arrest when evidence is not “palpable”
The Supreme Court on Thursday directed police and courts to carefully vet Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (Pocso) Act complaints against husbands or their family members in matrimonial disputes, and ordered that a child psychiatrist interact with the victim before arrest in cases where there is no “palpable” material against the accused.
The court felt the need to introduce this safeguard after it came across a case from Bengaluru where a mother filed a case under the Pocso Act against her husband after she lost a bitter and prolonged custody battle.
A bench of justices JB Pardiwala and KV Viswanathan said, “We are observing an alarming trend that is on the rise where one parent misuses the legal provisions to gain strategic legal advantage.”
Besides the incalculable harm caused to the child victim, the court said, “The only objective is to tie up the accused spouse and their family members in knots with the foisted criminal case and ensure that they are kept busy with the court process for a considerable period.”
This serves two ends - the accused suffers prolonged incarceration and such an accusation adversely affects guardianship or custody proceedings, the court said as it went on to quash the criminal proceedings under Pocso registered in 2024 against the husband. To arrive at this conclusion, the court ordered the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to conduct an enquiry into the victim child’s allegations. An expert team of child psychologists interacted with the victim and what came out was an “eye opener” for the court as the allegations were found to be false and the evidence non-supportive of the charges levelled by the child’s mother.
Laying down the safeguards for all cases investigated by police or where summons are yet to be issued by courts on private complaints, the bench directed the investigating officer or the Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU) to engage the services of an expert in child and adolescent psychiatry or clinical psychology from the District Child Protection Unit (DCPU) or the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) to interact with the victim.
The court said that such a measure shall be resorted to in cases where there is no “palpable” material against the accused and the police is in a dilemma if there is “reason to believe” to arrest the husband or his family members under Pocso offences.
Further, the court said, “Safeguards would apply only when an offence under the Pocso Act is alleged to have been committed by a parent, or any other family member who is living under the same roof as the child victim and a matrimonial dispute of some form, exists between the parents of the child victim, indicating the possibility of a strained relationship.”
Upon interaction with the victim, a report shall be filed by the experts with the police or SJPU, which will then consider how to proceed with the matter, the court said.
Under Pocso, the court noted that a complainant can approach the Special Pocso court under Section 33 of the Act. Directing the Special Court to apply its judicial mind to the contents of the complaint, the bench said, “The court has to prima facie be satisfied that there are sufficient grounds to look further into the allegations. However, in exceptional cases, where the material is palpable, the Special Court may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, dispense with the involvement of the services of an expert in child and adolescent psychiatry/psychology.”
The bench clarified that its directions will apply to police complaints where investigation is in progress or in cases under Section 33 of the Pocso Act where the Special Court is yet to issue summons (as on the date of judgment), indicating clearly that the judgment will not disturb pending trials or decided cases.
Further, the court clarified that the present directions will not disturb the procedure under Pocso Rules, which require assessment by the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) on whether the child needs to be taken out of the custody of the father or shared household.
It also clarified that the report by the child experts will not bind the police in arriving at any decision and will not be the sole basis for filing the chargesheet or closure report, as the case may be.
Justice Viswanathan, writing for the bench, said, “What is alarming is that this tendency of making false accusations is on the rise. Instances are not infrequent where gullible parties are misguided by their advisors, including in some cases by recalcitrant legal professionals, who in their pursuit of the motto of ‘win at any cost’, end up fuelling the fire.”
Terming it as a “growing menace”, the court said it has been seen in some cases that such provisions are invoked as a “pressure tactic” or used simply to settle scores or seek revenge.
In the case before the court, the child was born in 2015 and after the marriage between the spouses was dissolved in 2023, the father initiated a case for the child’s custody in which he was successful in June 2023. In March 2024, the child’s mother filed the Pocso case naming the husband. In April this year, the court handed over the probe to CBI which, along with two experts from NIMHANS Bengaluru, concluded, “The testimony of the victim does not appear reliable or trustworthy.”
Based on their report, the court quashed the criminal case. Before handing over the physical custody of the child to the father, the court sent the matter back to the Family Court to smoothly ensure the process of re-integration in the best interest of the child.

Bungie shares more detail about Marathon's Symbiosis update and 2027 plans
Another big overhaul to the game is now due in March.
Bungie is having a busy week. After the game studio shared its broad strategy for keeping players happy with its two main franchises, the team has gone into a little more detail about the next phase for its latest shooter, Marathon. Following on the previously announced Nightfall refresh in October, Bungie offered more insight on the new game modes coming in December and revealed that another big update is slated for March.
The team said that December's Symbiosis update will add a team deathmatch mode as well as a permanently available PvE mode. Details are still being finalized for the latter, but the goal of the PvE mode will allow people to experiment with their builds and fine-tune their skills without being attacked by other players. Bungie will also overhaul the Perimeter zone, which is the first one players see, to give it a more unique visual identity and new gameplay encounters, including a boss dubbed the Tick Queen. For the experienced players, a new shell archetype is coming. The Bishop is being billed as a "high-performance robot samurai," which certainly sounds fun. For the less experienced players, Marathon will add a social space with a firing range to help make the onboarding smoother.
Looking ahead to 2027, the March update hasn't been given a name yet, but Bungie says it will be "meaningfully larger than Symbiosis." The planned additions for that patch include "an interconnected system of permanent PvE, PvP, and PvEvP experiences," more onboarding improvements, a new zone and new alien enemies. The game will also add deeper progression to the shell system and "more focused questlines and narrative." That amounts to a pretty extensive set of changes, which Bungie says will lay a foundation for Marathon to continue growing over the course of 2027. It's a lot of big promises for a game that has already been facing a lot of scrutiny from the jump.

సౌదీ అరేబియా రాజధాని రియాద్లోని విమానాశ్రయంపై వైమానిక దాడి జరగడంతో భారీగా మంటలు, దట్టమైన నల్లటి పొగ వ్యాపించాయంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సౌదీ అరేబియాలోని రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై జరిగిన వైమానిక దాడికి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో రియాద్కు చెందినది కాదు. ఇది రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జూన్ 2026లో డ్రోన్ దాడి వల్ల జరిగిన అగ్నిప్రమాదానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై హౌతీలు దాడి చేసినట్లు వార్తలు వస్తున్నప్పటికీ, వైరల్ వీడియో దానికి సంబంధించినది కాదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇవే దృశ్యాలను చూపుతున్న వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 18 జూన్ 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోకు చెందినది. మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్పై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడి కారణంగా వ్యాపించిన మంటలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతోంది.
వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 18 జూన్ 2026న మాస్కోపై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడిలో సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో మంటలు, పొగ వ్యాపించాయి. వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న ప్రదేశాన్ని గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పరిశీలించగా, అది మాస్కోలో ఉన్నట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
అయితే, 19 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న రియాద్లోని కింగ్ ఖలీద్ అంతర్జాతీయ విమానాశ్రయంలోని ఇంధన డిపోపై తాము దాడి చేసినట్లు హౌతీలు పేర్కొన్నారంటూ పలు అంతర్జాతీయ వార్తా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) వెల్లడించాయి.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జరిగిన ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది.

Jammu and Kashmir Bank is set to issue a recruitment notification for assistant and officer-level positions within the next few days, Managing Director and CEO Amitava Chatterjee said on Tuesday.
Speaking during the bank’s 88th Annual General Meeting (AGM) at the Sher-i-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC) here, Chatterjee said the bank had finalised negotiations with the agency that would conduct the recruitment examinations for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
“After 2021, the bank is going for recruitment of both assistants as well as officers. The agreement for conducting the examinations for Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh is being finalised, and the bank will come out with a notification in a few days,” Chatterjee said.
He said the recruitment would be carried out in accordance with the bank’s operational requirements and would also take into account the need for employees with proficiency in local languages.
“As far as the bank is concerned, we will do what we have done in the past. There is a requirement for people with local language proficiency, though the numbers will be limited,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank’s presence across 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir had created a requirement for personnel familiar with local languages.
“The bank is present in 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir, and we need people with local language proficiency to serve customers there. So, the bank may decide in future to hire a few employees to support our existing staff strength,” he said.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, which was chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.
The AGM was held under the theme “Trust, Tradition and Transformation”. Addressing shareholders, Krishnan said the bank’s future growth would have to be aligned with its wider economic and social contribution to the region.
“Our past gives us identity. Our present gives us strength. Our future gives us responsibility. Trust is our inheritance. Tradition is our anchor. Transformation is our obligation,” he said.
He also highlighted the bank’s role in supporting entrepreneurship and said its participation in Mission YUVA was significant in creating economic opportunities for a new generation of entrepreneurs.
On digital transformation, Krishnan said technology should ultimately serve the objective of improving customer experience and making banking “simpler, safer and more accessible”.
Chatterjee, meanwhile, said the bank had maintained its growth trajectory despite challenging circumstances and had recorded its fourth consecutive year of record profitability.
“Notwithstanding the challenging circumstances, your Bank maintained its growth trajectory and delivered a fourth consecutive year of record profitability. Net profit reached an all-time high of Rs 2,363 crore, registering year-on-year growth of 13.5%. The growth momentum has continued into the current financial year. By June 2026, the Bank crossed the historic milestone of Rs 3 trillion in total business,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank’s performance reflected improvements across profitability, asset quality, efficiency and capital strength.
“These outcomes demonstrate that our progress is broad-based, with profitability, asset quality, efficiency and capital strength advancing together. For our investors, this represents a resilient and increasingly diversified franchise, supported by strong fundamentals and a clear strategy for long-term value creation. As we grow, our focus will remain on the quality and sustainability of earnings rather than growth in isolation,” he said.
On digital banking, he said investments in digital platforms, data analytics, cybersecurity and process automation were improving customer experience and operational efficiency.
“The rapid growth of up to 94% in digital transactions during FY 2025-26 demonstrates the increasing trust customers place in our digital ecosystem,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank would continue to invest in its workforce and technology while strengthening cybersecurity and customer experience.
“As we reflect with pride on a legacy spanning nearly nine decades, we remain conscious of the responsibility that accompanies it. Our aspiration is clear: to become the ‘Bank of Choice’. Towards this goal, we will continue to invest in our people and technology, reinforce cybersecurity, improve customer experience and institutionalise a culture of innovation and excellence,” he said.
During the question-and-answer session, shareholders raised queries on various aspects of the bank’s operations, including recruitment. Chatterjee responded to the questions.
DGM and Company Secretary Mohammad Shafi Mir also read out the Auditor’s Report, comments of the Comptroller and Auditor General and the Secretarial Audit Report. He informed shareholders that the e-voting results and Scrutinizer’s Report would be made available on the websites of the bank, its registrar and transfer agent, and the stock exchanges within two working days of the conclusion of the AGM.
The AGM concluded with shareholders appreciating the bank’s performance during the financial year 2025-26.

A delegation of the Kashmir Traders and Manufacturers Federation (KTMF), led by its president Mohammad Yaseen Khan, on Tuesday called on newly appointed Inspector General of Police, Kashmir Zone, Sujit Kumar Singh and discussed issues concerning the trade community across the Valley.
The delegation congratulated Singh on assuming charge as IGP Kashmir and expressed hope that his experience and leadership would further strengthen police-public coordination.
The meeting focused on traffic management, parking, policing, movement of commercial vehicles and timely resolution of traders’ grievances at the district level.
Representatives of various district trade bodies apprised the IGP of local issues affecting traders and business establishments and stressed the need for regular coordination between the police and the trading community.
The IGP gave a patient hearing to the delegation and, according to KTMF, issued on-the-spot directions on several issues. He also directed the concerned district SSPs to examine and address the grievances raised by traders from their respective areas.
KTMF senior member Javaid Ahmad Zargar, representing the Jamia Masjid and Downtown Srinagar area, raised the long-pending demand for a fire station near Jamia Masjid, citing the congestion in the area and the need for an effective emergency response mechanism.
Zargar also highlighted the shortage of adequate parking facilities in Downtown Srinagar, saying traffic and parking difficulties continue to affect traders, residents and visitors.
KTMF president Mohammad Yaseen Khan described the interaction as constructive and appreciated the IGP’s prompt response to the issues raised by the delegation.
He said traders were important stakeholders in maintaining a peaceful and orderly commercial environment and stressed that regular interaction between police and trade bodies could help resolve genuine issues before they escalate.
The delegation included Qazi Tauseef, Bashir Ahmad Rather, Javaid Ahmad Zargar, president Jamia Traders Federation; Ghulam Hassan Parra, president Traders Federation Ganderbal; Mohammad Usman Turray, senior vice president Traders Federation Shopian; Mohammad Iqbal Dhobi, acting president Traders Federation Kulgam; Rouf Ahmad Reshi, general secretary Traders Federation Pulwama; Nasir Bashir, president Traders Federation Pattan; and Asif Ahmad, president Traders Federation Tangmarg.
KTMF assured the police administration of continued cooperation in matters concerning public safety, traffic management, peace and a conducive environment for trade and commerce.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently
- Published
The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.
Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".
The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.
Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.
The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.
"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external.
"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."
His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.
Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."
"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.
Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.
This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".
Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".
For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".
British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.
They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.
After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.
The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.
The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.
Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.
Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.
Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.
The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.
Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.
