Sometimes you can win an argument just by repeating yourself over and over.
That’s a lesson from the tobacco industry’s battle with the Biden-era Food and Drug Administration over its proposed ban on menthol cigarettes.
After the FDA drafted language to outlaw the manufacture of the mint-flavored cigarettes in 2022, it asked for public comments — and was hit with an avalanche of 175,000 messages over three months.
Of those, 97% were form letters opposing the ban, according to a new study by researchers at Rutgers University that was published last month in JAMA Network Open. Nearly half of the letters had the same language as campaigns run by tobacco giants Altria Group Inc. or Reynolds American, researchers found. Most of the rest echoed industry talking points. Just 2% of the letters were unique.
The tactic of showering regulators with the same talking points is not new. The tobacco industry has done it since at least the 1980s, when it bombarded a federal agency with letters opposing airline smoking restrictions. Nor is it limited to cigarettes: When the Federal Communications Commission considered “net neutrality” rules in 2017, one college student filed more than 7.7 million comments.
Such campaigns usually have little effect on rulemaking because agencies typically consider the substance of comments rather than the volume, said Steven Balla, co-director of the Regulatory Studies Center at George Washington University. “You can imagine a case where there are a million ‘I hate this rule’ comments,” Balla said. “But the agency’s response will mostly be to the handful that are substantive.”
What’s novel about the menthol campaign is that the tactic seems to have worked.
After the public comment period closed in August 2022, the FDA issued a statement saying it would “need ample time to comprehensively review and analyze all of the comments.” The agency, which did not respond to requests for comment for this article, missed its deadline to issue the rule the following August and set a new deadline of March 2024.
By then, the FDA’s public health concerns about menthol cigarettes, which make up more than a third of all cigarettes sold in the U.S., had run head-on into efforts to get President Biden re-elected. He needed the support of Black Americans, a key market for menthol cigarettes.
In late 2023, a conservative organization bought television ads criticizing the proposal. Meanwhile, the White House scheduled dozens of meetings with various groups. Among them were law enforcement and civil rights organizations that had received money from the tobacco industry and opposed the ban over concerns it would lead to illicit sales and biased policing. (Researchers have not found any such outcome in Canada or the European Union after governments there banned menthols.)
The March 2024 deadline passed without action. That April, the Biden administration indefinitely postponed the ban, citing the vast public response — one that the Rutgers study concluded were nearly all form letters.
“This rule has garnered historic attention and the public comment period has yielded an immense amount of feedback,” said Xavier Becerra, secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services at the time. “It’s clear that there are still more conversations to have, and that will take significantly more time.”
Becerra, now a candidate for governor of California, did not respond to requests for comment sent to his campaign.
The proposed ban was officially scrapped the following year, after President Trump took office.
‘Genuine responses’
The Biden administration had proposed the ban in part because of menthol cigarettes’ disproportionate effect on the health of Black Americans.
The tobacco industry has cultivated the appeal of menthols in the Black community for decades. Starting in the 1960s, Brown & Williamson and rival tobacco companies used tactics like sponsoring jazz festivals, advertising in magazines like Ebony and distributing free samples to Black residents and even children. The industry also built ties with Black leaders by donating to civil rights groups and Black politicians.
Today, about 80% of Black smokers use menthols. Though Black smokers tend to start later in life and consume fewer cigarettes each day than their white counterparts, they fall ill and die at higher rates, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Between 1980 and 2018, menthols were responsible for 157,000 smoking-related deaths among Black Americans, according to research by the University of Michigan.
The proposed rule would have banned manufacturers from using the menthol compound, which cools and numbs the throat and airway, making cigarette smoke less harsh. Research has shown that menthols are more likely to addict young smokers and that a ban could avert 650,000 early deaths over four decades.
The letters opposing the ban largely didn’t address health concerns, the Rutgers researchers concluded.
Instead, those letters repeated industry arguments that smoking menthols is “a matter of adult choice” or that a ban would “increase crime, reduce tax revenues, and hurt small businesses.”
Tens of thousands of the letters were generated by public relations campaigns by Reynolds American, maker of Newport, and Altria, maker of Marlboro Menthol, researchers found. Newport and Marlboro Menthol are the two largest menthol brands in the U.S., according to Tobacco Insider, an industry advisory firm.
The study noted that because most letters didn’t have identifying information, “it is unclear whether these comments reflect genuine responses from citizens.”
Neither Altria nor Reynolds American responded to requests for comment about the form letters.
Phillip Gardiner, the co-chair of the African American Tobacco Control Leadership Council, placed part of the blame for the ban’s defeat on lobbying by civil rights leaders with ties to the tobacco industry. But the barrage of comments was also key, he said. Between the menthol cigarette rule and a related proposal to end the sale of flavored cigars, the FDA received nearly a quarter million form letters.
“They sent in 250,000 letters and our organization sent in one,” said Gardiner, whose group unsuccessfully sued the FDA in 2024 to try to force it to implement the menthol ban. “How do you counter that?”
In this case, the flood of public comments gave the Biden administration a way to back away from a policy it previously supported, said Eric Lindblom, a former senior official at the FDA’s Center for Tobacco Products in the Obama administration.
The idea that the White House or the FDA needed more time to consider form letters is “absolute nonsense,” he said. The law allows an agency to issue a single response to millions of identical comments, he said. And the FDA had conducted extensive reviews of menthols twice in the prior decade, concluding as early as 2013 they likely posed a bigger public health risk than other cigarettes.
“They always cite something like that: ‘We need more time to consider these arguments,’” said Lindblom, who is now at the O’Neill Institute for National and Global Health Law at Georgetown University. “Nobody’s going to come out and say, ‘We’re not going to issue this rule because it’s going to hurt us in the election.’”

The White House has blocked CNN and MS NOW from covering Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner with Donald Trump, according to the networks.
CNN and MS NOW both said their reporters were denied access to the White House to cover Xi’s arrival Thursday night, despite a federal judge temporarily reversing Trump’s ban on the outlets covering such events.
A reporter and producer with CNN were stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to enter the greeting ceremony between Trump and first lady Melania and Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, the network reported.
The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that they could cover Xi’s arrival but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.
MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López said she was also stopped by a press wrangler when trying to cover Xi’s arrival.
“I was told, ‘I’m sorry, I can’t let you in,’” Barrón-López told MS NOW host Symone Sanders Townsend, recalling the incident.
“The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” Barrón-López asked.

'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
- Published
Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

Why Trump gave Xi an ornate bald eagle statue at the state dinner
- Published
US President Donald Trump has presented Chinese President Xi Jinping with a sculpture of a bald eagle, a bird native to North America and his country's national symbol, during a lavish state dinner in Washington.
The gift, which was unveiled before VIP guests at the Thursday dinner, embodies "the free and soaring spirit of America", said Trump.
He said that he and First Lady Melania Trump participated in its design. The statue is part of a valuable - but sometimes tricky - aspect of international diplomacy: gift-giving.
Such gifts are a small but meaningful element of the larger aim of Xi and Trump's three-day summit – forging personal relationships between heads of two global superpowers.
"They're going to discuss all of these complicated issues," Daniel Kritenbrink, partner at The Asia Group says. "But at the end of the day, these are still two human beings.
"So that personal relationship means something," he says. "I think the gift exchange is one key part of that."
Kritenbrink, who spent over 30 years as a US diplomat, mostly in Asia, says personal relationships are of particular importance to Xi.
He believes the direct Trump-Xi bond is the glue that is holding together "the most complex and the most consequential relationship in the world".
He says Trump, too, values what Kritenbrink calls "leader-level diplomacy".
Gifts have had a unique presence in the Trump presidency.
The US president has received a luxury jumbo jet, an engraved gold bar, a diamond-and-jewel encrusted gold ring, and more.
Ole Jacob Sending from the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs says: "You think about the Trump presidency in that way, I think gift giving, certainly broadly defined, is very much part of how he operates."
On Thursday morning, Xi announced a gift of two Chinese pandas to a zoo in Atlanta - and a new student exchange programme, which will welcome 100,000 US students to study in China over five years.
"The giant panda have been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and the Americans," Xi said. "In a few days, two pandas - Ping Ping and Fu Shuang - will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people."
It's unclear if he gave any further presents. The BBC has contacted the White House.
Today, the practice of giving lavish gifts mostly exists in Gulf states and autocratic governments.
"Autocracies like China give much more expensive gifts," says Morten Skumsrud Anderson, who co-authored a study on diplomacy and gifts with Sending.
In the West, Anderson says, the tradition has been watered down by democratic guardrails and restrictions.
For example, the US Constitution has an emoluments clause that puts a dollar-value limit on gifts a president can receive from a foreign government.
Currently, the limit is $525 (£397). Anything higher and it becomes federal property, unless the president chooses to buy it back with his own money.
Also, when giving a gift beyond a certain amount, a US president would have to go through Congress, unless he was paying for it personally.
"There are a lot of rules and protocols involved," Sending says, "A lot of thought and process relating to what type of gift to to give, where should the gift exchange happen? How should it happen? When?
"All of this is highly scripted, and involves negotiation at lower levels that goes on for weeks and weeks in advance," Sending says.
Anderson adds: "This is not a last-minute purchase at the airport."
During Xi's state visit to the US in 2013, then-President Barack Obama gifted him an inscribed bench made of redwood, native to California where the two had met. They sat on it together afterwards, smiling for cameras.
It was a more shining example than in 2009, when then-British Prime Minister Gordon Brown gifted Obama an ornamental desk pen holder made from the timbers of a historic anti-slave ship; while Obama gave Brown a set of DVDs, which reportedly were not formatted for UK DVD players.
"That's one example of a kind of an embarrassing exchange," Sending says.
Fortunately, Brown and Obama were allied leaders and not deep rivals looking to resolve seemingly intractable differences.
"You don't want to mess up," Sending says, adding that the wrong gift could potentially derail any larger objectives.
In this case, there is potentially a lot at stake between Trump and Xi.
Their third face-to-face encounter since the start of Trump's second term, this summit is happening amid growing fears of an AI-led apocalypse as both countries race for dominance in the quickly growing industry.
It's also taking place in the wake of a bitter US-China trade war that has only been resolved by a temporary truce, extended on this trip.
So, do the military plane flyovers, cue the performances, fill the wine the glasses, Kritenbrink says. Exchange the gifts.
"It's protocol and it's optics and it's gift giving all as a means to an end, which is stable US-China relations," Kritenbrink says.
"I'll take a fragile truce over a white-hot trade war any day of the week."

Netherlands vs Germany. UEFA Nations League Group A2.

Netherlands 1-1 Germany: Jurgen Klopp's first game in charge ends all square after late Cody Gakpo equaliser
Report from the UEFA Nations League Group A2 match between the Netherlands and Germany in Amsterdam; Felix Nmecha put the visitors in front, but Cody Gakpo's 92nd-minute equaliser prevented a perfect start for Jurgen Klopp
Thursday 24 September 2026 22:50, UK
Cody Gakpo hit a stoppage-time volley to earn the Netherlands a 1-1 draw against Germany in their Nations League Group A2 opener on Thursday, denying Jurgen Klopp victory in his first match as Germany boss.
Former Liverpool manager Klopp took charge in July after their surprise early exit from the World Cup against Paraguay in the last 32 under Julian Nagelsmann.
His side appeared set to give him the perfect start after Felix Nmecha put Germany ahead, but Gakpo finished off a swift counter-attack in the closing stages to level the contest.
The result also gave Xavi Hernandez something to celebrate in his first game in charge of the Netherlands. He was appointed in August after Ronald Koeman stepped down following the Dutch side's elimination at the same stage of the World Cup.
Germany suffered an early blow when Jamal Musiala was ruled out before kick-off, after experiencing muscle pain - and they were given a scare when Virgil van Dijk headed in from a corner inside the first 15 minutes.
The goal was ruled out following a VAR review, however, with the Netherlands captain adjudged to have fouled Germany goalkeeper Marc-Andre ter Stegen.
Klopp's side were hit by another injury in the 30th minute when Arsenal's Kai Havertz was forced off, but they took the lead just two minutes later.
Philipp Treu's cutback found Nmecha, who made no mistake from close range to put Germany ahead.
The Netherlands had an injury concern of their own to contend with soon after, with Sunderland's Brian Brobbey taken off with what appeared to be a hamstring injury.
Germany almost doubled their advantage before half-time when Karim Adeyemi somehow failed to find the target from inside the six-yard box.
The Netherlands increased the pressure after the break and created a succession of chances, with Ter Stegen producing several important saves to preserve his side's lead.
Germany eventually succumbed in the closing stages, though, as Gakpo's late volley completed the Netherlands' comeback and secured an opening point.

Virtually every Android device comes with the Play Store preloaded, but there are other ways to get apps. F-Droid bills itself as a community-driven source for free and open source Android apps, but its official app store has gone 10 years without a major update. That’s finally changing: After a multiyear effort, the team has just announced F-Droid 2.0 is rolling out.
The new F-Droid client was redesigned from scratch in Kotlin Compose, which is the standard for modern Android apps. This makes the store much more responsive, and there’s optional support for Android’s Material theming. The interface has also been cleaned up considerably, making the most important functions easier to access and hiding some others in overflow menus.
While the new F-Droid looks nicer, the update was largely about making it easier to find and install apps. When F-Droid first appeared, there wasn’t much to see, but now it has thousands of open source apps. Unlike the Play Store, F-Droid doesn’t track your taps and installs to push ads and suggestions—it helps you find things and gets out of the way.
F-Droid now includes a huge number of categories, drilling down to specialized niches like firewalls, password managers, and VPNs. You can see all these groups in the search tab. There are also higher-level categories listed on the main Discover page. When searching for apps, F-Droid will now be able to return results based on app descriptions rather than just names.
When you find an app, F-Droid 2.0 will make the installation process easier. Google has long put up roadblocks for sideloaded apps, citing the security implications. This is also the rationale behind its upcoming developer verification system. For now at least, apps will be easier to install from F-Droid thanks to the use of Google’s pre-approval API. Instead of downloading an APK, opening it, and confirming the scary sideloading pop-up, you’ll just be able to verify that you want to install an app before the download. So you tap “Install” in F-Droid, and then tap “Install” again in a system pop-up. That’s one more click than the Play Store, but it’s still an improvement.

Italy decrees limits on non-Italian speakers and veils in school classrooms
Italy’s conservative government on Thursday has approved a school decree limiting classrooms to 30% of students with insufficient Italian-language skills and banning full-face Islamic veils, including burqas and niqabs
ROME -- Italy’s government passed a decree Thursday to place an upper limit on the number of students in each school classroom who have only limited Italian language skills and to ban face-covering Islamic veils in schools.
Premier Giorgia Meloni’s conservative government said the package is aimed at strengthening integration through language learning and has drawn support from right-wing allies.
Opponents including some educators, unions and opposition parties warn that new rules could force students to attend schools far from their neighborhoods, while critics accuse the government of turning immigration into a political issue.
With elections possible as early as next spring, analysts say the measures allow the premier to reassert her credentials on issues central to her conservative base, even though their impact is likely to be limited and significant questions remain about how they would be enforced.
Under the plan, a limit of 30% of foreign students lacking sufficient Italian proficiency would be allowed in any individual classroom.
The government decree goes into effect immediately but needs to be endorsed within 60 days in parliament, where Meloni's coalition commands a majority.
Meloni wrote on social media that they are “common-sense measures that do not divide but help foster genuine integration, avoiding ‘ghetto’ classrooms and giving all students equal opportunities.”
The decree comes as Meloni faces mounting pressure on her right flank from a new hard-line challenger, retired army Gen. Roberto Vannacci, who has been seeking to capitalize on voter concerns over immigration and national identity.
Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said local school authorities will coordinate student placements to avoid concentrations of non-Italian-speaking pupils, while schools unable to comply would be eligible for exemptions and additional language-support funding.
The minister says it would affect around 1,000 classrooms, about 0.3% of the total nationwide, and primarily those with high concentrations of recently arrived students with little or no Italian-language proficiency.
School principals questioned how the measure could work in areas with large migrant populations.
“From an educational perspective, the issue is well-founded and valid, but it’s difficult to turn it into a practical solution,” said Antonello Giannelli, president of the National Association of Principals.
"We have situations in which there is a district, a neighborhood that is mainly inhabited by immigrants and maybe there is only one school. So, since these are children, presumably young children in primary school, it is evident that they will hardly be able to go kilometers from their home,” Giannelli added.
Teachers’ unions criticized what they called a lack of both consultation and resources for the measure. They argued that the government’s 14-million-euro ($16 million) funding package would not be enough to hire specialized language teachers and cultural mediators needed to support students.
“Differences mean opportunities, and as with every opportunity one must be able to catch it. In most cases they (foreign students) allow the class to enrich their view of the world,” said Giovanni Castagno, a 52-year-old primary school teacher in central Rome.
According to Education Ministry data, students without Italian citizenship accounted for 11.2% of Italy’s school population in the 2022-23 academic year, while classes with more than 30% foreign students represented 7.6% of the total.
Foreign students who were born in the country would be exempt from the cap, along with those who attended Italian preschool or have already progressed through the school system.
The decree also bans burqas and niqabs in schools while continuing to allow hijabs.
The measure is narrower than restrictions adopted in some other European countries.
France banned full-face veils in public spaces in 2011, citing public security concerns, despite the small number of women affected. France also prohibits students from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, including Islamic headscarves, in public schools under its strict secularism doctrine.
Critics in Italy said the provision addresses a phenomenon rarely seen in Italian classrooms. Educators noted that while headscarves are common among some Muslim students, full-face veils are seldom seen in schools, and they argued that the provision risks becoming a symbolic political issue rather than an educational one.
Opposition parties also said the 30% threshold largely mirrors guidance already introduced by the Education Ministry in 2010, noting the government was repackaging an existing policy rather than investing in struggling schools. Center-left leader Elly Schlein accused the government of using schools to advance a political message on migration.
Valditara, the education minister, rejected those criticisms, saying the goal is integration through language acquisition and stronger educational support.
The decree provides additional teaching resources for schools where newly arrived foreign students exceed 20% of enrollment and additional language-learning funds for schools exceeding the 30% threshold.
It also would require some parents of foreign students to attend Italian-language courses when language barriers within families contribute to educational or behavioral difficulties.
Schools would refer eligible families to social services, which could enroll them in a tailored support program through adult education centers. Parents who fail to attend the courses could face fines ranging from 200 to 1,000 euros, although exemptions are included for those with certified age-related, medical or disability-related barriers to language learning.

SC reserves order on Centre plea against retrospective OBC creamy layer ruling
The Supreme Court reserved its order on the Centre’s plea seeking to defer its March 11 OBC creamy layer ruling by two years and apply it prospectively.
The Supreme Court on Thursday reserved its order on the Centre’s plea seeking prospective application of its March 11 judgment that held other backward classes (OBC) candidates cannot be excluded from reservation benefits solely on the basis of their parents’ salary income.
Stating that the judgment’s operation to all appointments and admissions made in the past will result in a “complete administrative chaos” the Centre urged the court to make the decision to apply prospectively and requested for a two-year period to work out equivalent posts similar to Group A and B officers in the government for identifying creamy layer among persons employed with public sector undertakings (PSU) and private employment.
A bench of justices PS Narasimha and R Mahadevan told the Centre that its judgment gave them six months time to implement the judgment. Yet, their application seeking modification came to be filed in the fag end of August as it questioned what the Centre did during the past few months.
The Centre led by solicitor general Tushar Mehta and additional solicitor general (ASG) Aishwarya Bhati said that the application does not question the judgment. “The Union government is only praying for a limited deferral of the operationalisation of the law laid down by this court for a period of two years so that the competing rights can be adjusted consistent with the administrative contingencies and an effective equivalence exercise is carried out.”
It further said, “The application of the present judgment to past and ongoing recruitments will gravely prejudice the competing rights of persons who were not even a party to the present litigation and will result in reopening of seniority, cadre allocation of appointees and candidates and result in complete administrative chaos.”
Further, Bhati pointed out that the Civil Service Examination recruitment rules for the past year and this year have already been issued and some candidates are citing this judgment to seek enhanced allocation opportunities based on the benefits under the March 11 judgment.
By virtue of this judgment getting implemented, she said that some candidates whose parents are earning even more than ₹1 crore annually would be benefitted and considered as OBC non creamy layer category
The court judgment came to be passed in a set of appeals filed by the Centre against orders passed by the Madras high court. In one such case, the high court permitted an OBC candidate to be treated as a non-creamy layer candidate which furthered his career prospects. He was earlier recommended for Indian Police Service by the UPSC but under OBC reservation, he became entitled for allocation under the Indian Foreign Service.
The top court approved the high court order and discarded the Centre’s objection that his father worked with a multinational and having a high income, he would come under creamy layer. Similarly, the court permitted another candidate to obtain benefit under the Civil Services after he was initially refused OBC reservation owing to his father’s PSU employment which fetched higher income. Both the candidates argued that their parents were excluded on income criteria while for government servants, creamy layer classification was based on their parents’ posts by which Group A or B, C or D officers stood excluded as creamy layer. They argued that similar “equalisation” based on posts should apply to OBC parents working in PSUs and private employment.
The judgment said, “Treating the children of those employed in PSUs or private employment, etc., as being excluded from the benefit of reservation only on the basis of their income derived from salaries, and without reference to their posts (whether Group A or B, or Group C or D) would certainly lead to hostile discrimination between parties who are similarly placed and would amount to equals being treated unequally.”
The creamy layer notification was issued in 1993 following the landmark Indra Sawhney judgment of 1992 which allowed 27% reservation for OBCs subject to exclusion of creamy layer. The 1993 order identified five occupational categories as creamy layer and a sixth category based on income/wealth test.
Later in 2004, the Centre issued a clarificatory order which explained that income from salaries and income from other sources (excluding salaries and agricultural land) are to be assessed separately, and exclusion would follow only if either component exceeds the prescribed limit for three consecutive years.
The March judgment held that the evolution of the non-creamy layer principle demonstrates that both the 1993 office memorandum and 2004 letter preserves the “primacy of status- based exclusion” and confines economic exclusion to those falling under the sixth category. “Salary income cannot be mechanically aggregated in a manner that defeats the constitutional objective articulated in Indra Sawhney,” the court said while justifying its conclusion.
The Centre’s application was opposed by those who benefited from the March judgment. Senior advocates Basav Prabhu Patil, Sanjay Hedge, P Wilson and advocate Prateek Chadha said that the application of the Centre was in the nature of review and should not be entertained.
Early this month, the court had refused to stay its judgment while issuing notice on Centre’s plea. It said that a decision will be taken after hearing both sides.

U.S. health regulators will review the scientific evidence on testosterone use in menopausal women on Thursday, including its benefits, risks, dosing and role in female health, as well as perspectives from doctors and patients.
The public meeting, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said could help guide future research and drug development, comes as a growing number of women are turning to testosterone to manage menopause symptoms.
There is no FDA-approved testosterone therapy for women, despite years of off-label use to treat low sexual desire, known as hypoactive sexual desire disorder, or HSDD.
Last year, the FDA removed the boxed warning about increased cardiovascular risk from testosterone products for men after reviewing post-marketing studies, though the products still carry warnings about increased blood pressure.
Physicians who prescribe testosterone to women typically rely on low doses of products approved for men, often dividing existing products such as AbbVie's AndroGel and Keenova Therapeutics' Testim, or on compounded formulations.
The lack of a female-specific product creates practical challenges for clinicians, said Diana Tordoff, an instructor in obstetrics and gynecology at Stanford, noting that an approved product could provide standardised dosing, labeling and safety-monitoring guidance and potentially improve insurance coverage.
Still, some experts say key questions remain unresolved. More long-term safety data are needed, said Stephanie Faubion, director of Mayo Clinic's Center for Women's Health.
The United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have approved or licensed testosterone products specifically for women.
The FDA's request for public comments ahead of the meeting attracted hundreds of submissions, many from women describing improved libido, energy and quality of life while using testosterone.
Evidence and safety gaps
Interest in testosterone among menopausal women has grown alongside claims on social media that it can improve energy, muscle mass, bone health and cognition, though specialists say the evidence is strongest for HSDD.
"We do not have any evidence in women that it will improve muscle mass or bone density or mood or well-being or really any other metric," Faubion said.
Karen Adams, director of Stanford Medicine's Program in Menopause and Healthy Aging, said testosterone has been reviewed by the FDA four times for use in women but has never been approved because of a lack of long-term safety data and concerns about cardiovascular and breast cancer risks.
The FDA has approved non-testosterone options like Sprout Pharmaceuticals' Addyi and Cosette Pharmaceuticals' Vyleesi for certain patients with HSDD.
Testosterone is generally not recommended for women with a history of breast cancer because it can be converted to estrogen in the body that can drive some cancers.
Excessive testosterone exposure can cause acne and increased hair growth, physicians said, while rarer effects such as voice deepening and hair loss may be irreversible.
Studies show that testosterone therapy is generally considered safe for men with medically diagnosed low levels of the hormone when prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
Tordoff and Adams are leading Stanford's MIX-T pilot study examining how low-dose testosterone affects vaginal health and the vaginal microbiome in postmenopausal women. Results are expected within the next two years.

Netanyahu defends Israeli military actions in Middle East in UN speech

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly.
After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice."
In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now."
The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.
Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland".
He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians.
Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military.
The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because had been denied a US entry visa.
Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him.
"They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said.
He went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity".
New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader.
"Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said.
In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians".
Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February.
"Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said.
A number of people protesting against Netanyahu's visit were detained in New York City. Among them were the Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and Emmy-winning actress Hannah Einbinder.
The Israeli military launched a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack against Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostages.
During the Israeli military campaign more than 73,920 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.
A resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) stated that Israel's conduct meets the legal definition as laid out in the UN convention on genocide.
Israel has regularly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence.
On 28 February, Israel and the US started launching massive air strikes on Iran, suspecting it of secretly building a nuclear weapon - a claim denied by Tehran.
Iran retaliated by carrying out missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases.

From Nagaland to a path to the Oscars: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema
- Published
There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh.
The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's northeastern frontier, and is in Konyak, a tribal language unfamiliar to most Indians, never mind audiences abroad. It was director Theja Rio's first feature and most of its cast faced a camera for the first time.
And yet, at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, this quiet film won the Platform Prize, a major juried award.
The award is intended to recognise films with a particularly distinctive directorial voice. The jury praised Rio's "refreshing perspective" and the film's portrait of a world rarely encountered on the international screen.
The win also gives Angh an unusual route towards the 2027 Academy Awards. Under new rules, winners of designated prizes at six international festivals can qualify for consideration in the International Feature Film category without relying solely on their country's official submission.
This does not make Angh an Oscar nominee. But it does place a Konyak-language film from one of India's smallest states inside a global conversation from which such stories have been almost entirely absent.
Rio still sounds slightly startled by it. When we speak in Delhi, roughly 72 hours after the win, he has barely had a moment to breathe - Toronto, flights, interviews, more interviews.
"There were a lot of good films in the competition", he says, including films by far more seasoned directors. His producers were confident.
"They thought we were going to win. I wasn't."
He is also less solemn than Angh might suggest. Before cinema, he wanted to be a rapper - "a kid from Compton instead of a kid from Nagaland", as he puts it. His tastes still range happily from Black Thought, the lead rapper of American hip-hop group The Roots, to his favourite filmmaker, the Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami.
But for his first feature, he turned close to home.
Set in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba, the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village, and his young son, as the world around them changes. The Konyaks are one of Nagaland's 17 major tribes, concentrated in the eastern district of Mon, where such chiefs are known as Anghs. Even today, some older men bear facial tattoos associated with the Konyaks' historical practice of headhunting.
Anghba and his son are among the last in their region to hold to an ancestral faith as Christianity spreads.
Then an American missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall, arrives. The father resists but the son is now curious.
Rio says the idea for the film came a few years ago, when he was visiting Mon for another project. What struck him was how closely different generations seemed to live alongside one another there.
Within a single family, he says, a grandfather might be a former headhunter, his face still tattooed; two generations later, his grandson might play guitar in a rock band.
"It feels like you've jumped on a time machine," Rio says. "The past and the present sort of coexist together."
The year also matters. Nagaland, which was earlier part of Assam state, formally became an Indian state in December 1963, during a period of profound political and social change.
By then, Christianity had been spreading among Naga communities for decades, bringing changes extending beyond religious belief into customs, rituals and everyday life.
Dr B Amo Konyak, a scholar of Konyak society, says the changes during this period were almost like a disappearance.
Some practices were lost; others "survived in fragments" - in the memories of elders, in family heirlooms. What had once been part of everyday life became heritage.
But Dr Konyak says culture did not simply stop. People carried parts of it into new religious and social worlds. Traditions survived, but changed meaning as they changed form.
It's this moment of transition that Rio wanted to capture.
"The past 50 or 60 years have brought extraordinary churn," he says, widening the distance between generations.
In Angh, he explores this through the relationship between the father and son who "intimately love and care about each other very deeply", even as their worlds begin to pull apart.
Critic Siddhant Adlakha was struck by the ambiguity the film captures. "Progress and tradition can be nonlinear, even entwined," he says, "rather than strictly opposing forces."
The film is yet to reach a wider audience, but its brief trailer offers a glimpse of how Rio constructed this world. Mist hangs over steep green hills; figures move through forests and village paths; fire and lamplight pick faces out of the darkness.
The landscape is beautiful but not merely picturesque - a small world held together by ritual, family and geography, while something larger presses in from beyond its edges.
Adlakha singles out the quiet close-ups of Anghlong Konyak, the first-time actor who plays the chief, and the "gentleness" with which Rio captures his "subdued rage".
What the camera saw mattered almost as much as where it was looking from.
Konyak people have long been viewed from the outside.
Dr Konyak points to explorers, colonial officials, missionaries and photographers drawn to tattooed faces, ornaments, weapons and headhunting, while the lives behind them often receded from view.
Rio was conscious of inheriting that history. "There have been several films and documentaries made about Nagaland," he says, "but these sort of films tend to follow the gaze of the explorer rather than the subject."
With Angh, he wanted to reverse that gaze, asking viewers to "step inside the shoes of these characters".
The change is subtle but consequential. The Konyaks are no longer an exotic remnant of the past, but people living through what Dr Konyak describes as "love, grief, conflict, faith, uncertainty and generational change".
Konyak advisers worked on dialogue, costume and production design, and much of the cast was drawn from first-time Konyak performers. The forest, too, belongs to the people moving through it. Adlakha says Rio treats it "not just as a setting, but as a home with a history", much as an urban filmmaker might treat Mumbai or New York.
Rio and cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz shot Angh on 16mm film, drawing on photographs and footage of missionaries and Naga communities from the 1950s and 60s.
They wanted to recreate the grain, texture and atmosphere of those archival images, while shifting the point of view from outsider to subject.
It was an evocative choice - and a logistical headache.
Unlike digital footage, the exposed film could not simply be reviewed on set. Every four or five days, the cans had to be sent to Mumbai for processing, while the crew carried on shooting without knowing exactly what they had captured.
There were more prosaic problems too.
During a night shoot with Henshall, an old Second World War Jeep was supposed to be driven into frame. It behaved perfectly through rehearsals. But when the cameras began rolling, the engine refused to start. After repeated attempts, the crew managed to capture just one take of the Jeep entering the frame.
"It was a very difficult night," Rio says.
Angh may be Rio's first feature, but its journey places it within a widening map of Indian cinema, especially in the northeast.
Adlakha points to filmmakers such as Assam's Rima Das and Meghalaya's Dominic Sangma whose work, he says, reveals "how complex and multifaceted the idea of Indian cinema happens to be".
Rio thinks Nagaland still remains at the edge of that scene. Its film industry is, as he puts it, "at a very nascent stage", with little of the reach enjoyed by India's established filmmaking centres.
But he hopes some of the attention around Angh travels back with it.
There are, he says, "so many talented filmmakers with so many beautiful stories that are yet to be told".
For now, though, Rio is looking forward to something more ordinary - getting back to Nagaland.
"I want to play football with my friends."

With time running out, new poll suggests Alberta separatism support is slipping
Poll also suggests decline in people who say they feel mainly attached to Alberta
With a little more than three weeks to go until the Oct. 19 referendum, a new poll done for CBC News suggests support for separation has softened since spring.
Janet Brown Opinion Research, in a random survey of 1,200 Albertans between Sept. 8 and 21, asked respondents the same question they’ll face on referendum day: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”
Twenty-three per cent of respondents said they’d vote to start the legal process to hold a binding referendum, while 72 per cent said they’d vote to remain in Canada. Four per cent said they were unsure.
That stands in contrast to Brown’s poll in the spring, which asked Albertans if a referendum were held today on whether Alberta should separate from the rest of Canada, would you vote for or against separation?
The April survey found 27 per cent of respondents would vote for separation, while 67 per cent would vote against.
"It’s part of this overall trend that we’re seeing," said Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown.
“People are feeling more comfortable with Alberta’s role in Canada, more comfortable with Ottawa, more comfortable with the prime minister.
“And all of those things seem to have caused a slight dip in the proportion of Albertans ready to vote to separate,” said Brown.
The survey has a margin of error of +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
Over the past months, the remain and leave sides have sought to win over hearts and minds with advertising and large rallies. They’ve criss-crossed the province in RVs decorated with maple leafs and Alberta flags, delivering lawn signs to front yards in cities and small towns.
But according to Brown’s polling, how Albertans feel about the prospect of separation has been largely baked-in for years.
“There’s a slight decline in people who are interested in the separatist option, but these numbers have been very consistent over time,” Brown said.
Lori Thorlakson, a political science professor at the University of Alberta, said as referendum day approaches, the meaning of the separatism question may be changing.
“This most recent shift, I think, really reflects that people are focusing more on what it would actually mean if we were to leave Canada,” she said.
A majority of respondents across the province voiced support for remaining a province of Canada.
Support was highest to remain in Canada in Alberta's big cities, at 74 per cent. In small centres, including in smaller towns and rural areas, support to remain in Canada sat at 69 per cent.
Attachment to Alberta and Canada
Since 2020, Brown has also been asking Albertans whether they feel more attached to the province, more attached to Canada, or attached to both equally.
Her most recent polling saw a decline in people who said they felt mainly attached to Alberta, and a corresponding increase in people who said they felt mainly attached to Canada or attached to both equally.
Some of that could be attributed to Alberta’s relationship with Ottawa, in Brown’s view. Last month, the federal government moved toward listing the West Coast pipeline as a national interest project ahead of an Oct. 1 deadline.
Brown believes the increased positive feelings Albertans have for Canada could also be attributed to the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S. and tensions with U.S. President Donald Trump.
“It’s made Albertans more focused on their Canadian identity,” she said.
The polling found that 23 per cent of respondents said they were more attached to Alberta than to Canada, down from 33 per cent in April 2026.
Forty per cent of respondents said they were more attached to Canada than to Alberta, up from 34 per cent in April 2026.
The polling also focused on the partisan divide found around the separation question.
At 98 per cent, nearly all respondents who said they would vote for the Alberta NDP if an election were held today said they wanted to stay in Canada.
But among those polled who said they would vote for the United Conservative Party, 53 per cent said they would vote for the separation option, while 40 per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada.
“That really speaks to the very delicate line that the premier is walking right now,” Brown said. “A bare majority of the people who say they would vote for her party in the next election, they are separatists.
“The premier has taken the ‘stay’ side. That’s making her job very difficult at the moment.”
A focus on mobilization
With sentiment seemingly baked in and with few undecideds remaining, Brown said she anticipates that the final weeks of the campaign are likely to revolve around mobilization, rather than persuasion.
“The game will be about both sides trying to make sure they get their voters out to vote on this referendum,” she said.
Separatist groups have spent recent weeks trying to make their case with voters. As referendum day has drawn closer, separatist group Let Alberta Decide has ramped up its messaging on social media, attempting to gear its campaign toward different demographics.
Speaking to CBC News in late August, Let Alberta Decide leader Keith Wilson said that while he’s not entirely convinced the polls over past months have been accurate, his group assumes they are from a strategic point of view.
“We see this with our signs as well. People are concerned about sharing with other people that they support a better deal for Alberta, or that they support Alberta independence,” Wilson said. “There’s a lot of polarization in our politics, as we know.”
Stephen Carter, a federalist with the group Alberta’s Voice, has said he’s worried about voters seeing consistent polls showing low support for separation and then staying home on referendum day.
"If it's close, we deal with this forever. And that’s the worst-case scenario,” he previously told CBC News.
Other polling across past months has been consistent with Brown’s findings, largely showing that the two sides in the separation debate have been entrenched, with the majority wanting to remain in Canada.
The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.
The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers.
Telephone numbers were dialed up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.

After months of controversy about the privacy of its smart glasses, Meta has unveiled the next iteration of its product lineup. At its Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced all the new glasses the company is putting out into the world.
Its popular Meta Ray-Ban glasses are now in their third generation, but two new models steal the show: a powerful, slimmed-down version of Meta's Quest headsets capable of virtual and augmented reality modes, and a camera-free pair of Ray-Ban–branded smart glasses, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Meta is also bringing its Muse AI agent to its smart glasses platform.
Meta VR Glasses
The next evolution of Meta’s Quest VR headset is something truly different. Instead of a heavy helmet-like headset, the new Meta VR Glasses look like big goggles. They’re five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3. They sit on the nose, right in front of your face like glasses, with no headstrap needed.
They look and feel more like the virtual display glasses made by companies like Viture, and what Xreal’s Project Aura seems to be shaping up to be—lightweight mixed-reality lenses that let you access virtual spaces without the burden of a VR headset.
There are no included controllers, though the device can connect to Meta’s previous Quest controllers or gamepads like an Xbox controller. Instead, the wearer controls the device with hand movements and finger pinches, similar to Android XR and Apple’s Vision Pro. Eye tracking pinpoints what you’re trying to access. You can pinch with two fingers to open an app or interact with something on the screen. Form a fist and flick your thumb up or down to scroll the screen.
Inside, the lenses feature a 5K micro-OLED display with a resolution of 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye. The computing power is offloaded to an attached compute puck, which also houses the battery.
Small prescription lens inserts can be magnetically clipped inside the lenses. (Meta has not shared how much those will cost.)
The software is the same that runs on Meta’s Quest VR devices, so movie and game titles in the Quest ecosystem will work on the VR Glasses. That includes games like Beat Saber, live sports apps, and streaming services like Disney+. There are digital workspace modes that let you have multiple monitor screens around you. The VR Glasses can also display a virtual keyboard on a surface in front of you, then use the embedded cameras to track specific finger placements.
The only immediate downside compared to other VR headsets—at least that I could tell from a brief demo at Meta Connect—is that the VR glasses don’t cover your entire field of vision, so it doesn’t feel as immersive as a traditional VR headset.
Meta says the VR Glasses cost $1,300 and will ship in the spring of 2027.
Ray-Ban Meta Audio
Meta has spent the past few months being absolutely pummeled by controversy about the privacy issues inherent in its camera-enabled smart glasses. The solution? A pair of smart glasses with no cameras.
The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses have all the audio capabilities of a standard pair of Meta’s smart glasses, minus image and video capture. At 43 grams, they’re also lighter than the others. They have better battery life—12 hours on a single charge and up to 48 hours with the included charging case.
They come in 23 different color and style options, including the retro Ray-Ban Clubmaster frame and a more rectangular Burbank. The Audio glasses cost $349 and are available for preorder now. They start shipping on October 10.
Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3
Meta's flagship line of smart glasses is getting a “Gen 3” upgrade. They have 12-MP cameras, like last year, plus 3K Dolby Atmos–enabled video capture. The glasses will get up to nine hours of battery life, two more than their predecessors. A new six-microphone array offers better sound and can cut out background noise more easily.
A new hearing aid feature called Hearing Enhancement uses the speakers in Meta's glasses to enhance speech and audio around the wearer, similar to the Nuance glasses from EssilorLuxottica.
Earlier this summer, Meta debuted smart glasses under its own branding, which cost a little less but were functionally identical to the Ray-Ban models. Now, it is already following them up with Gen 3 versions. These Meta-branded glasses come in a cat-eye shape called Capri and a rounder lens called Nova.
The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 glasses start at $449. Special-edition aviator glasses are $579. There are also additional models with colors and styles designed in collaboration with Kylie Jenner and rapper Lisa. (They come with optional charms.) They're available now. The Meta-branded Gen 3 glasses are also on sale now for $299.
Muse Charm
For folks who don't wear glasses, Meta has teased a new product altogether: the Muse Charm. Zuckerberg says it's the “fastest way to talk to your Muse,” referring to the company's AI agent, and show it the world around you. That likely means it has a camera on the back. Zuckerberg says Meta still needs to finalize the hardware, but plans to have it ready by the holiday season.
Meta Ray-Ban Display
Meta's Display glasses are also getting some updates. With the implementation of Meta AI, users can create photorealistic holograms of their faces, which can be helpful for video calls. There are better cycling options and improved navigation apps.

Chelsea Women: Sonia Bompastor and Carly Telford discuss new fertility and player maternity policies in WSL first
Chelsea are the first team in the WSL to introduce fertility and Player Maternity policies; it gives players the choice to have a family in whichever way they want to, with support during and after starting a family; Sonia Bompastor and Carly Telford explain more to Sky Sports
Thursday 24 September 2026 16:28, UK
Chelsea are used to being the first. While plenty of that has come on the pitch, it is the behind the scenes work that is truly leading the way for female players and women's health.
Now, the Blues are the first team in the WSL to introduced new fertility and maternity policies, giving their players the choice to start a family in whichever way they want to, and the post-natal support to balance the demands of elite sport and motherhood.
The Blues were also the first club in the world to starting tracking menstrual cycles - introduced by Emma Hayes in February 2020 - and how they impact performance. This is the next step in that process.
"As a club, it's always been really important for us to support our players the best way possible," Chelsea head coach Sonia Bompastor exclusively told Sky Sports.
"We want to be a club who always supports the players to have more knowledge around different opportunities... it's more for them to be able to make a choice and a decision about what they want for them.
"Every player is different, every individual is different, they have a different journey and you can make a choice based on what you know and what is available for you.
