"You don't have to choose anymore between your professional career and your personal life being a mum. Now, both are possible."
Chelsea have partnered with leading London fertility clinic Fertility Plus - and former goalkeeper and commercial manager for the women's team, Carly Telford, has led the way it that collaboration.
She exclusively told Sky Sports: "I've seen first-hand the kind of experiences that women, girls and athletes have when it comes to making choices around fertility and I wanted us to be a leading club in that.
"I wanted to find someone that understood us as athletes first, but also understood us as women and what that comes with. I wanted to find a fertility clinic that offered more than just egg freezing and more than just optional things, but to give choices around hormones, endometriosis, cycle tracking, testing - something all-encompassing around the female body.
"Then what the players do with that is completely up to the individual. That was really important to the club and to the players in terms of having options outside of their careers for how their families or how the individual look at themselves.
"It brings comfort and a thought process that we as a club are looking at them differently and are treating them as people as well as footballers. They will give their whole bodies to this club for the amount of time they're with us and it's an extra option for them to think about themselves.
"It's an important thing to have that every club should be looking at, the league should be looking at, the FA should be looking at in terms of making sure that women have a choice when it comes to their whole body and what that looks like during and after their careers."
'I thought there was only one way for me to becoming a mum and be a footballer'
Bompastor herself has four children with her partner, Chelsea assistant coach Camille Abily. She always knew she wanted to have a family, but a lack of options during her own player career led her to believe there was only one way for her to have children.
"When I reflect on my own story and experience, I didn't really have the choice," she explained. "I wanted to have a really good career as a player and I decided to carry on and to finish maybe a little bit earlier than what I should have done because I also wanted to become a mum and have a family.
"With the knowledge I had in that moment and everything that was available for me, I thought it was almost the only way for me to do that, because when we talk about becoming a mum when you are still an athlete, there are lot of questions to answer.
"It's about the pregnancy, but also everything after that. How can you look after your kid when you are an athlete and you play at the highest level? All these things were really difficult questions for me and I didn't have all the answers.
"Now, to have a club who is able to support the players, bringing them the knowledge, allowing them to talk about that subject is really important for us and giving them different opportunities to become a mum when they decide to. I'm really proud to be the head coach at Chelsea and to offer that opportunity to the players."
'Players are feeling comfortable with new policies'
No Chelsea players have yet revealed their intention to use the new resources available to them which, of course, should remain their own private decisions.
But Telford - who remains close with the squad from her own playing days - gave some insight into how the policies have been received.
She explained: "We touched base with some of the players and I'm lucky enough to be friends with a lot of them, so I leant on a few of them just to see what they felt about what this would look like for them. A lot of the feedback was 'this would be really good, keep us across it'.
"As soon as we knew the deal with Fertility Plus deal was close, we informed the leadership group who then informed the team and since then, we've had a lot of good feedback. The players are feeling very comfortable with it and then how they act upon that based on their own individual needs.
"Any information will confidentially be shared amongst the doctors at Fertility Plus and the doctors within the club and it will stay like that."
Chelsea have had pregnant players before. Melanie Leupolz had a baby in 2022 before returning to play for the club, while Zecira Musovic moved back to Sweden in June 2025 before giving birth later that year.
Telford said their pregnancies made her and the club consider how older players in the squad might be approaching their fertility and future families. For example, former Blues captain Millie Bright recently announced her pregnancy having retired from playing earlier this year.
"The 30-plus-year-olds are probably the last group of women that have had to maybe put those things on hold," Telford hopes.
How the policies work in tandem to offer players options
Ultimately, the two programmes offer players choice in whatever they decide, whether that is to start a family or looking after their gynaecological health. There is a clear link between fertility and maternity care and the two will work in tandem to give the players the support they need.
Bompastor said: "Having a family is something no one can teach you. You just learn to be a mum when you have your first child and even if someone is trying to tell you how you have to deal with the situation, you only learn when you have a baby.
"Having the opportunity to have platforms where you have information you can share with different people who already experienced that is already a big thing.
"Also, giving the support to players after having a baby. They need that because when you are a high-level athlete and you become a mum, those are two full-time jobs and you need that support to be able to do both at your best level.
"All these elements are really important for the players to have, but also for them to know there are different opportunities and they are available for them."
'All women should know about their bodies'
While Chelsea's announcements are player-focused, Telford is hoping that the club's profile can help raise the importance of women's health across the board.
She explained: "We want to be followed for the things we're doing around the team that have a wider impact when it comes to women in general and that's the impact that our sport has.
"We're very lucky to play one of the most popular sports in the world and be part of one of the biggest clubs and biggest brands. If we can make businesses, other football clubs and other sports think differently around their women, that is what we want to do.
"As women, we need to take more control of ourselves and have more viewership of what our bodies are doing, what they look like during womanhood and how that changes in terms of genetics, lifestyle, all these things that impact our bodies.
"And it's not just the athletes. They take a bigger toll on their bodies because of what they do, but general womanhood and what that looks like for us, that is the thing that I wanted to echo outside of football.
"I would have loved to have known more about my body for lots of different reasons while I was playing - how I get the best out of it as an athlete, what it's like during menstruation, what it's like in terms of longevity of my cycle and fertility and what that looks like moving forward, the options I then have during my career and what it looks like later on in life and in my career.
"Now they have that, I am really proud of it. I do hope this sparks a big conversation around what that looks like, not just for the future of women's sport, but for the future of women in general."

I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. Not all are winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or how cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.
For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.
Updated September 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations after testing the Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 Ultra and Framework Laptop 13 Pro. I've also reevaluated my picks based on the latest price changes.
The Laptops I Recommend Most
When friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that new price, it remains my top pick because it nails the big picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.
With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.
While the lower price of the new MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.)
Speaking of price, I have to mention the new Dell XPS 13 next. I like just about everything about this laptop, whether it's the compact size, the excellent build quality, or the gorgeous screen. It's not OLED, but it's sharp, bright, and color-accurate. It also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don't normally end up in a laptop at this price. While it doesn't have what I'd call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done for basic, day-to-day computing tasks. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. Just don't try to play games, edit high-resolution video, or take it to engineering school.
The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact device to travel with. With its tiny bezels, it's still one of the best laptops to use on a plane. But even beyond that, it's just one of the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. The Dell XPS 13 is primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its original $700 starting configuration. But that model comes with only 8 GB of RAM, which limited performance in my testing, and unfortunately, it's now $800. You'll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Most people will want the upgraded 16 GB model, which has also been increased by $100 to $1,000. It's still a good deal for the hardware.
If you want a Windows laptop that still feels high-end but has a bit more performance, I would point you to the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It's usually quite expensive, but we're finally seeing discounts that bring it to a more reasonable price. There's also an Intel model with a very efficient, powerful chip that would be a good choice. I'd go with whichever is cheaper right now.
And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I'd recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It's a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with the 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000, on sale at Amazon. While it's slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports including HDMI, USB-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided.
Lenovo also sells a cheaper version directly, but it has a lower-resolution IPS screen that I haven't tested. While the other specs are good, you might want to consider one of the cheaper options that I've tested below, such as the HP OmniBook 5. The IdeaPad Slim 5x has stronger performance and a better touchpad, though.
Cheap Laptops That Are Actually Good
While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but HP always has some version of the OmniBook 5 with a Snapdragon CPU at under $700. The specific discounted configuration seems to change every few days, though, so shop carefully.
I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for around $550. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.
The MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It initially started at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently been raised to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly prioritized the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a far better choice for remote workers—the Neo is an extremely premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual users. Thanks to the lower-powered A18 Pro chip, though, performance does take a hit. So, be careful about buying this laptop if you work at a computer all day.
Given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. The standout option is still the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14. It’s the most premium Chromebook available, with an OLED screen, 16 GB of RAM, and battery life that rivals the MacBook Neo. Its price just keeps going up, though, now at $849. That’s far too expensive for what you get. Instead, I'd recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514, which uses the same efficient (and responsive) MediaTek Kompanio Ultra that delivers excellent battery life. This one is also a 2-in-1, with a touchscreen, a 360-degree hinge, and a quality touchpad. The retail price of $749 is way too much, but it frequently drops down to $549, which is a great deal for this hardware. For a true budget Chromebook under $400, there are significant compromises, but I'd recommend the Asus Chromebook CX15. The screen isn't the best, and neither is the touchpad. But the specs are solid for the price, and I liked the more modern look compared to other ultra-cheap Chromebooks.
Windows laptops are about to get much stronger in this category, however, just as higher-priced Chromebooks will be seemingly phased out over time and replaced by the upcoming Googlebooks. Personally, I wouldn't spend more than $500 for a Chromebook and would instead opt for one of the cheaper HP OmniBooks mentioned above if you're already spending close to this price.
Powerful Laptops for Those Who Need It
While the laptops above are great for the average person, content creators and gamers need extra performance. For the former, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro is the ultimate choice. It combines immense power with surprising portability and fantastic battery life—a rare feat. The M5 generation is the most impressive yet, with a greatly expanded GPU and significantly boosted on-device AI processing thanks to a more efficient Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth. While it is one of the most powerful AI laptops available, the MacBook Pro isn’t for everyone; it is built specifically for professional creatives and engineers running heavy, demanding applications. It’s become more expensive in 2026, but there’s still nothing quite like it on the market.
There are a number of Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro, including the Asus ProArt P16 and Lenovo Yoga Pro 9i. And while both are powerful, they take an old-school approach to performance, using hot-and-heavy discrete graphics cards that significantly reduce battery life to achieve that level of performance. We'll probably need to wait for Nvidia's anticipated RTX Spark laptops for a true MacBook Pro competitor later this year. The Dell XPS 14 takes a different approach, ditching the discrete GPU for Intel’s new X7 or X9 chip (also known as B390 or Intel Arc graphics). The results are seriously impressive, replicating the performance of an RTX 4050 without the downsides of using a discrete GPU. Moreover, the Dell XPS 14 has a level of design polish you usually see only on MacBooks—and it even surpasses them in some areas. The more affordable configurations with the Core Ultra 5 or 7 don't have as strong graphics, but you still get the premium design and excellent battery life.
The most common use for laptop performance, however, is for playing games. If you plan on booting up any graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, I've come back to the Lenovo LOQ 15 as my top pick. There are cheaper RTX 5050 models out there, such as the Alienware 15 or MSI Cyborg A15, but prices have been increasing on these laptops over the past few months. The Alienware 15 with the RTX 5050, in particular, has seen a $600 price increase, which makes it incredibly overpriced. That's led me back to the LOQ 15, which has stayed steady at $1,300 at Walmart and gives you an RTX 5060 for graphics and a bright, colorful screen.
You won't find a cheaper gaming laptop that doesn't make some significant compromises in either performance or screen quality, both of which can sour the gaming experience. And while I wish the LOQ 15 were still selling for under $1,000 like it was when it first launched, it remains the absolute best gaming laptop for the money right now. It's really the only gaming laptop under $1,500 I'd currently buy, given where prices are.
There’s also a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, they have rightfully earned their reputation as the MacBooks of PC gaming—along with the MacBook Pro–like price tag. Their sleek design means they work just as well for school or work as they do for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While there are more powerful options out there, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade. They're expensive, but if you've got the money to spend, they're as premium as gaming laptops get. I'll soon be testing the latest version of the Blade 16, which includes Intel's latest Panther Lake chips and should have vastly improved battery life.
Other Good Laptops I’ve Tested
If you choose one of the laptops above, you will be very happy with your purchase. However, if you are looking for a specific feature or a different price point, I have included a few other options below that I've recently reviewed and enjoyed using. I've tested dozens of laptops this year already, but I've included some of the standouts below. Each of these recently tested laptops has at least one minor drawback, but they could still be the perfect choice depending on your needs and current discounts.
Framework Laptop 13 Pro for $1,599: We've always loved the Framework laptops here at WIRED, primarily because of how repairable and upgradable the internal components are. Unlike every other laptop on this list, nearly every part can be easily swapped out by the user, including the CPU. The Framework Laptop 13 Pro uses the same internal structure as the basic Framework Laptop 13, but upgraded with a haptic touchpad, an aluminum chassis, and a brighter (and sharper) display. The result is the Framework Laptop I've always wanted, especially with an all-black aesthetic that hints at ThinkPad inspiration. But most of all, if you're going to try and make a laptop last for many years, it makes sense that it would be something more premium. This one actually feels like it's worth the investment.
Microsoft Surface Laptop 13.8 for $1,500: The Surface Laptop 13.8 (also known as the 7th Edition) was one of my favorite laptops throughout 2024 and 2025, primarily because of its premium build quality, great battery life, and 3:2 aspect ratio screen. And while I still love this laptop, it’s risen in price dramatically and no longer feels like as good of a value, especially since it’s two years old at this point. The 2024 model now starts at $1,200, though I've occasionally seen it dip under $1,000. The next-generation model with the Snapdragon X2 chips costs $1,700. I have seen that price come down as low as $1,350 on discount.
Dell 14 Plus for $1,030: There was a time in 2025 when the Dell 14 Plus was as affordable as $600. It was easily the best deal in the world of Windows laptops, primarily because the Dell 14 Plus has a 2560 x 1600 display and a smooth touchpad—two things laptops at that price typically lack. These days, it's up to over $1,000, though for a 1 TB configuration, that is still a fabulous price. The XPS 13 is the better overall laptop, but the Dell 14 Plus has more ports and comes with more storage for the money.
Lenovo Yoga Slim 7 Ultra for $2,250: I like this laptop quite a bit. The OLED screen is sharp, bright, and quite colorful—very similar to the HP OmniBook Ultra. It also has a lot of the other great features on premium Windows laptops these days, including a haptic feedback touchpad and a very slim profile. Unfortunately, it's only available right now in a very expensive, maxed-out configuration with 32 GB of RAM and at least a terabyte of storage. I don't think that's a good pairing for this ultra-light laptop. Even with half the memory and storage, though, this would be too expensive compared to the competition.
Asus Zenbook A16 for $2,200: The Zenbook A14 and A16 are Asus' ultralight laptops, weighing just 2.16 pounds, making them some of the lightest laptops you can buy right now. This second edition of the Zenbook A16 is still incredibly light, and it now comes with second-generation Snapdragon X2 chips. It’s unique for its portability, and the Qualcomm chips deliver great battery life and performance. However, given the dramatic price increase, I’d suggest buying the 2025 model instead, which consistently comes in under $1,000.
Alienware 16X Aurora for $1,099: Another solid gaming laptop, this one comes with the typical Alienware flair. Its standout features are its higher-resolution display and great build quality. The price fluctuates frequently, though, and in most cases, the LOQ 15 is the better option (unless you really want that higher-resolution screen). This Walmart deal for the RTX 5050 model, however, is really fantastic.
Laptops to Avoid
Dell 14S: This is the 2026 successor to the Dell 14 Plus, which I recommended above. This is a solid laptop, sporting a premium design and a very reflective OLED display. It performs well too, thanks to the latest Intel Core Ultra Series 3 chip. But it's far too expensive right now. Until the price comes down, I prefer just about every other Dell option, including the Dell 14 Plus, Dell XPS 13, or Dell XPS 14.
Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential: This is a “new” model that came out this year, even though it uses a CPU from 2023. But honestly, this is just too expensive. I've seen it on sale for under $1,400, but even so, the standard LOQ 15 is a similar price and has a far superior display.
MacBook Pro M5: It’s not a significant step up from the MacBook Air in performance, and it’s much thicker. You're paying for the Mini-LED screen and extra ports. Unfortunately, it got the biggest price bump, up $300 to $1,999. It’s not a bad laptop, but you’re better off with the MacBook Air or a more powerful M5 Pro/Max configuration.
Acer Swift 16 AI: This is one of the few laptops you can buy with the powerful, efficient new Intel Core Ultra X9 chips. However, the Acer Swift 16 AI took an experimental approach with its oversized trackpad, making it very difficult to use. Even at a discount, you'll find it frustrating.
Asus TUF Gaming A14: There’s a lot I like about this gaming laptop. The design is portable yet modern, and the display is sharp. And while the TUF Gaming A14 is impressive technically (using the interesting AMD Strix Point chip), the lack of a discrete graphics card doesn’t provide enough gaming performance to justify its very high price. I haven't tested the options with dedicated graphics cards, but they tend to be more expensive than counterparts from Lenovo, Acer, or Alienware.
Asus Vivobook 14: I recommended this laptop a lot throughout 2025, but it doesn’t hold up as well these days. While the Vivobook 14 has great battery life, the HP OmniBook 5 14 offers a much better display and similar specs, making it a better laptop.
How Much Should You Spend on a Laptop?
If you’re shopping for a laptop, you probably already have a budget. But some context might help put things in perspective. The cheapest laptops cost around $200, but laptop prices can range as high as $5,000. Meanwhile, the average amount people spend, according to the best data we have, is around $750. That lands decidedly in the midrange, splitting between the more expensive devices that are more than $1,000 and the budget-tier machines you find below $700.
When we talk about pricing, it’s often the “starting” price of the laptop, meaning the lowest-priced configuration. This is really important to consider, as you want to compare devices apples to apples as much as possible. For example, a cheaper laptop might start at $750 with 256 GB of storage, while a more premium laptop might start at this same price but come with 512 GB or even 1 TB of storage. Increasingly, you can find some really decent laptops around this price, some of which we’ve listed.
If your budget needs to be under $750, though, there are still good options. Laptops below this price tend to come with compromises. Most commonly, it’s the quality of the display and touchpad that suffers, as these are things you can’t gauge from a spec sheet or reference photo. Or it might be a performance-related issue, such as the 8 GB of memory in the MacBook Neo. If you’re shopping for something under $500, Chromebooks often give you the best bang for your buck.
So, why spend more? Well, there are two primary reasons. First, you might want a more premium design, perhaps one that has a more daring aesthetic or high-end components. Take the MacBook Pro, for example. It starts at $600 more than the MacBook Air but comes with a brighter mini-LED screen, significantly better speakers, and more ports. The second primary reason to spend more than $750 or so is to get more performance. Whether for gaming or content creation, laptops with discrete GPUs cost more, which is why it’s hard to find a worthwhile gaming laptop for less than $1,000. If you’re buying a gaming laptop, plan to spend a few hundred bucks more (outside of the Lenovo LOQ 15).
What Are the Best Laptop Brands?
Unlike the smartphone world, the biggest laptop brands have been around in the tech industry for more than 40 years now. Besides Apple, four laptop brands stand out for their ability to adopt the latest technology and trends while providing reliable support and service.
Lenovo is the biggest PC brand in the world, at least in terms of global shipments. It’s perhaps most well-known for its familiar sub-brands like ThinkPad and Yoga, but it also isn’t afraid to take risks with more experimental designs and advanced technology. Lenovo has also made a name for itself in the gaming space with its Legion laptops, known for balancing performance and features at competitive prices.
Asus has quickly become a favorite, notable for the sheer number of laptops available in the consumer market. The company takes a similar approach to Lenovo, which has led Asus to innovate quickly on new technology and designs while also launching premium laptops at more affordable prices than its competitors. Gaming, in particular, is a space Asus has come to dominate, with the ROG Zephyrus, Strix, and TUF brands leading the way.
Dell and HP are generally more conservative, but both have recently undergone significant rebranding. In 2024, HP replaced its Spectre and Envy lines with the OmniBook name. Meanwhile, Dell briefly retired its well-known Inspiron and XPS sub-brands in 2025, though it has since reversed course and brought the XPS line back.
Other notable laptop brands include Microsoft Surface, Samsung, Acer, LG, and MSI, though none have the same global footprint as the top four.
How Do I Choose the Right Laptop?
If none of these laptops quite rings your bell, that’s OK! There are far more laptops than we have time to test. To help you make smart choices, we put together a complete laptop buying guide. We also cover the CPUs and GPUs you need to know. We recommend sticking to these guidelines:
RAM: It’s recommended that you get 16 GB of RAM. That’s become the new standard, even in more affordable laptops. Upgrading to 32 GB is even better and means you never have to worry about running out of memory, especially if you’re a gamer or video editor. The recent memory shortage may change RAM configuration options soon (and overall laptop pricing), however, though we haven’t yet seen how exactly that will play out. Apple’s launch of the 8 GB MacBook Neo may indicate the direction things are headed.
CPU: In the world of Windows laptops, you have three CPU brands to choose from: Intel, AMD, or Qualcomm. Intel’s Core Ultra Series 2 launched in late 2024 delivers a huge boost to battery life. It also has the best integrated graphics of the three. Core Ultra Series 3 is just now rolling out and, based on my own testing, is extremely impressive in performance and efficiency. While AMD chips are primarily used in gaming laptops, they’ve struggled to gain ground on Intel. AMD’s next-gen Ryzen AI 400 series is also rumored to launch in 2026. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, however, have seriously challenged Intel over the past year with their ARM architecture, offering some of the best battery life we’ve ever seen on Windows machines. The second generation of these chips, Snapdragon X2, was announced last fall and will launch in devices in 2026.
Discrete graphics: Want to play AAA PC games or edit video on your laptop? You’ll want a standalone graphics processor. At this point, Nvidia is the primary option. The RTX 5090 launched in 2025 as the most powerful new GPU available, but the 40-series remains a good option. Integrated graphics have improved significantly over the years though, especially on processors made by Apple, AMD, and Intel, such as the Apple M5 or the Intel Core Ultra X9 388H.
Screen: The display depends on the size of the laptop. A 1,200-pixel resolution (HD+) screen on a 13- or 14-inch laptop looks sharp enough, but you’ll want more pixels on larger displays, such as a 2560 x 1600, 2880 x 1800, or 3840 x 2400. While IPS screens will be good enough for most people, OLED or Mini-LED are becoming more common, offering better color accuracy, deeper contrast, and excellent HDR performance.
Connectivity: While port needs vary by user, we generally recommend at least two USB-C ports, along with one HDMI and one USB-A port for legacy devices. (Remember that nearly all laptops today use one of those USB-C ports for the power adapter.) Thankfully, most laptops still have headphone jacks, but always check, because a few daring machines have dropped them. Lastly, make sure it supports Wi-Fi 6E or newer. Even if you don’t have a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 router yet, it’s a good bet you will in the future (see our Best Routers or Best Mesh Systems guides if you need a new one).
Battery life: Battery life is extremely competitive these days, with Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel all making highly ambitious battery-life claims. Most laptops with the latest chips (and without discrete graphics) will get you more than 10 hours of battery life, or many more if your workload is lighter.
Intel vs. AMD vs. Qualcomm
In the world of Windows laptops, there are three primary options for CPUs: Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. All three companies offer good options, but it really depends on the type of laptop. For premium laptops, you’ll want something like the Intel Core Ultra 258V or Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite. Meanwhile, for budget laptops, Snapdragon X is the best choice. And for gaming laptops, I’d recommend something from AMD, such as the Ryzen AI 9 365. All three companies have announced next-gen chips for 2026, and there’s some exciting stuff coming soon.
Intel’s latest chips, known as either Core Ultra Series 3 or codename Panther Lake, are slowly rolling out in new laptops, such as the Dell XPS 14. These chips represent a massive leap forward in both CPU and integrated graphics performance. While highly impressive, they will soon face fresh competition from upcoming AMD and Qualcomm releases.
Qualcomm made a major impact in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips. Similar to Apple's M-series, these ARM-based processors prioritize efficiency to drastically improve battery life. This has been a game-changer for Windows laptops across different price points. The Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite is the highest-end option for performance, but the Snapdragon X Plus and base Snapdragon X still offer equally strong battery life, despite showing up in much cheaper laptops. The sequel was unveiled in late 2025, and now in 2026, we’re seeing those laptops roll out. Unfortunately, like Intel’s latest chips, laptops with this next-gen silicon tend to be significantly more expensive than their predecessors.
Over on Team Red, AMD has grown into a competitive player in the gaming laptop space. Its latest processors, including the Ryzen 9 9950X3D and 9900X3D, are the most powerful gaming chips you can find in a laptop. Unfortunately, it’s still hard to find many laptops supporting these killer chips. AMD also offers its Ryzen AI 300 H and HX chips, which are more commonly found in gaming laptops. While they also offer a mainstream Ryzen AI 300 series, these chips aren’t found in many laptops and currently fall short of the battery life offered by Intel and Qualcomm. AMD’s new Ryzen AI 400 series will be arriving soon.
How I Test Laptops
I have been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, and WIRED contributor Chris Null has been testing these machines for 25 years. We test each laptop we review in a variety of situations, including both synthetic benchmark tests and real-world use cases. We make comparisons against similar equipment. We don’t just look at the specs—our reviews evaluate performance, usability, portability, and price to help you find the right laptop for your needs.
We put every laptop through a gauntlet of tests before writing a review and assigning a rating.
Hands-on use: We evaluate the exterior of the device. We compare how thin and light it is against other laptops. We repeatedly open and close the lid to test the quality and ease of the hinge. We push on weak points like the keyboard and lid to test build quality. We also extensively test the keyboard and touchpad for comfort and precision. By using each laptop as our daily driver for days or even weeks, we can spot real-world quirks—like awkward port placement, excessive bloatware, or unexpected problems that may make the laptop difficult to use—that you won’t see on a spec sheet.
Sights and sounds: Once we boot up the device, it’s all about the sights and sounds. The screen is paramount, as it’s your window into everything the laptop has to offer. While you can tell a lot about brightness, color, and contrast just by looking, we go beyond subjective testing. We use a Spyder colorimeter to precisely measure brightness, contrast, color saturation, and accuracy. For HDR-capable screens, we also test peak brightness with HDR content. Finally, we evaluate the webcam and speakers to ensure they are ready for your video calls and streaming sessions.
Performance testing: Finally, we test performance. We always evaluate a laptop based on what it’s intended for—we don’t expect a $500 budget laptop to run like a gaming powerhouse, or a gaming rig to get 18 hours of battery life. Our testbed includes more than 20 synthetic benchmarks, which we constantly adapt based on the device's CPU and operating system. These include tests within Geekbench, PCMark, 3DMark, Procyon, GFXBench, Puget Bench, Superposition, Cinebench, and various gaming-related tests such as 3DMark and Cyberpunk 2077. While we don’t generally report raw scores, we pay close attention to what they tell us. We also monitor fan noise, surface temperature, and overall battery life during these tests.
It’s a lot, I know. But we’re thorough, because we want to stand by our recommendations and ensure that the laptops we rate highly are worth the money.

Trump and Xi clash over AI at tense US state visit
Chinese leader warns US president both countries can and must ensure technology remains under human control, two days after Trump dubbed fears ‘a hoax’

China and the US can and must develop and manage AI “for good”, Chinese leader Xi Jinping has toldDonald Trump, further ramping up tensions with the American president who has dubbed fears over the technology “a hoax”.
On his first state visit to the US in more than a decade, Mr Xi told Mr Trump: “Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence. [We must] ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people.”
The US president had rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese leader amid friction between the two superpowers, largely over global trade.
Thursday's lavish state summit at the White House appeared heavy on symbolism but light on substance, with no sign of major breakthroughs between the world's biggest economies, even as Mr Trump highlighted progress under a bilateral trade mechanism.
Both leaders also identified AI as an area of cooperation.
AI bosses have sounded the alarm in recent weeks over the potential of the technology to threaten the future of the human race. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI maker ChatGPT, said the world was right to be afraid of AI, and the warnings have led to new calls for regulation of the technology.
But at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Mr Trump dismissed calls for stricter controls, branding the warnings “a hoax”, setting up a clash with the Chinese leader. He also said he wanted AI to be renamed “super-intelligence”.
Mr Xi’s visit began in Washington on Thursday with much fanfare, including a military ceremony, a flyover at the Rose Garden and Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof.
However, the meeting between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies comes as Mr Trump faces international backlash for inviting Russian president Vladimir Putin to Miami’s G20 gathering in December despite the war in Ukraine.
Mr Trump, who has dubbed his relationship with Mr Xi the “G2”, said their meeting would have an impact on the world for decades to come.
“During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and 'super-intelligence’,” Mr Trump said.
“The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.”
Mr Xi was treated to a state dinner on Thursday evening with tech executives including Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Open AI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai.
But analysts cautioned that the intense competition between the two countries in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements.
Mr Xi used his initial address to emphasise that the US has the “capability and responsibility to manage AI for good”.
“China-US cooperation may not solve every problem in the world, but without our cooperation, it would be hard to solve many of the world's problems,” he said.
He voiced hope for a more stable relationship with the US, saying Beijing and Washington should be “partners, not rivals” and that the “historical logic of peaceful coexistence” between the two countries had not changed.
The two are expected to discuss the ongoing Iran war but there has been little sign China is willing to exert pressure on its ally to yield to US demands.
Mr Trump has been warned about the relationship between Tehran and Beijing as the war he started in February continues with no end in sight.
“The president needs to tell Xi Jinping that this is a dangerous alliance,” Jonathan Schanzer, executive director of the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, told Fox News before the visit.
“The Chinese assistance to the Iranian regime has actually expanded on a number of fronts,” he warned, citing the provision of drone parts and motors, dual use chemicals, alleged assistance with targeting and an economic relationship.
Disputes over Taiwan remained the most contentious issue as China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own. Mr Xi is keen to press Mr Trump to halt arms sales to the democratically governed island.
As expected, the Chinese president pressed Mr Trump on Taiwan on Thursday, saying he hoped the US would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence."
After his May summit with Mr Xi, MrTrump, whose administration in December approved an $11bn arms sale package to Taiwan, said he was holding a second package, worth some $14bn, in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip".
Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank said Beijing may believe it has established a new baseline on Taiwan with Mr Trump.
Mr Xi's use of the word "adhere" was revealing because "it implies Beijing believes Washington is already behaving in ways it wants”, he told the Associated Press.
"In the context of the current stand-down on Taiwan arms sales, China may increasingly view that restraint as a new baseline rather than a temporary pause," he said.
"Beijing's objective is to get Trump to absorb Chinese red lines into his own definition of a stable relationship."
Sources told Reuters said that Beijing is offering to help put pressure on Iran in return.
After their previous meeting earlier this year, Mr Trump had said he was holding in abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth $14 billion and called it a “very good negotiating chip”.
Mr Trump, known to be impressed with ceremony and symbolic gestures, has attempted to reciprocate the grand welcome he received when he made his own state visit to China in May.
On Wednesday evening he greeted Mr Xi with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews – the first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader in that manner since President Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015.
The Chinese leader’s visit comes at the end of busy week for international diplomacy in the US, with the UN General Assembly still taking place in New York.
Secretary of state Marco Rubio announced the Putin invite after meeting Russia’s outspoken foreign secretary Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the event Wednesday, and soon faced international backlash.
“It's clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalise people who are starting wars, who are going against the UN charter, who are killing and giving orders to kill civilians,” the EU’s representative for foreign affairs Kaja Kallas told Sky News in response.
The European Commission also issued thinly veiled criticism of the US invitation.
“Russia is escalating attacks on Ukrainian civilians as we speak. July and August were the deadliest months since the war started,” deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill said.
“Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion and to call for it to end.
“What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting.”
The state dinner wrapped up with Mr Xi saying that the two leaders shared a “sincere and indepth exchange”.
Mr Trump will take the Chinese leader on Friday to the US National archives. They would also see "artefacts testifying to the long and cherished relationship" between China and the US and their "cultural exchanges,” he said in remarks welcoming Mr Xi.

The Eiffel Tower has reopened after a one-day strike was called in response to the landmark’s management ordering female staff to keep out of sight at the request of a visiting religious group.
City Hall, which operates the Paris landmark, has apologised for breaching France’s republican principle of equality and ordered a full inquiry.
Workers at the tower walked out on Monday, closing the landmark to visitors, after female colleagues were sidelined and replaced during a visit organised by a Hindu religious group at the weekend.
In a statement, staff said they objected to “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit.
“Some were asked to leave their posts and wait in separate rooms. In some posts, women were replaced by men. All female employees were instructed not to pass through or enter certain areas while the [Hindu] delegation was present,” they said in a statement.
Employees said they were shocked to find themselves in a situation that was “deeply contrary to the values of equality and nondiscrimination”.
“The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France. We believe it must also be exemplary in the values it promotes and the way it treats staff,” the statement said.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement, whose members made the request in advance of a visit on Saturday, apologised.
“To our knowledge, nobody was refused access to the Eiffel Tower at any moment. Nevertheless, We offer our sincere apologies to anyone who may have been hurt or offended by this situation,” it wrote in a statement.
BAPS is close to India’s ruling Hindu nationalist party, Bharatiya Janata, and was in France to consecrate its first major temple in the country on Sunday.
The public-owned Eiffel Tower operating company (SETE) acknowledged that BAPS had requested that “interactions with women” be limited, and said it should not have accepted these conditions. “They are not in keeping with SETE’s values or the principles of equality between women and men and the neutrality that must guide the organisation of visits to the monument,” it said.
Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor of Paris, has promised an investigation to “get to the bottom of this as soon as possible”.
He said moving female staff out of sight was unacceptable.
“These are not my values nor those the Eiffel Tower must represent,” he wrote on X.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the Paris Centre district and president of SETE, said he was unaware of the “shocking and unacceptable” conditions afforded the visiting group.
“I confirm again the Eiffel Tower’s commitment to republican values and gender equality,” he said.

Vladimir Putin has arrived in India’s capital of Delhi ahead of an 11-member Brics summit set to be dominated by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as economic challenges.
The Russian president and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, were due to hold talks with India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, while Chinese leader Xi Jinping was also expected to attend the two-day meeting.
Putin arrived at Palam air force Station in Delhi, where he was greeted by India’s minister of state for external affairs, Kirti Vardhan Singh, according to footage broadcast by Russia’s Ria Novosti news agency.
The summit will mark Xi’s first visit to India since 2019 and is seen as the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border.
Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again recently, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.
However, deep mistrust remains, with their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.
On Friday posters of a beaming Modi lined streets in Delhi, along with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions in central districts. Delhi police have urged people to be patient and cooperative.
Brics was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by western powers.
It has since expanded and now includes Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
“The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the Brics summit,” said Harsh V Pant of India’s Observer Research Foundation. “What was seen until last year as an achievement – the expansion of Brics – today looks like a big constraint on Brics”.
It will be Pezeshkian’s first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.
“The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the [expanded] group’s cohesion,” said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the Brics foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in Delhi in May.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important strategic partners and its most controversial fuel supplier in recent years as the war against Ukraine drags on.
Putin last visited India in December 2025 but he also met Modi in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, this month.
India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, visited Kyiv this month, when the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war”.

A group of 31 Democratic members of the US Congress has sent a letter to the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, criticising the Trump administration over “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections.
Latin America’s largest country will hold the first round of its presidential election on 4 October, with polls showing a technical tie between the incumbent leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro.
In the letter sent to Rubio on Thursday, 30 members of the House of Representatives and the senator Bernie Sanders listed a series of measures the US government took that they interpret as attempts to secure a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
They wrote that those actions “reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America”, citing the recent midterm elections in Argentina and presidential elections in Honduras and Colombia.
In July, a group of 11 Democratic members of Congress sent a similar letter arguing that Trump was trying to interfere in Colombia’s election in favour of the far-right millionaire and former lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who went on to win the second round.
In Thursday’s letter, the lawmakers wrote that US officials under Trump have engaged in a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil”.
They noted that when Trump imposed his first tariffs on Brazil last year, he made clear that one reason was Bolsonaro’s trial over his attempt to stage a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The former president was ultimately convicted and, unable to run because he is under house arrest, named his son to take his place.
They also cited new tariffs that Trump imposed on Brazil in July under section 301 of US trade law, as well as plans by the US government to send two officials to Brazil to “cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s voting system, considered by many experts to be among the most reliable in the world”. The Lula administration ultimately denied the US delegation visas.
The Brazilian president has repeatedly complained that Trump is trying to interfere in Brazil’s elections and, in his speech opening the UN general assembly this week, said, without naming anyone: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy, internal or external, to act against the will of the people.”
In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US is “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.
They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October.
The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

Dengue and influenza viruses are currently in circulation, with a number of hospitals in the city reporting a steady flow of patients with fever, though doctors say the numbers remain in line with the seasonal trend.
“Currently, both flu and dengue viruses are in circulation. Flu spreads from person to person, while dengue is a vector-borne infection. We need to deal with both the infections carefully. If a person has fever, they should look out for respiratory symptoms such as cold, cough, and throat pain. These are the primary symptoms of Influenza-Like Illness (ILI). If there is a high-grade fever with no respiratory symptoms but body pain and headache, it is a sign of dengue,” a senior government doctor said.
Hidden cases
Epidemiologically, if one case of dengue is notified in a particular area or village, it means there are hidden cases, he said, adding: “There is no need to test everyone, and persons with typical symptoms can be treated appropriately based on a physician consultation. Laboratory tests can be initiated if doctors prescribe.”
He said that in the case of flu, it is mostly self-limiting, but utmost care should be taken for elderly and pregnant women. “ILI can lead to Severe Acute Respiratory Infection and people could land in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome. Early treatment is important for flu-like symptoms. For dengue, a basic blood test — Complete Blood Count — will give us clues, especially a drop in the platelet count. So, with two viruses in circulation, which happens naturally during this season, people should be prepared and alert,” he said. However, there are no official institution-wise figures on fever outpatients or admissions. Authorities of at least two government hospitals in Chennai said the number of fever cases were not rampant and admissions for fever had not increased. In another hospital, senior doctors said all beds in the fever ward were full, and that the patients were recovering.
Seasonal trend
S. Chandrasekar, Professor and Head, Department of Medicine and Critical Care Services, Government Stanley Medical College Hospital, said that at present, the situation was not alarming and the rise in fever cases was in line with the expected seasonal trend typically observed from September to November.
“A mild variant of flu is also in circulation. Dengue cases slowly peak after rainfall in mid-November and usually settle by February-end every year. There is a small excess of cases this year. Many persons, especially adolescents/teenagers, are being referred late, and with complications such as capillary leak syndrome on the fifth or sixth day of illness. We are closely watching the situation. It is important to know the warning symptoms of dengue,” he said.
At Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital, medical director Janani Sankar said they were seeing a lot of dengue and influenza A cases as well as a few Respiratory Syncytial Virus infections. “The cases are quite rampant. Our beds are full. We are seeing children with dengue, respiratory infections, wheezing, and bronchiolitis. Some children with dengue are requiring admissions for 24 to 48 hours, but none with complications,” she said.
Dr. Sankar said parents should ensure there are no water collections in and around their homes. As dengue virus is transmitted by a day-biting mosquito, schools must ensure that they take mosquito control measures. “If a child is dull after a fever subsides, they should seek medical help. The warning signs of dengue are abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness, and refusal to take feeds,” she said.

Senior Judicial Officer, Yash Paul Bourney was sworn in as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at a solemn ceremony held in the Chief Justice’s Court at the Srinagar Wing of the High Court on Tuesday.
Dr. Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, administered the oath of office to Justice Yash Paul Bourney.
The Warrant of Appointment was read out by M. K. Sharma, Registrar General, High Court of J&K and Ladakh, who also conducted the proceedings of the ceremony.
The ceremony was graced by Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Justice Mohd. Akram Chowdhary, Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal, Justice Rajesh Sekhri, Justice Mohd. Yousuf Wani and Justice Sanjay Parihar. Justice Sanjeev Kumar, Justice Sindhu Sharma, Justice Sanjay Dhar, Justice Rahul Bharti, Justice Moksha Khajuria Kazmi and Justice Shahzad Azeem joined the ceremony through virtual mode from Jammu wing of the High Court.
The family members, close relatives and friends of Justice Yash Paul Bourney were also present on the occasion, lending special significance to the ceremony.
Among other dignitaries present were Mir Syed Latif, Judicial Member (HOD) of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Srinagar Bench, Shaleen Kabra, Additional Chief Secretary, M.K. Sinha, ADGP CID, Achal Sethi, Commissioner Secretary Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Divisional Commissioner, Kashmir, IGP Kashmir, IGP Security, Senior Advocates; Executive Members of the Kashmir Advocates’ Association and the J&K High Court Bar Association, Jammu; Law Officers; Judicial Officers; and officers of the High Court Registry.
The Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India, issued the notification appointing Justice Yash Paul Bourney as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh on September 19, 2026.
Born on August 25, 1967, Justice Yash Paul Bourney hails from village Dadwara, Bhaddu, Billawar, District Kathua. During his distinguished judicial career, he has held several important judicial and administrative assignments. He served as Principal District & Sessions Judge at Leh, Baramulla, Udhampur and Jammu, besides serving as Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Srinagar and Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Jammu.
Justice Bourney also served in key institutional positions as Member Secretary, J&K Legal Services Authority; Registrar Vigilance, High Court of J&K and Ladakh; and Director, J&K Judicial Academy.
After serving as Principal District & Sessions Judge, Jammu, Justice Bourney was appointed on deputation as Member, J&K Special Tribunal, Jammu. He was serving in the said capacity immediately prior to his elevation as a Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

The Pixel Watch 5's blood pressure and insulin resistance trends are rolling out this week
The first trend reports for the health data will be available in early October.
When Google debuted its latest Pixel smartwatch last month, one of the standout features the company announced was the Health Guardian toolset. This platform promised to bring a new layer of insight to the wearer's blood pressure, insulin resistance and sleep breathing. Those health tracking tools were not available at the time of our review, but considering we rated the Pixel Watch 5 highly at its launch date, the rollout of these new tools should further increase the device's appeal — provided they work well. About 40 calves dead in structure fire at beloved B.C. highway stop D Dutchmen Dairy
Longstanding family business started in 1978
A well-known ice cream shop and family dairy farm in Sicamous, B.C., has lost multiple structures and dozens of animals in an overnight fire.
Bianca Colonna, whose parents run D Dutchmen Dairy, said the fire started at around 1 a.m. PT, burning three buildings including a barn housing about 40 calves, which all died in the flames.
"So in the words of my mom — her babies passed away last night," she said.
The animals were like family, she said, and each one had a name.
"My four-year-old son hugged and kissed every calf."
D Dutchmen Dairy was established in 1978 by Chris and Nellie Dewitt, according to its website.
Located just off the Trans-Canada Highway, the business has become a popular roadside stop over the years, known for its ice cream and farm animals.
The ice cream shop was not burned, but it is closed as the family assesses its next steps.
Colonna said the fire moved quickly in the old wooden barns, but that firefighters were able to save the milking parlour and cow section.
They even rescued one cow who fell down in the havoc of the night.
"They said, 'We're not going to let her burn,'" Colonna said.
The cause of the fire isn't yet known, and the business is asking for people to avoid the farm at this time.
'Not just a business': mayor
Sicamous Mayor Colleen Anderson said the fire was "devastating," calling the business "iconic."
"Not just a business but family friends, community supporters. Just a big part of Sicamous," she said.
Laurie Kubos of Askew's Food, which sells milk from the farm, said she has many memories of stopping at the dairy farm as a child growing up in neighbouring Revelstoke.
"It was a big deal," she said.
Both said the entire community was rallying around the family-owned business, which has been a major support of charities and organizations over the years.
A community fixture for nearly 50 years
Owner Jake Dewitt, the son of the business's founders, said in an interview with CBC News in 2021 that 180,000 customers stopped at D Dutchmen each year. At peak times, the business employed 25 workers, according to Dewitt.
He attributed the stop's popularity to its "beautiful yard and store," its quality products and its ice cream — which he said is particularly well-known in Alberta, where most of their customers come from.
Reacting to news of the fire Thursday, Jennifer Tirschman, executive director of the Sicamous and District Chamber of Commerce, emphasized what an important role D Dutchmen has played in the area.
"They're part of the very fabric of the soul of this community," she said.
She noted that many people have memories of going to D Dutchmen over the years.
"We're all very saddened to hear about the devastating fire that has occurred, and the community is here to support them in any way we can."

Ecommerce giant Amazon India reportedly plans to invest $3 Bn (₹28,790 Cr) to expand its quick commerce business, Amazon Now, over the course of next four years. Sources told Reuters that the ecommerce giant will invest $1 Bn in the vertical by the 2027-end, and an additional $2 Bn by 2030. According to the report, Amazon plans to utilise the fresh proceeds to add new dark stores, strengthen inventory management software at stores, deploy AI tools for demand prediction and expand product mix. The focus will be on stocking daily essentials rather than iPhones, added a source. Another source reportedly added that the ecommerce major is looking to expand its dark store network to around 1,300 stores by April 2027 from 750 currently. Amazon India first launched ‘Now’ in Bengaluru in June 2025 and later expanded the service to parts of Delhi in July 2025 and subsequently to Mumbai. While the platform has been comparatively late in entering the quick commerce market, it is picking up momentum. In April this year, Amazon India’s vice president of operations Abhinav Singh, in a blog post, said that the company would invest ₹2,800 Cr (around $300 Mn) to expand its quick commerce vertical and strengthen its logistics network. Notably, this is not the first time that the ecommerce giant has poured in capital into the country in the past year. Last year, Amazon India had announced a ₹2,000 Cr investment to add 17 new fulfilment centres, six sortation centres, and 75 last-mile delivery stations across India. Prior to this, it had also committed an investment of $35 Bn across its India businesses till 2030 to help boost its cumulative exports from the country to $80 Bn by 2030 The investment comes amid rising competition in the quick commerce segment. While the likes of Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart and Zepto continue to dominate the segment, the entry of new players has intensified the fight. From Walmart-backed Flipkart’s Minutes to Reliance’s JioMart, deep-pocketed giants are aggressively attempting to capture a larger piece of the pie. The new entrants are spending heavily to expand their dark store networks to compete with early movers. For instance, Flipkart Minutes has scaled to 1,000 dark stores across 130 cities, with brokerage UBS estimating that the platform could add another 1,000 dark stores by mid-2027 ahead of the Big Billion Days sale of 2027. Meanwhile, the biggest incumbent Blinkit continues to lead the category with over 2,600 dark stores across 300 cities. Zepto and Instamart, on the other hand, operate over 1,100 fulfilment centres each. At the heart of all this is the homegrown quick commerce ecosystem, which as per Inc42 data, is projected to become a $40 Bn market opportunity by 2030.

'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia
- Published
Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.
Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".
European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental.
"Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame".
"It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.
'Sex positivity'
Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".
Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.
The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.
Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.
But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.
Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice.
However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.
- Language around birth should be less judgemental 
  - Published15 June 2022
The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen".
Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.
When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame.
"Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.
Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.
'Virginity membrane'
Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.
The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.
The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once.
"With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.
Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".
In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".
She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."
The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."
'Judgmental words'
Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first.
"Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"
New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.
Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.
One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue.
"Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.
Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected.
"Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."
In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.
But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress.
"I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."

Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack
- Published
Australia made a dramatic revelation on Wednesday during the United Nations General Assembly.
Rogue AI agents had hacked one of its government bodies - the first known incident of its kind in the world. Private data, but not sensitive information, was taken from Medicare, Australia's universal healthcare scheme.
The breach happened in June, but OpenAI says it only became aware of it in August - and then took until 10 September to alert Australia's government, by sending an email to an address used by researchers and academics to alert authorities to concerns of vulnerabilities.
While worrying, the timing of the incident is somewhat of a gift for Australia.
A middle power that doesn't usually get as much of a platform as its influential allies, the country wants to be seen as punching above its weight on one of the most defining issues of our time - big tech regulation.
In the past year alone, it has implemented the world's strictest social media ban, announced what it says are the world's strongest algorithm controls, floated the possibility of "world-leading" limits on smart glasses, and is now the first government to confront AI firms over a rogue attack on its data.
It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents.
Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon told the BBC he'd heard whispers that several others have been notified of similar recent breaches by OpenAI agents.
"Some have chosen to not be public – that's every government's choice on how it wants to handle these things," the CyberCX chief strategy officer said. "The [Australian] government chose a time to release this to gain maximum publicity which is their wont to do."
Revealing a data breach can of course be a risky strategy for governments - it leaves them vulnerable to criticism that their security systems aren't up to scratch. But the fact that no sensitive information was leaked put Australia in a stronger position to use the incident.
"Nobody has died," says the University of Queensland's associate professor Michael Noetel, who studies AI risks. "This is another canary in the coal mine. This sort of loss-of-control incident, even though it's minor now, is what CEOs are worried about getting worse over time."
Though Australia has made a name for itself by taking a stand against social media companies, taking up the AI mantle now is another way for Australia to rein in big tech, says Tama Leaver, professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth.
"It's impossible to say for sure, but it seems incredibly likely that this was very carefully planned."
The fact that leaders were all together in New York this week has probably helped.
Albanese says he had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to express Australia's "extreme concern" about what happened. Altman acknowledged "issues with protocols" at OpenAI, he said.
The Australian leader also posed with Donald Trump for a selfie - and the two may have had face-to-face talks. But Australia risks the ire of the US president, who wants to encourage AI, "not rein it in", and even rename it "super intelligence".
Earlier this week, the Albanese had to deflect criticism from the Trump administration over his government's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms. The US said it amounted to "censorship of protected speech".
Back home, Australia's very own eSafety commission is currently arming itself with lawyers, preparing to take on social media platforms objecting to its social media law for under 16s.
Australia isn't popular with big tech. But its bold policies on social media and internet safety have been largely supported among Australians themselves, especially parents.
The government is taking advantage of the hack to position itself as a leader on one of the biggest talking points of our time. And it's wasting no time in using the incident to advance the country's broader crusade.
Within hours of the announcement, Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters: "This is an example of an unregulated industry where big tech clearly feels like they can do whatever they like, and that's not going to wash here in Australia."

Alzheimer’s blood tests are advancing diagnosis. What can they really tell us?
Blood tests such as p-tau217 and p-tau181 can help identify changes linked to Alzheimer’s disease. Neurologists explain what these tests can detect, how they aid diagnosis and what the results can and cannot tell patients
For now, the important question is not simply whether a blood test is positive or negative, but what the result means in the context of the person’s symptoms, clinical assessment and the specific test used.
| Photo Credit: AFP
Changes in the brain linked to Alzheimer’s disease can begin years before memory and other cognitive symptoms appear. Blood-based biomarkers offer a less invasive way to detect some of these biological changes. These include phosphorylated tau (p-tau), such as p-tau217 and p-tau181, and amyloid-beta measures such as the Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio. However, these tests do not directly measure memory loss, brain-cell loss or the severity of cognitive impairment.
Tau is a protein found in nerve cells. In Alzheimer’s disease, abnormal tau is linked to the formation of neurofibrillary tangles. The build-up of amyloid-beta is another biological change associated with the disease.
