Over the past five years, at least three meetings involving all stakeholders were convened to address the occupational safety and health concerns faced by workers in the unorganised sector. However, despite these consultations and a plan for a dedicated policy or guidelines, a comprehensive framework to ensure their health and safety is still pending in Tamil Nadu, with health officials noting that a number of recommendations remained on paper.
With Tamil Nadu witnessing a steady increase in the migrant worker population across various sectors, the need for a comprehensive occupational safety and health (OSH) framework has become increasingly important.
What exists
On its part, the Directorate of Medical and Rural Health Services had created the Occupational, Social and Environmental Health Wing for screening, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation and compensation of the unorganised sector workers including micro, small and medium enterprises and inter-State migrant workers nearly a decade ago. Based on its proposal, the Health department constituted State and district-level inter department co-ordination committees and 21 disease and speciality-specific expert (technical) committees. The wing was later made into the State Nodal Centre for Occupational Health and Safety of Unorganised Workers (SNC-OSH).
Health officials said that the State Planning Commission had convened meetings on OSH of unorganised sector workers during which various aspects were discussed. A wider stakeholder consultation with trade union representatives, employers, NGOs and unorganised workers was suggested. Based on the recommendations of these meetings, the need to formulate a policy was also planned but no headway was made.
Key discussion and action points on OSH in Tamil Nadu
Key focus areas
Among the key focus areas was the health of the unorganised sector workers. Officials had raised the need for the inclusion of basic occupational health services and universal health coverage as per World Health Organization/International Labour Organization standards and mandatory health screening on job entry and regular check ups for all unorganised labourers. Maintenance of log book/health profile for all workers including inter-State migrants employed for over 30 years to track long-term illnesses like silicosis, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, noise-induced hearing loss, contact dermatitis and occupational cancers to ensure health coverage was also put forward.
One of the key action points was that all departments must provide inputs to outline OSH guidelines for unorganised sector labourers. Industrial and economic units should be required to maintain log books, ensure mandatory health screening/check ups for workers. The need to integrate OSH components into all National Health Mission programmes was another key point.
Apart from these, the need for Tamil Nadu to notify 107 diseases/hazards under OSH for unorganised workers [ILO and WHO have notified 107 diseases/hazards under occupational safety and health administration], sensitisation of workers on NCD management and conducting medical camps for NCD screening were among the other discussion points.
Independent OSH cell
A source privy to these meetings said that a series of discussions were held and one of the proposals was to have a slightly independent OSH cell. “It should have a broader perspective and a larger compass to operate on. This is an important area but least attended to. New industries are coming up and new problems will crop up. It is better to have a Standard Operating Procedure in the beginning to protect workers’ health,” he said.

Pharmacy-focused quick commerce startup Rio Health has raised $4.5 Mn (around ₹43 Cr) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Version One Ventures. Existing investors Xeed Ventures, Good Capital and Amplify also participated in the all-equity round. The startup intends to use the fresh capital to expand its presence across Delhi NCR by setting up 12 more dark stores as well as strengthen its tech abilities across ordering, inventory and delivery operations. The startup is also targeting an annual recurring revenue (ARR) of more than ₹150 Cr over the next nine to 12 months. “This funding will help us strengthen our technology, improve how we predict neighbourhood-level demand, and make reliable medicine delivery available to many more customers across Delhi NCR,” said Rio Health cofounder Ankur Agrawal. Founded by Agrawal and Amit Ahuja, Rio Health delivers medicines and healthcare essentials in Delhi NCR within 20-30 minutes. Customers can place orders by typing or speaking in Hindi, English or Hinglish, or by uploading a photograph of a prescription. The startup’s AI system identifies the medicines prescribed and creates an order, which is subsequently verified by a licensed pharmacist. Rio Health currently processes more than 30,000 orders a month, with an average order value of ₹600-700. The startup claims that nearly 80% of its orders come from repeat customers. Rio Health currently offers access to more than 20,000 SKUs, while long-tail medicines are sourced through its distributor network. Its dark stores serve a radius of around three kilometres, with neighbourhood-level demand data used to forecast medicine requirements and stock its stores accordingly. Prior to the latest round, Rio Health had raised ₹19.2 Cr across earlier funding rounds. The latest investment takes its total funding raised to ₹62.2 Cr ($6.5 Mn). The fundraise comes as quick commerce players and specialised startups are stepping up their bets on faster medicine delivery, even as the category comes with higher operational and regulatory complexities than grocery within the booming quick commerce market. Broadly, the Indian quick commerce market is expected to become a $30 Bn to $40 Bn opportunity in the next three to five years. Quick commerce players are expected to clock $68 Bn in gross merchandise value (GMV) by 2031, up from $8.3 Bn in 2026 — an almost 8X rise at a 52% CAGR. Quick commerce giants Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart are already exploring 10-minute medicine delivery as they look beyond grocery for higher-value categories. However, unlike grocery, pharma requires licensed entities, prescription verification and tighter controls around inventory, storage and fulfilment. The complexity has also created room for specialised players. Plazza, which operates technology-enabled neighbourhood pharmacies, raised $15 Mn in July 2026 to strengthen its technology and AI-led inventory systems and expand beyond its two Bengaluru stores.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.

— Vikas Pandey (Sankrityayan) (@MODIfiedVikas) June 9, 2024
We also found an X post from 2015 where Bhatt can be seen with the Prime Minister.

— Vishnu Dhanuka (Modi ka Parivar) (@VishnuDhanuka) July 2, 2015
In April 2022, Right-wing influencer Shefali Vaidya, who has been fact-checked by Alt News several times in the past, posted an image with Bhatt on X saying that she had met the latter and “his lovely family” in Uttarakhand.
No Uttarakhand trip would have been complete without meeting @alok_bhatt and his lovely family! pic.twitter.com/1QHMaJk9OY

X Handle Suspended for Violating Guidelines
Alt News found at least three instances, in 2018, 2019, and 2020, where X (then Twitter) had initiated action against Bhatt’s handle for violation of community guidelines, and at least two of those three actions were owing to hateful content.
In 2018, Bhatt declared that all the “killers of Pandits, Rapists of Pandits, Terrorists killing in Kashmir, instigators of Godhra, and bombers of Mumbai were all Muslims, and thus Islam was the problem”. His account had then been ‘limited’.
Why is @alok_bhatt blocked by twitter for a week when blue-ticked racist bigots like Audrey Truschke are still on Twitter despite their naked Hinduphobia? @TwitterIndia pic.twitter.com/3qlnNiVWhj

In 2019, Bhatt declared in a post that “their boys could take on Jihadis” but needed police action for “rumour mongers” like activist Shehla Rashid. “These jihadi accomplices are running a hate campaign aided and abetted by Media…please help our state dispel rumours,” the tweet read. His account was suspended after this. Political analyst and Right-wing influencer Suresh Nakhua took to Twitter to condemn the move.

— संवैधानिक डकैत (@Shivam_h9) May 29, 2020
The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.
ठीक 2 साल पहले देहरादून में आज ही के दिन @Pamphlet_in ऑफिस निर्माण की शुरुआत हो गई थी, उत्तराखण्ड चुनाव निपटने के बाद मैं २० दिन के अपने नैनीताल और लैंसडाउन प्रवास के बाद दून घाटी में उतरा था।
आज ही के दिन साल 2019 में लोकसभा चुनाव का रिजल्ट भी आया था और प्रधानमंत्री… pic.twitter.com/6lAVSW3twN
— V Ashish Nautiyal (@ashu_nauty) May 15, 2024
The Pamphlet claims to “cut through the noise of the modern information ecosystem by offering readers and viewers clarity, depth and perspective on issues that shape India and the world.” Its reports have seem to be echoing pro-BJP narratives. An August 11 video report, for instance, was captioned: “Questions raised in the public domain regarding the credentials of two CJP leaders, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, have brought up several serious concerns”. It questioned Dipke’s Boston University degree, academic timeline and funding, as well as Das’ property, tenancy, rent, police verification, and electoral records.
During the CJP protests, another report took a swipe at Mohammed Junaid, who had been feeding protesters, with the reporter noting that “such bhaijaans were also seen” at the protest sites in Shaheen Bagh and Farmers’ stir. Thumbnails of these reports carried AI-generated visuals of individuals critical of the Union government, their faces distorted through AI to portray them in a negative light. This is a tactic common across Right-wing outlets and social media troll handles.
More recently, the outlet, alongside Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, Law Beat, The Jaipur Dialogues and The Sunday Guardian, was summoned by the Delhi high court over a Rs 2 crore privacy suit by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das, who alleged that they had disclosed his home address and other personal details online. The case will be heard on September 14.
The video below depicts a time when the outlet was still called The Indian Affairs, and Nautiyal (in striped shirt) can be seen with his colleagues alongside educator Pawan Gupta.
The Indian Affairs @ForIndiaMatters Coming Soon
Subscribe our Youtube Channel: https://t.co/orjioxscXy #TIA #TheIndianAffairs pic.twitter.com/v1VVtf83XZ
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) July 22, 2022
Nautiyal’s last video with The Pamphlet was uploaded in December 2024. In June 2025, Nautiyal was pictured with the OpIndia team. His first video for OpIndia, an interview with Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Dhami, came a month later, in July 2025.
Nautiyal is now the multimedia & digital head and editor at OpIndia, and is no longer listed as a director of Savitr on the MCA website.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. Its ‘About Us’ page offers only a description of what it does, while calling itself ‘an independent digital media platform’. The only publicly mentioned funding source we could find was YouTube memberships of The Pamphlet costing Rs. 119 to Rs. 3199 per month.
Nautiyal is not the only link between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet. An individual named Shiv Kumar Mishra was appointed the director of Savitr Analytics in April 2023. In March 2023, Mishra was announced as the CEO of The Pamphlet.
Please welcome @shivkmishr, Founder & CEO, The Pamphlet https://t.co/U53aK62Fzo
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) March 14, 2023
In other words, two of the three directors of Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. And in both cases, the appointments to Savitr and The Pamphlet came in close succession. This raises the question of whether the two entities are formally linked.
We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

After a nearly monthlong delay, states are now able to order this season’s COVID-19 vaccines through a federal program that provides free immunizations to low-income children, the US health department says. Trump officials have still not provided a clear explanation for the delay, raising concerns about meddling from anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
On Wednesday, Ars Technica reported that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had still not opened ordering for 2026–2027 COVID-19 vaccines through the Vaccines for Children program. That was despite the vaccines having been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in late August.
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told Ars on Wednesday that “CDC has not yet finalized procurement decisions” for the shots. The department’s statement further suggested Trump officials were questioning whether children should receive them. “HHS and CDC are committed to responsible stewardship of taxpayer resources and to ensuring that vaccines purchased through federally funded programs are appropriate for the populations those programs serve,” the department said.
However, The Washington Post reported late Wednesday that ordering was opening. An unnamed source told the Post that part of the reason the vaccine ordering was held up was a delay in finalizing the CDC’s clinical guidance, which is written for health care professionals and public health officials. The guidance reportedly needed to be reviewed by an external expert.
Lingering questions
The Post also reported that CDC career officials had previously finished preparations for making the vaccines available. All Trump officials needed to do was essentially push a button to open ordering, sources said. Further, a spokesperson for the Minnesota Department of Health suggested to the Post that CDC leadership was behind the hold, saying the state had been told “that CDC leadership approval is needed before distribution of the vaccine can begin.”

In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
- Published
For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.
As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.
Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table.
"A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department.
"When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."
The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.
The state health department told the BBC it has administered nearly 4,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at pop-up clinics near the epicentre of the outbreak since it began in late April.
But even as health officials see success in their vaccine programmes, the state has reported four deaths from measles complications, marking the most deadly outbreak the US has seen since 1992.
The infections have led to tensions between state and federal health officials, including vaccine-skeptic Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
Those politics are back of mind in the Amish community, where people are growing fearful of more deaths as they watch their friends and family fall sick with the disease, which for decades has been eliminated in the US.
"They're not a community that's as easy to reach - we can't just put up a social media post," Weiser said. "They are suffering at the moment, and we're trying to reach out and make connections."
Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.
About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.
There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said.
"A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.
Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated.
"Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."
He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials.
Boots on the ground
Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.
Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings.
"People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"
The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.
In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.
Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it.
"You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.
People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.
But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children.
"There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."
Kennedy casts doubt on deaths
The ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has once again sparked political debate in the US.
After the state health department announced the first two deaths - both in infants - Kennedy, the top health official, took to social media to dispute at least one of the deaths. The BBC has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.
Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro took aim at Kennedy, saying he told the top US health official that he was spreading misinformation that was worsening the outbreak.
Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican, has said one of the two infants died of a ruptured spleen rather than measles itself. Measles can cause the spleen to enlarge, making it more likely to rupture. Several doctors have said the measles infection made the child vulnerable.
"I think the measles very much contributed to that child's demise," said William Moss, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Public health experts said a number of actions taken by Kennedy and the Trump administration have sowed doubts about vaccine safety and worsened outbreaks.
Last month, Trump passed an executive order recommending the MMR shot be split into three separate shots, a move doctors say is costly and unnecessary for a vaccine that is already safe.
"What he's doing is casting doubt," said Dr Moss. "He basically said the vaccine could be dangerous in its current combined form."
The tensions are not helpful for experts working to combat misinformation in a so-far unrelenting outbreak, they said. They worry for the start of the school year, which will provide even more opportunities for the highly contagious virus to spread.
"I think we're in this for six to 12 months. It does feel like it's spreading and accelerating," Weiser said. "We're in community transmission now. We can't stop it easily."

Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MLA from Agra's Fatehabad constituency, Chotelal Verma, died on Thursday at a hospital in Noida, PTI reported. He was 73.
Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath paid tribute to Verma in a post on X, describing his death as "extremely sad". He prayed to Lord Shri Ram to grant salvation to the departed soul and strength to Verma's family to bear the loss.
Verma was first elected as an MLA from the Fatehabad constituency in 1993 on a BJP ticket at the age of 40. He contested the 1996 election on a BJP ticket but lost to Janata Dal's Vijay Pal Singh. He returned to the assembly in 2002 after winning the seat on a BJP ticket.
Verma's political legacy
He contested the 2007 election on a Samajwadi Party (SP) ticket but was unsuccessful. He later joined the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) and won the Fatehabad seat in 2012. Verma subsequently returned to the BJP and won the constituency for a fourth time in 2022, securing more than 50,000 votes.
According to Live Hindustan, in 2008, Verma was appointed vice-chairman of the Ramganga Command Project, Kanpur-Lucknow, a position carrying the rank of a minister of state. In May 2009, he was appointed chairman of the Uttar Pradesh State Integration Council, a post carrying the rank of deputy minister.
Verma is survived by three sons and three daughters.
Final rites at ancestral village
His son Mahendra Verma told Live Hindustan that after a post-mortem in Noida, Verma's body reached Agra at around 3 am on Friday. The final viewing will take place at the family's residence in Vibhav Nagar until around 3 pm, after which his body will be taken to his ancestral village, Nagla Devhans.
Verma was overseeing the construction of a temple in the village. His body will be kept at the temple premises for people to pay their last respects before his last rites are performed with state honours at a cremation ground on the banks of the Yamuna.

How Carsley aims to lead England to U21 glory - for third time in row
- Published
Lee Carsley has yet to get his picture on the wall at St George's Park.
At England's base, there are framed photographs of every senior England manager, which line opposite sides of a corridor. All of them - from Walter Winterbottom to Sam Allardyce, who was in charge for only one game - are included.
Despite winning back-to-back European Championships with England Under-21s, however, the Young Lions boss is still absent. He even managed the senior side for six games after Gareth Southgate's departure.
Yet Carsley is not concerned with personal accolades as he plots a treble with the under-21s.
Victories against Kazakhstan, at Wolves' Molineux Stadium on Friday, and Slovakia next week will book a spot at Euro 2027 - and keep Carsley and his players on course for history.
Embracing the expectation of two-time champions
England lifted successive trophies in 1982 and 1984 but then had to wait 39 years until Carsley's men won in Georgia and Romania in 2023, beating Spain in the final.
Last summer's extra-time victory over Germany in Bratislava sealed their title defence, thanks to Jonathan Rowe's strike.
Winning the tournament three times in a row has only ever been done once before, by Italy in the 1990s, although never in the competition's current guise of 16 teams.
Carsley is aware of the challenge ahead - but also the lasting impact more success could have.
"The older you get, you want to leave a legacy, don't you?" He said, with England top of Group D and three points clear of Slovakia.
"There would have been an easy move, after the first win, to go and do club management and go and accept a few of the offers.
"But I enjoy the job I'm doing and I enjoy that I'm part of a bigger quest to win a major tournament. I want to be part of the FA when we do that."
Carsley also says he welcomes the pressure of attempting to do something no Young Lions team has done before.
"I think we have to embrace that," said the former Everton and Derby midfielder. "They come to play for the under-21s, you're back-to-back champions. There's a bullseye that goes with that. We have to be aware of that and go for it.
"The expectancy, we'll just get through the group and then we'll win the quarters, we'll win the semis and then we'll just win the final... it's very difficult.
"My priority is definitely qualifying and then that's something I'll think about."

England started their qualifying campaign with a 2-0 win in Kazakhstan last September, although they have not played since beating Moldova in March.
The Young Lions host Slovakia in Stoke on 2 October before travelling to Cork to wrap up Group D against Ireland four days later.

Like Lewis, there are plenty of recognisable names within the current squad, including Tottenham's Archie Gray and Dortmund's Jobe Bellingham.

Noni Madueke, who featured in this year's World Cup, could not even get in the starting XI.

They only won Group F by a point in Euro 2025 qualifying, needing two late goals by James McAtee to beat Ukraine in their penultimate game to take the race for top spot to the final match.
They then beat Azerbaijan 7-0, as Ukraine lost 1-0 to Serbia, to overhaul their rivals and top the group.
Carsley is refusing to take anything for granted this time.
"We can't just be arrogant and think, we'll just turn up, we've got better players," he said.
"We've got to make sure we constantly make these players aware we are a big scalp, this is a chance for them to make a big deal in their own country, so it's important mentally and physically you're ready to challenge.
"It's very difficult to qualify. I've never known an easy qualification process, but sometimes you forget - when you're on the pitch and you've got the trophy in your hands - the journey you've gone on to get there."

To establish a comprehensive framework for registration of allied and healthcare professionals (AHP) in both the State Registers and the Central Register, the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions (NCAHP) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare notified the Registration of Allied and Healthcare Professionals Regulations, 2026 on August 31, 2026, and published it in the Gazette of India on September 15, 2026.
(Sign up for THEdge, The Hindu’s weekly education newsletter.)
Under the new regulations, all allied and healthcare professionals spanning 57 vocations across 10 broad disciplines, including physiotherapists, dietitians, lab technologists, forensic psychologists, among others, will soon have to register in the State and Central registers to practise in their chosen fields.
Registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the Unique Identification (UID) number and a secure QR code, will be issued to the professionals by the Commission or the respective State Council. This will facilitate identification and verification of registered professionals and support greater transparency in the delivery of allied and healthcare services. The registration and payment of the fee will be processed on a dedicated online portal developed by the Commission.
“These regulations mark a leap towards streamlining the allied and healthcare workforce. Unless and until the professional gets the UID, he/she will not be able to practise/work. There is a penalty of up to 6 months to two years’ jail term under the NCAHP Act-21 if the professional practices without registration,” Dr. Yagna Unmesh Shukla, chairperson of NCAHP said.
“The regulations also aim to bring uniformity in the registration of allied and healthcare professionals and ensure renewal. With this registration, the actual number of qualified professionals will be available, as well as the difference between qualified and non-qualified professionals, which is also one of the key objectives of the NCAHP Act-21,” she added.
Public access
Highlighting that the registration process is the first of its kind in the history of allied and healthcare professions, Dr. Shukla says that the regulations provide a real-time synchronisation between the State Registers and the Central Register through an integrated online system.
Further, the Central and State Registers will be accessible to the public through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils, which will display the prescribed particulars of registered professionals.
Since only persons meeting the prescribed eligibility requirements, including recognised qualifications and the applicable exit examination requirements, will be eligible for regular registration, this will provide an important safeguard for patients and service users by promoting the practice of appropriately qualified professionals.
The public will be able to verify the registration status and relevant details of allied and healthcare professionals through the websites of the Commission and the respective State Councils. Professionals residing in a State or Union Territory where a functional State Council has not yet been established may register directly with the Central Register.
A key feature of the Regulations is the flexibility they give to allied and healthcare professionals to register in one State and practise in another State. “This will mitigate the hassles professionals face when applying for registration in another state. All they now need to do is fill out the form and inform the state in which they reside of the state where they intend to practise, so that this information remains on record. Since each registered professional is provided with a UID number, all their records are documented, facilitating the smooth transfer of registration details from one state to another,” Dr. Shukla said.
Apart from registration certificates, including digital certificates featuring the UID and a secure QR code, registered allied and healthcare professionals will also have access to a Good Standing Certificate. It will help professionals pursue any foreign education or profession or participate in student exchange programmes outside India. “There is a big difference between registration and a Good Standing Certificate. Registration is the licence to practise in India, whereas a Certificate of Good Standing is issued by the State Council when required by various countries for professionals who wish to work or study in those countries,” Dr. Shukla says.
Registration of foreign-qualified professionals
The Regulations establish a pathway for Indian citizens holding foreign qualifications in allied and healthcare. A foreign-qualified allied and healthcare professional will be considered eligible to apply for registration provided his qualification is recognised by the Commission, or he has completed the prescribed credential equivalency evaluation, and has also passed the relevant exit examination, where applicable. “It is important to have an equivalence process of foreign qualified professionals in place for the safety of the patients,” Dr. Shukla adds.
There is also provision for temporary registration for eligible foreign-qualified Indian professionals for specific, time-bound purposes, including postgraduate or specialty education, fellowships, clinical research, observerships, advanced workshops, expert visits, and voluntary community service. Such registration remains subject to the conditions laid down in the Regulations and applicable regulatory guidelines.
Validity period
Under the regulations, the registration will remain valid for five years, renewable upon the fulfilment of Continuing Professional Development (CPD) requirements through approved online and offline modes. This means that professionals must upgrade themselves professionally (15 hours per year) by attending seminars, conferences, workshops, training programmes and faculty development programmes.
“It is important for professionals to update and upgrade themselves in their respective professions. Since the regulations are being implemented for the first time, flexibility in the CPD programme is being permitted. This explains why 50% of these participations in online mode are being considered,” Dr. Shukla said.
Additionally, the Commission is making efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications. Such professionals will be provided with an option to undergo a bridge course to attain eligibility for regular registration. The Commission is making concerted efforts to introduce provisional registration for professionals currently practising in the allied and healthcare sector who lack the prescribed primary qualifications.
“Those who are practising for many years and are not qualified as per the provisions of the Act will be registered under the Provisional Registration Act and will have to undergo a prescribed Bridge course within the given time period to attain eligibility for regular registration,” Dr. Shukla said.
Interim registrations
The Regulations have also introduced provisions for interim registration for students enrolled in recognised institutions who are undertaking internships, clinical training, observerships, or practical coursework required to complete an allied and healthcare qualification. Interim registration must be initiated by the recognised institution and obtained from the concerned State Council. No fee will be charged for interim registration applications, the NCAHP regulations stated.

Karnataka on Tuesday (September 22) launched a State action plan aimed at reducing population salt intake by 30% by 2030 and promoting healthier dietary habits as part of efforts to prevent non-communicable diseases (NCDs).
The Karnataka State Multisectoral Action Plan for Salt Reduction and Promotion of Healthy Dietary Habits focuses on reducing salt consumption at three levels — households, food consumed outside the home, and processed and packaged foods. It also seeks to encourage healthier food choices and strengthen dietary counselling through the health system.
The plan proposes measures to reduce the use of discretionary salt, encourage food manufacturers to reduce salt in processed and packaged foods, and promote awareness of healthier diets. It also envisages strengthening research and evidence on potassium-enriched low-sodium salt.
The action plan seeks to align Karnataka’s efforts with India’s commitment to the global target of reducing population salt intake by 30% by 2030, while encouraging progress towards the World Health Organisation (WHO) recommendation of less than five grams of salt per person per day.
TAG meeting
Health Minister U.T. Khader launched the plan at a Technical Advisory Group (TAG) meeting at Vidhana Soudha. Former Health Minister Dinesh Gundu Rao and Rajya Sabha member Mansoor Ali Khan were present.
The TAG was constituted under the chairpersonship of Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences (RGUHS) Vice-Chancellor Bhagavan B.C. to provide technical guidance and support evidence-based action on salt reduction and healthier dietary practices.
The TAG brings together experts and representatives from the State Health department, Sri Jayadeva Institute of Cardiovascular Sciences and Research, NIMHANS, academic and nutrition institutions, and public health organisations including the Institute of Public Health (IPH), Resolve to Save Lives and Vision for Social Development.
The Minister said the plan would build on existing initiatives, including salt-reduction measures under PM POSHAN, dietary counselling through Gruha Arogya and dietary risk-factor counselling under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD).
State steering committee
Mr. Khader called for a State Steering Committee involving multiple departments to ensure coordinated and sustained action on healthier diets. Karnataka has already introduced measures addressing foods high in fat, sugar and salt, providing a basis for strengthening healthier food environments, the government said.
Jayadeva institute director Dinesha B. participated in the technical deliberations and stressed the need for coordinated action to address dietary risk factors.
Jnanesh Kamath, State Joint Director, presented the key priorities, objectives and proposed actions under the State plan. Raghunandan, State Deputy Director - Non-Communicable Diseases (NCD), Amrut Kadam of RGUHS; U.S. Vishal Rao, member of the Consultative Group to the Principal Scientific Adviser to the Government of India; Syed Imran Farooq, Executive Director, and Manika Sharma, Principal Advisor, Food Policy, Resolve to Save Lives; and Amit Karnik, Director, Vision for Social Development, were among those present.

Thiruvananthapuram, TDB president K Jayakumar on Friday met Devaswom Minister K Muraleedharan and briefed him on preparations for the upcoming Sabarimala pilgrimage season.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Muraleedharan said the government and the TDB would work together to ensure that devotees do not face difficulties during the pilgrimage season.
"The Board and the government are working together. He has given an assurance that this season's pilgrimage will be made smoothly. Therefore, there is no scope for apprehension. We will move forward together," the minister said.

'Like our sweatshirts?'
The news comes in the wake of the backlash over a photo Smith had posted to Facebook on her way to Halifax, in which she and three family members pose wearing "Lake America" sweatshirts that Smith later said were AI-generated.
"Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will," said the Sept. 11 photo originally posted by Smith, and later shared by her sister, followed by "lol lol."
- Michigan tourist who posted about wearing 'Lake America' sweatshirts to Halifax says it was AI
- 'Lake America' change highlights Canada's reliance on U.S. tech
Judging by the reaction online, just weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" amid the trade war between the two countries, Canadians were not lol-ing.
In a previous interview with ABC12 News in Michigan, Smith said the image was AI-generated and meant to be a joke.
"We weren't trying to make a political statement," Smith told the news outlet.
"However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun at the fact that, you know, one of the Great Lakes's names were getting changed."
She further explained that the sweatshirts weren't real, saying she ran a photo of them through ChatGPT to add the "Lake America" gear, then posted it to her private Facebook page with an AI label.
When they arrived in Halifax, it was her sister who reposted it publicly, added the comment and didn't include the AI warning, Smith said.
"We never had actual sweatshirts. We never wore sweatshirts."
There's been ongoing backlash over Trump's proposed name-change on both sides of the border. Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canadians will call it Lake Ontario "now and always." In the U.S., three members of Congress have introduced a bill aimed at stopping Trump's renaming, titled "Hands off our Great Lakes."

The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

On a cold February morning, Jassuram Khanna, a farmer from Sujau village in Chakrata in Uttarakhand, felt a tightness in his chest on his way to the market. After waiting a few minutes, he called his son Suresh to come and take him to the doctor. They hired a private car and went to the local Primary Health Centre (PHC), where the health worker checked his blood pressure and sent him to Vikasnagar, a nearby Tehsil town.
On reaching Vikasnagar’s Community Health Centre (CHC), 55 km away, they found no doctor there. Finally, at around 3 pm, they found help at the Swami Vivekanand Charitable Hospital in Dharamwala, about 70 km from their hometown. This is where Jassuram finally got an electrocardiogram (ECG) done, which indicated he had suffered a heart attack. The doctors rushed him for an angiography, where they found he had a 100% blockage in one of his heart vessels. They performed an angioplasty where a balloon was sent to the blocked heart blood vessel to widen it, and a mesh tube called a stent was placed there. The time taken from his first symptoms at 10:30 am to his first ECG was 4.5 hours, and it would be another 40 minutes before he the angioplasty procedure was done.
The ideal time that guidelines recommend for a patient with a heart attack to get an ECG and have it interpreted is 10 minutes of contact with a medical team.
Jassuram’s long journey for an ECG is typical of what patients in rural areas face.
While poor access to healthcare in rural India is a well-known fact, does living in a city guarantee timely care? In December 2025, Usha Amin, a retired teacher, felt breathless for two consecutive days on her morning walk; she found her pulse to be 33 on her electronic BP machine (normal pulse being 60-80beats/min). Alarmed, she called her son and rushed to the nearest multispecialty hospital in Thane, which falls in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region.
An ECG showed Usha had developed a third degree heart block, a serious condition where the electrical signals from the upper chambers of the heart are completely blocked from reaching the lower chambers of the heart that can lead to cardiac arrest. However the doctor on duty informed them that the cardiologist was unavailable at the moment. Since Amin looked stable, the family was told that there was no need to worry, and she was advised to schedule an appointment with the cardiologist and return the next day. Amin’s daughter, an occupational therapist, realised the possible gravity of the extremely low pulse rate and asked them to go to another hospital’s emergency department, which correctly diagnosed her. They immediately admitted her and fitted her with a temporary pacemaker and scheduled her for surgery to fit a permanent pacemaker the next day. “I feel extremely lucky that my mother did not face complications due to the delay, and we could refer her to another hospital,” her daughter Kritika Amin said.
Heart disease is the most common cause of death in India, accounting for 28.6 lakh deaths according to the Global Burden of Disease, 2021. It is estimated that nearly 27% of all deaths in India are due to heart disease, while 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease (CVD) in the country are premature between the ages of 40 and 69 years. In 2014, the World Economic Forum and Harvard School of Public Health estimated India’s economic loss due to CVD between 2012 and 2030 to be approximately $2.17 trillion--about half of India’s 2025 GDP of $4.5 trillion. Yet, despite the rapid development of medical facilities in the country, there remains a lacuna when it comes to an appropriate and timely response to emergency heart conditions. Here, we look at the various gaps in the healthcare system that delay treatment for heart disease and the cost that we pay for it.
Most PHCs not equipped
The first step in diagnosing a heart attack is undergoing an ECG test, which records the heart’s electrical activity using sticky patches called electrodes, and gives out a report as a wave graph. This test can help diagnose heart attacks, irregular heartbeats (arrhythmias) and problems with blood flow. An ECG can detect a heart attack as ST-segment elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) cases -- or non-STEMI within minutes, and help doctors plan further treatment. However, even access to this ECG is not common in India.
ECGs are currently available in district hospitals and community health centres in India, which are tertiary healthcare centres. Most primary health centres (PHCs), which are the first point of contact for patients in rural areas and are equipped with medical officers, do not have ECG machines. While the 2025 National Essential Diagnostic List recommends that ECG be available at the PHC level, its implementation is expected to take time, time which millions in India do not have.
Meanwhile the availability in higher centres is also not guaranteed. “ECGs are not available in many of the CHCs here and patients have to travel all the way to the district hospital (2-3 hours away) to get an ECG done, ” said a doctor who works at a non-profit in the tribal district of Surguja in north Chhattisgarh. 
Despite being comparatively inexpensive and easy to conduct, the availability of ECGs is restricted to big metros and hospitals in India, and there is a shortage of trained personnel to interpret the results, says Yogendra Singh, director-interventional cardiology at Max Healthcare, Dehradun. “If a patient gets chest pain in Uttarkashi [in Uttarakhand], he has to travel at least 40-50 km to get an ECG done without which he cannot even be given an Ecospirin [a blood thinner]”, he says, emphasising the need to make ECGs available and accessible to people to detect heart attacks early.
Doctors are not necessary to be present to read the ECGs, several studies (here and here) have shown how tele-ECGs, conducted by frontline health workers, can be electronically sent to doctors and nurses for further interpretation and advice, saving crucial time and money, in reaching higher centres.
Heart attack mortality
Indians suffer from heart disease about 10 years before the Western population, while our deaths due to heart attacks is twice that of Sweden, even as their patients are 15 years older, said S. Ramakrishnan, senior cardiologist at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi.
While the average age at first heart attack in Western Europe, China, and Hong Kong is 63 years, it is 53 years in South Asia, and about 10% of our patients are below the age of 40 years. A number of factors, like high blood pressure, poor cholesterol control, diabetes, sedentary lifestyles, high abdominal fat, poor diet, as well as genetic factors, play a role, along with lifestyle factors such as smoking and prolonged stress. Poverty also plays a role -- poor people are more likely to consume tobacco and alcohol and not consume fruits, vegetables, fish and fibre -- and this increases risk for heart disease.
What’s worse is that most people do not know that they are at risk for heart disease due to inadequate screening and poor awareness. “In India, major heart attacks and death are often the first symptoms of heart disease,” said Dr. Ramakrishnan. Despite having 315 million with high blood pressure and 101 million with diabetes according to the Indian Council of Medical Research’s INDIAB study, there is low awareness of blood pressure and blood glucose, even among those with the disease, and 57% of the population does not meet the WHO guidelines for physical activity.
Further, various studies have shown that patients with heart disease in India have a higher proportion of STEMI cases. STEMI is a more severe type of heart attack caused by the complete blockage of a coronary artery, restricting blood to the major part of the heart and requiring urgent emergency care. The studies also show that STEMI patients in India are likely to be poorer, show symptoms late, get inappropriate treatment and have a higher likelihood of dying within a month of the first month.
While timely treatment of STEMI cases in India will improve the quality of life and also save lives, “the most common treatment an average Indian gets for a heart attack is no treatment,” says Dr. Ramakrishnan. Either patients do not reach the hospital in time, or the hospitals they reach do not have the infrastructure or expertise to treat heart attacks, he added. Late treatment increases the risk of death and complications, increases chances of muscle damage and even if the patient survives, he or she ends up having heart failure, adds.
‘Time is muscle’
When it comes to the heart, cardiologists often like to use the phrase ‘time is muscle.’ Every minute of delay in getting treatment causes irreversible death of the heart muscle. Restoring blood supply to the heart can reduce damage to the heart, improve survival rates and prevent deaths.
In STEMI cases, for example, the key treatment is reperfusion, which involves opening the blocked blood vessel. This can be done either by giving thrombolytic therapy, which is drugs that bust the clots in the artery or through primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or an angioplasty. While PCI is the gold standard of treatment, a very small percentage of Indian patients get PCI as treatment, and even getting thrombolytic therapy in the treatment window is not widespread. Various registry databases show that only 5 to 10 in 100 patients undergo timely PCI while 36-60 out of 100 undergo thrombolysis.
Another approach of combining the two, is called pharmaco-invasive therapy, where thrombolytic drugs are given to the patient till the patient can be transferred to a hospital with a cath lab. This has been successfully implemented as a hub-and-spoke model in many parts of the country.
In other cases such as in conduction defects, cardiac muscle dies because of the irregular pumping of the heart. Immediately addressing this via drugs or a temporary pacemaker ensures that the damage to the heart muscle is kept to a minimum.
In case of any emergency heart condition, detecting and treating immediately is of paramount importance to ensure that as much of the heart muscle as possible can be saved.
Treatment windows
The most critical time for intervention is between 1-3 hours of the heart attack. The ideal time to conduct an angioplasty is within 120 minutes or two hours of the first medical contact. Treatment most beneficial within three hours of a heart attack.
Jassuram and his son had to waste four and half precious hours travelling from one centre to another before getting the treatment that could save his life.Most Indian patients reach the hospital between 6 hours on average, and up to 12 hours in the hilly States of India, according to various heart registries, after suffering significant damage to their heart muscles. A study in Denmark has shown that a one hour delay in starting treatment after the first contact in the health system leads to a 15% increase in deaths within three-and-a-half years, while it is doubled if the delay is of three hours.
Treatment window in the Indian context
| Metric | Target time | Description |  | 
| Door-to-Needle (Thrombolysis) | ≤30 minutes | From hospital arrival to starting thrombolysis at spoke/non-PCI centres |  | 
| Door-to-Balloon (primary PCI) | ≤90 minutes | Arrival at PCI-capable hub to balloon inflation |  | 
| First Medical Contact (FMC) to Reperfusion | ≤120 minutes | FMC to PCI or thrombolysis; ≤90 min preferred for direct PCI |  | 
| Symptom Onset to Reperfusion | Within 12 hours | Best <6 hours; pharmacoinvasive PCI 3-24 hours post-thrombolysis |  | 
| First Medical Contact-to-Needle (prehospital) | ≤120 minutes | Community-level goal for thrombolysis initiation |  |

Why the delays
Lack of awareness: A 2023 study, which audited civil-registered premature (30–69 years) deaths due to acute cardiac events or strokes in Faridabad, Haryana, found that only about 11% of the patients reached an appropriate health facility within one hour. About 4 in 10 of them did not reach the correct facility due to a delay in recognising the symptom or its seriousness; 2 in 10 did not reach the correct facility due to a delay in reaching the hospital -- due to lack of transport, absence of an attendant or reaching a centre without appropriate facilities -- and lastly 1 in 10 due to unaffordability or lack of a specialist.
This was similar to what was found by analysing the results of the CREATE registry -- a prospective study of 20,937 acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients across 89 Indian hospitals between 2001-2005 -- poor awareness of symptoms, logistical challenges in reaching the hospitals and health system gaps were key reasons patients got delayed treatment.
“Sometimes there is ignorance, sometimes there is denial, [patients think] that it will get relieved with local treatment or an antacid,” says H. S. Isser, professor and head of cardiology, at Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, Delhi. If the heart attack is very severe, the patient may collapse and is immediately rushed to the nearest hospital, but if the symptoms are mild, like sweating, pain and breathlessness, patients often try home remedies and wait for one or two hours before reaching the hospital, he notes.
Lack of cath labs in public settings, over-crowded tertiary care centres: Even when patients reach hospitals, many hospitals are not equipped with ECG machines or the manpower to interpret them. Even if ECGs are available, patients are often referred to higher centres that have cardiologists and cath labs, where angioplasties are conducted. There are about 2,500 cath labs in the country, most of them in the metros of the developed States of Maharashtra, Kerala, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and New Delhi.
Thrombolysis use is also limited because non-specialist doctors do not want to risk giving clot-busting drugs, which can have side effects like internal bleeding, without the presence of cardiologists. There are about 6,500 cardiologists in India, less than 0.45 per 100,000 population and most of them are concentrated in urban cities.
Also, despite the increasing number of cath labs, 90% of them are in the private sector, and most States, especially in the North and the East, have to make-do with having only one tertiary centre in the State capital with a cath lab-- leading to overcrowding and long waiting times for patients.
Unaffordability: Even if the treatment is accessible and available, the question that bogs down most families is how expensive it would be. Given the lack of diagnostic facilities in the public sector and long waiting lines, most patients rely on private hospitals for hospitalisation of cardiac conditions, but this has led to high out-of-pocket expenses in patients. Nearly half of heart patients experience catastrophic health expenses -- when the health expense is greater than 40% of the family’s annual income -- due to hospitalisation, while 43% face it due to outpatient expenses.
The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PM JAY), India’s flagship health insurance scheme, has improved access to heart procedures that were out of reach for average Indians -- the rate of angioplasties rose by 61% and angiographies by 132% -- after the launch of the scheme in Kashmir, notes a 2025 study. While this is a welcome change, there is an over-reliance on the private sector -- 79% of all cardiac procedures under the scheme are conducted in the private sector. This has led to cases of malpractice on one hand and denial of the scheme on the other -- hospitals in several States have protested nonpayment of dues and refused to provide treatment under PMJAY, leaving millions without coverage.
Many patients we met outside Delhi’s public hospitals claimed to have been told the scheme is not available in the private hospitals in their districts, which forced them to seek care in crowded public hospitals, even if they face delays. One patient, 57-year-old Raiz, suffered a heart attack on December 30 in Bulandshahr’s Shikarpur but came all the way to Delhi government’s Govind Ballabh Pant Hospital 100 km away, because the treatment would be free of cost. Raiz, a labourer, had first done preliminary tests including an ECG and 2D ECHO at Jaypee Hospital, Chitta, but refused further treatment when he was told that an angiography would cost ₹30,000. While the hospital is empanelled under the PMJAY scheme for cardiology according to PMJAY’s website, Raiz says the hospital said they do not accept Ayushman Bharat card patients and Raiz decided to wait. Like most Indian patients who set out on a journey, he tried to attend to all his unfinished business first, which included getting one of his daughters married. A heart attack that should have been attended to within the first two hours, would only be treated a month later.
Sheespal Bhagel, head of medical operations at Jaypee Hospital says, “Our name has changed from Jaypee Hospital to Manush Jaypee Hospital on January 14, 2026 which has caused a change in the status on the [PMJAY] portal. We have sent applications to Lucknow so that the hospital, with its new name, is empanelled again.”
After a heart attack
Once a person has a heart attack, they have to take medicines for life. There is, however, no mechanism to ensure patients have access to affordable drugs in the public system. “Patients do not get their prescribed medicines in PHCs or CHCs but have to travel all the way to the district hospital to get them,” says the Chhattisgarh doctor. Given the cost, intermittent unavailability of medicines and the time involved, most patients have to buy the drugs out-of-pocket from the private sector, he adds.
The situation is not better in Delhi’s tertiary care hospitals, which cater to patients within the State and other neighbouring states. Many of the patients we met at the cardiology OPD of Delhi’s tertiary care hospitals did not know whether they had suffered a heart attack; they had been going from hospital to hospital without a clear diagnosis or a plan. It took them weeks to get their reports ready and get a chance to see the doctor while the waiting time for procedures was in weeks or months.
At AIIMS Delhi, the waiting period for cardio-thoracic and vascular surgery is up to two years due to heavy patient load, according to an answer given in Parliament in July 2025, by Prataprao Jadhav, Union Minister of State in the Health Ministry. Just a few metres away is another government tertiary care hospital, Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, with a fully equipped 12 bedded ‘Heart Command Centre’ that is trying to reduce delays in treatment for heart patients. While the patients in general emergency patients may suffer delays in getting identified and referred for angioplasty, they get quickly triaged and receive thrombolysis and angioplasty here. The centre boasts of four cath labs with two being available 24/7.
“This is a rare kind of set-up in the public setup; we do 20 angioplasties daily out of which 5-10 are heart attack patients receiving emergency angioplasties,” said Dr. Isser. The hospital, which gets patients from Delhi and other North Indian states, has a capacity of 110 beds for cardiac patients but sometimes faces a shortage, he says.
What if heart patients did not have to travel long distances to other cities and were treated near their homes? That is a question waiting to be answered.
(Swagata Yadavar is an independent journalist. swagatayadavar@gmail.com)

Second crane topples onto Florida home while trying to remove first fallen crane
The incident ‘caused ’significant structural damage’ to the home, according local officials
