Liam Neeson still remembers his shock and shame when he read a New York Times article about the mother and baby institution in Tuam, County Galway.
It was 2017 and the article chronicled the campaign by Catherine Corless, an amateur local historian, to expose abuse and neglect by Irish nuns that led to hundreds of children being buried in a mass, unmarked grave.
“I had such a visceral reaction,” Neeson told the Guardian. “I’m obviously Irish, I was raised in the Catholic church, and I had a deep sense of embarrassment and obligation for the truth to come out and for there to be some accountability.”
It prompted the actor – and former altar boy – to use his heft in the film industry to become a producer for the first time. He optioned the article, visited Corless at her home and assembled a team to put the story on screen.
The result, nine years later, is The Lost Children of Tuam, a feature film that is released in Ireland this week and in the UK next month. “This was such an important story for the world to know about and to give a voice to the hundreds of babies and children that died,” said Neeson.
The release coincides with the continuing excavation of a 5,000 sq metre (53,820 sq ft) site where the Bon Secours order is believed have interred 796 infants who died at the St Mary’s mother and baby home between 1925 and 1961.
An international team of forensic archaeologists and other specialists has found skeletal remains of 99 babies and children since starting work last year – the result of Corless’s research, a judicial commission and a promise by the Irish state to seek truth and justice for survivors and relatives of those who died.
It is part of a wider reckoning of the mistreatment of women and children in state- and religious-run institutions across Ireland. Tuam, however, stands out for its macabre details – some infants were buried in a disused subterranean septic tank – and the doggedness of the woman who exposed it.
In her quest for answers, Corless never accepted “no”, said Neeson. “The detective work she did to uncover this atrocity involving the relationship between the state and the church was extraordinary.”
The film, based on the New York Times article by Dan Barry, tells the story of how Corless, a former textile factory secretary with an interest in local history, began researching the site for an essay. Officials and the Bon Secours order fobbed her off but Corless discovered that 796 children had died without burial records before the institution was closed in 1961 and demolished.
Early reviews of the film, which was written by Rebecca Lenkiewicz and directed by Frank Berry, say it is sensitive and stirring, with the English actor Monica Dolan giving a powerful central performance.
“She’s brilliant – so natural, so down to earth,” said Corless. “She portrayed me as I am. She has an English accent so how on earth did she capture the way I speak?”
Andrew Bennett, who plays her husband, Aidan, has also captured his personality and the couple’s relationship, she said.
Corless has watched the film three times – two private viewings for her family and survivors, and the premiere at the Galway film Fleadh in July, where it won best Irish film. “I was so nervous I needed to see it a few times,” she said.
“We’re ordinary people. We have a farm. That a film would be made about us, it was out of this world. It’s done with great respect, with the odd little bit of humour in it too, and it just hits people, it hits you hard.”
Berry, the director, said the film showed Corless’s integrity and persistence. “Her work revealed a lot of very hard truths about Ireland. It’s a way of telling truths but with an inspirational central character. It shows that one person can achieve amazing things.”

It was at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona when the mutterings about a new "secret weapon" started.
Dozens of Great Britain athletes had been taking a new product that increased muscle mass and improved athletic performance – a "wonder pill" that didn't fall foul of any doping rules.
They were talking about creatine.
Now found in tubs and bags on many supermarket shelves and tagged in your social feeds, it is the supplement of choice for millions of people and one of the most scientifically researched.
But back then, when it came on the scene at the very top of British elite sport, there were suspicions and stigma around the use of any substance described as 'performance enhancing' – even if it was legal.
From the minute an athlete wakes, to the moment they go to bed, they are thinking about how they can optimise their performance and recovery.
Today, creatine is just one of a long list of supplements taken by elite athletes in this pursuit of marginal gains. Some help with muscle size and strength, while others correct deficiencies in the diet.
"There are various reports in the literature of some studies that say maybe up to 90% of athletes take supplements. I often jokingly say that means 10% are lying," says Prof Graeme Close, professor of human physiology at Liverpool John Moores University.
"The sports teams that I've worked in, I think that's probably closer to 100% of athletes will be taking some form of supplementation."
So, what do supplements actually do and why do athletes take them? And in the world of strict liability, where elite athletes are solely responsible for what they put in their bodies, how do they make sure they stay clean?
While experts like Close advocate for seeking to meet nutritional needs through food in the first instance, it may not always be possible or practical to do this - and that is where supplements come in.
Take, for example, creatine, which is found naturally in meat and fish.
"You would need the best part of a kilogram of raw chicken a day to get the amount of creatine you need," says Close. But it is unsafe to eat raw poultry because of the food poisoning risk from harmful bacteria.
Creatine is a natural compound in the body produced in the kidneys, liver and pancreas. It is a quick source of energy for muscles, which is especially important for short-duration, high intensity activities such as sprinting.
Its big break as a supplement came in the 1990s when two scientists who had been researching it for two decades shared their findings with Steve Jennings, whose Maxim sports nutrition company supplied products to the British Olympic team.
During the 1992 Barcelona Games, investigative reporter Doug Gillon had learned of a 'secret trial' involving British athletes and seen a box of their Ergomax C150 – effervescent creatine tablets. He wrote that if the scientists' claims - that creatine could improve explosive athletic performance by 1-3% - were true, then "sport may never be the same again".
In terms of sport supplements and nutrition, he was right. By the time of the next Olympics in 1996, an estimated 80% of athletes were taking creatine, and since then it has become mainstream, with research suggesting there may be cognitive benefits as well as physical.
According to the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, the creatine breakthrough of the 1990s had "launched a new era in sports nutrition" and "sparked exploration into other supplements".
The global dietary supplements market size was valued at $209.5bn (£154bn) in 2025 and is projected to grow to $431.7bn (£317.4bn) by 2033, according to Grand View Research., external
Close, who oversaw nutrition for last year's British and Irish Lions rugby union tour, sees supplements as the "final piece of the jigsaw" rather than a starting point.
"What we're talking about is small margins of benefit, where actually these athletes who focus on the food, I think what you often find is that they've got the big-ticket items right," he says.
"So they're seeing great performance benefits because their overall diet is immaculate.
"They might be missing out on the one per-centers, but they've really nailed the 99 per-centers. And they often do better than those who chase the one per-centers but have not given enough attention to the 99 per-centers."
Australian cyclist Nicole Frain agrees, adding: "I'm a pretty big believer that they are called sport supplements. They are there to supplement the things you already do right.
"I don't think supplements are the answer to fix my problems.
"You need to be eating a balanced diet, training well, sleeping right, recovering well, hydrating – all of those things – before we add in all of the extras."
Close puts protein powders top of the list of supplements taken by athletes he works with, followed by creatine and vitamin D.
Protein powders maximise muscle repair and contribute to muscle growth, while creatine is a quick source of energy for muscles and important in short-duration, high-intensity activities like sprinting. Vitamin D, meanwhile, is essential for bone health and supports muscle function.
Other popular supplements include carbohydrate gels, which Close says were key in the first sub-two hour marathon run earlier this year by Kenyan long-distance runner Sabastian Sawe.
"As sport nutritionists we were all fascinated at what the fuelling programme was, and it was the sports drinks and gels that played a huge part of that fuelling," Close says.
"There was a calculation done of what it would take to break the two-hour marathon, and that did involve making sure that over 100 grams of supplemental carbohydrate were ingested per hour.
"And the reports coming out of the recent sub-two-hour marathon was that it was 110 grams of carbohydrate per hour that was achieved."
Supplements can improve performance, but there is an uneasy ring to describing them as 'performance enhancing' because of the association with banned substances and anti-doping rule violations.
So what determines whether something is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's (Wada) banned list?
"For Wada to put anything on the list, it's got to hit two out of three criteria: dangerous to health, performance enhancing, and against the spirit of sport," Close explains.
"So just because something enhances performance, if it's not dangerous to health and not against the spirit of sport, Wada will not touch it.
"So creatine is a good example.
"Though something like an anabolic steroid, where it's against the spirit of sport to be injecting yourself for a performance benefit, it's dangerous to health and it's performance enhancing - that hits all three."
But taking a supplement still carries anti-doping risks.
"No guarantee can be given that any particular supplement is free from prohibited substances," UK Anti-Doping advice states, urging athletes to "be vigilant" in using them.
And if you test positive for a prohibited substance, consuming it unintentionally can result in the same four-year ban as if you deliberately took it.
There are supplement-testing programmes which batch test products before they are sold to make sure they do not contain any Wada-prohibited substances.
One of those is Informed Sport, which says as many as one in 10 supplements is contaminated with ingredients and compounds prohibited in sport and points to a study carried out by the Anti-Doping Knowledge Centre that showed product contamination was responsible for 8% of all anti-doping violations between 2005 and 2022.
While Informed Sport is a very well used system among athletes, Wada makes it clear that quality assurance schemes can reduce but do not eliminate the risk of an anti-doping infringement.
If you do accept the risk, you need to be organised to keep track.
In the case of Great Britain rower Heidi Long, it takes a spreadsheet.
"I've recorded the batch number of every product that I've taken and its expiry date because if you take it after the expiry date the Informed Sport [certification] is no longer viable," she says.
Close says he has also done site visits to factories to see where the supplements are made to check the manufacturing processes because "the risk of failing a drugs test is huge".
There are risks to the general population too, he adds, saying: "You can be buying supplements off the internet that are made in somebody's garage and you've got no idea of the manufacturing processes."
He points to studies on creatine products which have found there is no creatine in them and so "you're completely wasting your money" and that in the worst case scenario it may contain substances that are dangerous to your health.
"So it is really important that the message is that while they can play a small role, the safety considerations are the key factor," he says.
There is, however, more than one way for an elite athlete to chase a competitive edge – and some are going back to basics.
For every trending supplement, there is an unprocessed, wholefood alternative – from the anti-inflammatory benefits of turmeric, staving off cramp with pickle juice or consumption of high-nitrate foods like beetroot before competition.
It is what Close calls a "food-first" or "food-only" approach and something he says every athlete should use as a starting point.
The latest to have its moment in the spotlight is an ancient Ethiopian grain called teff.
Used for thousands of years in traditional east African diets, teff is now making its mark globally in performance nutrition.
In comparison to other popular grains like wheat, rice and quinoa, teff has a high mineral content and is rich in calcium, iron and vitamin C. Naturally gluten-free and good for the gut, it is also unique for being a 'complete' protein, meaning it provides all nine essential amino acids required for human nutrition.
These superfood credentials have caught the attention of some of the world's best athletes over the years, from Olympic champion marathon runner Haile Gebrselassie to seven-time Grand Slam singles champion Venus Williams, and it is now becoming a more common sight on UK supermarket shelves.
British boxer Fran Hennessy was introduced to teff by her nutritionist and it is now part of her daily routine.
"I've never looked back," she says. "What I'm putting in my body is good fuel and energy and teff has so much. It energises you so much before a workout and it gives you the fibre you need."
As well as boosting her performances, Hennessy credits teff with being key to recovery.
She says: "Each meal I'm having there's a reason behind and everything that's in it there's a reason behind... I know what I'm putting in my body is fuelling me, recovering me, energising me."
Cost is another consideration when athletes are deciding on supplements.
"The supplement industry is really expensive," says Long. "And we're definitely not made of money. So I think it's really picking and choosing when you want to put that investment in."
She says it makes sense to have more supplements around racing time "when the performance is super critical and very time dependent".
"[But] on a daily basis if I can get the protein intake from my dinner and a glass of milk or yoghurt and breakfast then actually I was going to be eating that food anyway so it's not as expensive."
And then there is taste.
"I would much rather enjoy a coffee in the morning with friends or while I'm working rather than have one of the gels," she says. "Some of the gels ... you'll end up holding your nose when you take it.
"I guess it's just like the enjoyment of what you're taking, you know, it's nicer to eat food than it is to take supplements."

Bushra Bano cleared the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission examination in 2017 with Rank 6, becoming a PCS Officer and later a sub-divisional magistrate. She studied on her own, without coaching, while working full-time and raising two children with her engineer husband. She sat for the UPSC exam twice — in 2019 and 2021 — before securing Rank 234 and clearing the Indian Police Service.
On September 14, 2026, she was transferred from her post as additional SP of Kharagpur in West Bengal’s Paschim Medinipur district, a day after propaganda news channels and Right-wing accounts targeted her for using the Arabic words, ‘Assalamu Alaikum’, ‘Jazakallah’, and ‘Inshallah’, in a video.
In the clip, Bushara is heard commending a government-aided residential coaching academy for minorities, women and SC/ST students at Aligarh Muslim University. While she spoke, she said the three phrases in Arabic. She said, “Assalamu Alaikum. My name is Bushra Bano… ” at first. Towards the end, she said, “…If they (the students) stay and study through the RCA then Inshallah many more people will move forward like me and get the opportunity to serve their country.” At the end she ended her video by saying, “Thank you, Jazakallah”.
“Assalamu Alaikum” is a common greeting which means “Peace be upon you”; “Inshallah” translates to “God willing”, and the phrase “Jazakallah” means “May God Reward You”. The reader might note that these are not religious phrases but greetings and wishes.
A simple video, made by a Muslim IPS officer who used a few Arabic phrases, sent ripples across the Right-wing ecosystem. On September 13, propaganda outlet Sudarshan News, which has its own national TV channel, shared the video on X and said, “Starting with ‘Assalamualaikum,’ slipping in ‘Inshallah’ midway, and wrapping up with ‘Jazakallah’, Bushra Bano… shared how she came from Saudi Arabia and became an IPS officer in India… She made full use of the scheme being run by the government at Aligarh Muslim University.”
“अस्सलाम वाले कुम” से शुरू कर बीच में “इंशाल्लाह” कहते हुए “जज़ाकल्लाह” पर किया खत्म,
खड़गपुर में एडिशनल एसपी के तौर पर तैनात बुशरा बानो ने बताया कि सऊदी अरब से आ कर वो कैसे भारत में बनीं IPS..
सरकार द्वारा अलीगढ़ मुस्लिम यूनिवर्सिटी में चलाई जा रही स्कीम का उठाया भरपूर फायदा.… pic.twitter.com/foYKjihMV2
— Sudarshan News (@SudarshanNewsTV) September 13, 2026
Soon, a barrage of online trolls started targeting Bano. An X handle called @HinduLegalFund posted on X that a complaint had been filed with the West Bengal home secretary regarding the video. “She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind…” the post read. Additionally, it stated that a serving officer should maintain “neutrality and national expressions in public communication”.
Complaint filed with West Bengal Home Secretary regarding IPS Bushra Bano’s official video statement.
She began with Assalamualaikum, used Inshallah, ended with Jazakallah — and did not use Vande Mataram or Jai Hind.
A serving officer representing the Indian state should…
— Hindu Legal Fund (@HinduLegalFund) September 13, 2026
Several Right-wing accounts, including @JaipurDialogues and @MeghUpdates, also shared the video and complained that no ‘Vande Mataram’ or ‘Jai Hind’ had been used by the IPS officer.
A notification issued by the government of West Bengal on Monday stated that Bano, alongside two other WBPS officers, was being transferred to a different posting “in public interest”. She has been made the deputy commandant of the state armed police 4th battalion. The notification does not state any reason behind the transfer.
West Bengal Government reshuffles 3 police officers with immediate effect; Partha Ghosh appointed as Addl SP, Kharagpur, Paschim Medinipur.
Subhendu Mandal posted as Addl DC, Chandannagar
Dr. Bushara Bano, transferred as Dy. CO, SAP 4th Bn. pic.twitter.com/MHu5WK4De1
— ANI (@ANI) September 14, 2026
It should be common knowledge that Arabic is a language and Islam is a religion. Muslims use Arabic extensively for religious purposes, but Arabic is not synonymous with Islam. In other words, none of these expressions is simply a ‘Muslim word’ in the narrow linguistic sense. They are Arabic phrases whose meanings and histories intersect with Islamic religious usage, but they are not exclusive to Islam. The tradition of greeting a person with ‘Peace be upon you’, for example, exists in other languages and religious traditions — the Hebrew expression ‘shalom aleichem’, for example, literally means ‘peace be upon you’ and is common in Jewish religious literature. None of this, however, came in the way of pro-BJP handles slamming the officer for her alleged religion posturing.
Sudarshan News editor Suresh Chavhanke, whose history of peddling misinformation and communal propaganda is well documented, called Bano’s case ‘UPSC Jihad’.
Even if one were to accept this as an instance of religious posturing, it would hardly be the first time a police officer has done so. What stands out, however, is how differently such conduct is received depending on the community to which the officer belongs.
In May 2026, IPS officer C V Anand invited priests to perform a puja in his office on the day he took charge as director general of police of Telangana.
Senior IPS officer CV Anand taking charge as Telangana DGP. pic.twitter.com/5ZSSAT6K3w
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) May 2, 2026
He himself posted about this on X. No one batted an eyelid. Anand is still serving as the DGP of Telangana.
Anand wrote, “As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.”
It was a very busy and perhaps the biggest day for me and my family . As per the muhurtham , I reached the DGP office at Lakdikapul with my family , took the salute and followed the pujari into the dgp chambers where the puja and blessings were done.
Then at 11:05 AM , signed… pic.twitter.com/wlkJX8hszp
— CV Anand IPS (@CVAnandIPS) May 1, 2026
More such instances are not difficult to find.
In Uttar Pradesh’s Sambhal, a circle officer named Anuj Chaudhary, who was an accused of firing during the violence at the Shahi Jama Masjid in November 2024, was pictured joining a Hindu religious procession in January 2025. He was accused of participating in religious rituals while on duty and violating service conduct rules. A complaint was filed by retired IPS officer and Azad Adhikar Sena president Amitabh Thakur, following which a probe was launched.
The same year, on Holi, Chaudhary had stated: “Holi comes once a year, Jumma comes 52 times. If you want to serve sevai, you must also eat gujiya.” Again, an investigation was initiated, and Chaudhary was eventually given a clean chit.
In May 2025, he was transferred from Sambhal to Chandausi, some 30 km away. Three months later, in August, Chaudhary was promoted to the role of additional superintendent of police (ASP). His colleagues and senior officers, including SP K K Bishnoi and ASP Rajesh Kumar Srivastava, marked the occasion with a felicitation ceremony.
Was there no outrage when Anuj Chaudhary carried a mace and marched in a religious procession in uniform? There was, from one section, but he went on to be promoted. Bano’s case panned out differently. The principle, presumably, is that the same rules apply to everyone. In practice, however, some seem to be considerably more equal than others. And if Bushra Bano’s transfer was, as the government put it, “in public interest”, one is left wondering exactly which ‘public’ that interest was meant to serve.
Bano’s transfer set off a series of critical reactions from the Opposition. Several politicians alleged that the transfer was a direct fallout of her use of Arabic phrases. Comparing the incident with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s inauguration of the Parliament “with sengol & bare chested sadhus”, Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra remarked, “…We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India”.
For a country whose Prime Minister inaugurated new Parliament with sengol & bare chested sadhus, transferring a Muslim IPS officer for saying Assalamalaikum & Inshallah is ridiculous. We are a nation gone mad, poisoned with hate & bigotry. God Save India.
— Mahua Moitra (@MahuaMoitra) September 15, 2026
Former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Mehbooba Mufti also criticised the move, saying the transfer, which was followed by the West Bengal CM “calling an election a ‘test’ of Muslim loyalty”, was “a veiled threat to the community”. “…First our food, clothes and marriages , now even our vocabulary and our votes are being policed”, she added.
Congress MP Imran Pratapgarhi took to X to condemn the move. “A hate-mongering TV channel first sensationalized that video by posting it and incited online trolling against the female IPS officer, and instead of standing by her, the state government transferred her the very next day. What kind of India are you building, @narendramodi ji? @IPS_Association, are you watching this?”, he wrote.

A pair of developers say that with very little prompting, Meta’s Muse will share its entire filesystem with you. Peter James and Jonny L. Saunders have said they both independently coaxed Muse into zipping up and sharing the entire contents of its root filesystem, Ubuntu system files, app templates, and internal documentation. Saunders posted on Mastodon that it was “extremely easy” to replicate James’ results and that Muse had “Almost no prompt injection resistance.”
Muse will apparently let you download its entire filesystem
With a little coaxing, Meta’s AI will reveal all its secrets.
Meta denies that the incident represents a security breach. As noted in its announcement post, Meta’s Muse runs in persistent Linux virtual machines for each user. Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said, “Just like with the laptop in front of you, of course you can see the files. Exporting virtual machine data doesn’t give people any privileged access to Meta infrastructure or to other people’s data.” Unlike with the average laptop, however, the data potentially reveals some interesting things about how Meta’s new AI platform functions.
This is the second Muse vulnerability disclosed this week, after security researcher Patrick Wardle discovered an exploit that would let attackers hijack the AI agent, redirect transcription processing, and access a user’s Muse account. Meta quickly issued a hotfix.
Both James and Saunders gained access to plain-text Markdown and JSON files describing in detail how Hatch (Meta’s internal name for Muse) processes requests, handles data, and connects to other services like Gmail. While it’s well documented that AI agents hallucinate and will provide false information about how they function, Saunders said that it is “generating hundreds of MB of accurate library code and compiled binaries” in a matter of seconds and that, “unless it synthesized a whole Ubuntu VM in less than a minute then I think this is a real dump.”
When I asked Muse to share its filesystem with me, it initially refused, saying it would be a security risk. When I shared links to evidence that it had created archives for others, it responded that it should not have done that and continued to say that it “can’t do a full / copy.” However, after starting a new session and prompting it with some flattery and curiosity, it created “safe” versions of /opt/hatch and /home/hatch for me, stripped of things like SSH keys. It also exposed its full directory tree to me and offered to “pull a safe copy” of “any specific subtree that looks interesting.” The resulting files seem to match what Saunders and James shared.
Roberts explained that while Meta isn’t seriously concerned about the leaks, “We’re continuing to make updates to the product, so users may see changes in how much information is available about their virtual machine.”
The developers’ dump potentially reveals a lot about Muse’s internal workings. For one, it stores its memory in plain Markdown files. It also performs a nightly “dream” review of recent conversations, which it then builds into guidance for future conversations, according to James. Saunders also found that many of Muse’s capabilities were hard-coded, including its ability to cancel subscriptions and “the machinery that manages runaway agent spawning.” Saunders speculates that many of the bash and Python scripts running Muse in the background were created using Claude, though that is unconfirmed.
James also found references to hardware integration called Meta Home Link, which appears to give Muse access to devices on a home network. Though Meta has not announced any feature by that name, and it’s not guaranteed that it will ship.

Srinagar has an estimated 64,416 stray dogs, according to a scientific survey conducted by the Srinagar Municipal Corporation (SMC) in 2023, the Government stated today. It said nearly one-fourth of the dogs in Srinagar, that is 15,266 stray dogs, were sterilised between June 2023 and September 2025.
The figures have been provided by the Housing & Urban Development Department (H&UDD) in a written reply to a starred question raised by MLA Zadibal Tanvir Sadiq. According to the reply, the 2023 survey carried out by SMC used the Lincoln-Petersen Formula to estimate the stray dog population within SMC limits. The Animal Welfare Board of India has recognised it as a scientific survey and it found approximately 64,416 in Srinagar.
The government has stated in the reply to the question of the legislator that from June 2023 to September 2025, SMC sterilised 15,266 stray dogs and immunised 15,725 dogs. The surgeries and vaccinations were carried out at Animal Birth Control (ABC) centres at Tengpora and Shuhama.
The government also said dog-bite cases in J&K were being recorded and monitored through the State Surveillance Officer under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP). The IDSP operates under the Directorate of Health Services, Kashmir.
It has also said that SMC currently has ABC centres at Tengpora Bypass and Shuhama in SKUAST. Together, these facilities have a combined kennel capacity of 121.
An additional ABC centre at Ahal Chatterhama is also coming up, with the kennel capacity of 60. The three centres will have an aggregate kennel capacity of 181, once the third one is ready, according to the government.
The department said ABC/ARV programmes are also being implemented in Jammu. The Jammu Municipal Corporation (JMC) has sterilized 50,000 dogs since 2014.
“However, keeping in view the scale and geographical spread of the stray dog population in the urban areas of the Union Territory, the existing infrastructure and operational capacity require further augmentation and strengthening to ensure wider, effective and sustained coverage,” the reply states while acknowledging gaps in efforts to control stray dog population.
It listed its strengthening efforts as: the expansion of ABC centres, strengthening veterinary manpower and dog-catching facilities, augmentation of holding/isolation and post-operative facilities, expansion of sterilisation and ARV coverage, scientific identification and record-keeping of sterilised/vaccinated dogs, regulation of designated feeding points, improved solid-waste management and intensified public awareness.
The government has said that veterinary surgeons/doctors have been deputed to municipal corporations and urban local bodies to for helping in ABC/ARV programme.

Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has celebrated a “historic” meeting with Donald Trump in New York, posing for a smiley photo with the US president less than nine months after he ordered the abduction of her boss, Nicolás Maduro.
The former foes met at a five-star hotel in Manhattan a few blocks from Trump Tower late on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly. The hotel is about 7 miles from the Brooklyn prison where Maduro has been held since he was snatched during a special forces raid on Caracas.
On the eve of Tuesday’s encounter, an American reporter asked Rodríguez if she would be visiting Maduro, under whom she served as vice-president, during her stay in New York. She did not reply.
But Venezuela’s interim leader did find time to meet Trump at the luxury Lotte New York Palace hotel, with the get-together seen as a key part of Rodríguez’s push for international legitimacy after years of diplomatic isolation under Maduro’s dictatorship. On Wednesday she is expected to address the annual UN assembly.
“We held a historic meeting with … Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, security and other matters of common interest,” Rodríguez wrote on Instagram, in a 133-word statement that made no mention of her incarcerated ally.
Oliver Blanco, one of Rodríguez’s top diplomats, claimed the meeting marked “a new stage of dialogue and understanding between both countries” and was “an important step toward new opportunities for our country and our people”. Blanco also posted a cheery photo in which both he and Trump smiled and gave the thumbs up to the camera.
A White House aide said the meeting was also attended by top US officials including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and the deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Hours earlier, Rodríguez had sat in the general assembly hall watching Trump celebrate the “massive military operation” during which Maduro – whom he called an “outlaw dictator” and “a real criminal” – was captured. “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils,” Trump bragged of the recent oil deal between the US and Venezuela, as she appeared to wince.
Some observers also detected signs of discomfort in the body language captured in the photo of Trump and Rodríguez, who appears to be clenching her left fist as she poses beside the grinning US president.
Some of Rodríguez’s critics in Venezuela called her treatment by Trump an unmitigated humiliation for a socialist party politician who has spent years railing against Yankee imperialism.
After Maduro’s capture, Trump warned that Rodríguez would “pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro” if she did not toe the US line. Since then, Rodríguez has made a series of major concessions, including ceding control of Venezuela’s oil revenues to Washington and agreeing to a controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal that Trump on Tuesday called “the largest oil deal in history”.
One opposition figure denounced the Rodríguez/Trump meeting as an encounter between a “shameless puppet and her unscrupulous puppeteer”.
But Rodríguez has succeeded in consolidating power, with Trump seemingly more focused on gaining access to Venezuela’s natural resources than pushing for a fresh presidential election that would move the South American country back towards democracy.
Trump has repeatedly praised Rodríguez’s “fantastic” and “terrific” leadership while sidelining her main rival, the opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado, who left Venezuela late last year to receive her Nobel peace prize in Oslo, has been unable to return and is exiled in Panama. She reportedly made three attempts to return to Venezuela this week, but failed.
Before Tuesday’s tête-à-tête, the presidents of the US and Venezuela had last met in 2015, when Barack Obama and Maduro spoke briefly during a regional summit in Panama. In the decade that followed, Maduro became an international pariah as he led his country into economic chaos and increasingly authoritarian rule, and Venezuela was hit by punishing international sanctions.
At the 2015 summit, Obama conceded that the days in which “the US could meddle with impunity” in Latin America were over. But Trump has dramatically different ideas and has been forging ahead with attempts to reassert US dominance in a region it has long considered its back yard.
As well as capturing Venezuela’s government and trying to topple Cuba’s communist government by strangling its economy, Trump’s push for hegemony has also seen the US accused of trying to swing Brazil’s presidential election in favour of the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro through diplomatic and economic pressure.
Addressing the UN assembly on Tuesday, the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, hit back at such efforts, without directly citing the US. “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians,” said Lula who is facing a tough battle to win re-election in October’s vote.
“Brazil doesn’t fit into anyone’s back yard,” added Lula, who also called for fresh elections in Venezuela. He did not meet Rodríguez during her visit to New York but said the “people of Venezuela deserve to decide their own future”.

Justice minister says miscarriage of justice likely occurred in Sask. murder case, orders new appeal
Neressa and Odelia Quewezance convicted by jury in 1994
The federal minister of justice has ordered a new appeal in the case of two sisters who were convicted of murder more than 30 years ago.
The appeal was announced on Thursday, after an "in-depth" review by the ministry that took more than four years and found "reasonable grounds to conclude that a miscarriage of justice likely occurred."
Odelia and Neressa Quewezance, sisters from Keeseekoose First Nation in Saskatchewan, were convicted in 1994 of second-degree murder in the death of Anthony Joseph Dolff, a farmer from Kamsack, Sask.
"My decision does not decide guilt or innocence, as that will rest with the courts," Justice Minister Sean Fraser said in a news release.
"Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts for new information to be considered."
The new information was not before the courts at the time of the sisters' trial or appeal, the government said.
In an emailed statement, Odelia Quewezance spoke on behalf of herself and her sister and thanked everyone who has "kept the faith" with them over the years.
"Neressa was 18 when she was arrested and is now 52. I was 21 and am now 55. But we have never stopped fighting," Odelia said.
"Today’s announcement by the minister is encouraging and now we will continue the fight in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal."
The murder
On Feb. 25, 1993, Dolff invited the two young Indigenous girls and their teenage cousin to his home in Kamsack, Sask.
Both girls had attended residential school and were victims of institutionalized violence, their lawyers have said. Dolff had worked at the St. Phillips Residential School on Keeseekoose First Nation.
Events that night led to Dolff's death. The cousin, who cannot be identified under the provisions of the Youth Criminal Justice Act, confessed to stabbing him.
Odelia and Neressa were also charged with second-degree murder and were convicted after a trial in Yorkton Court of King's Bench in 1994.
David Milgaard brought the sisters' cases to Innocence Canada, a non-profit organization that advocates for the exoneration of people who have been wrongly convicted. It filed an application with the justice minister on Dec. 21, 2021, asking for the review.
James Lockyer, founding director of Innocence Canada, is lead counsel for the Quewezance sisters.
He said the new information they'll be bringing on appeal has to do with the period of time after Odelia and Neressa's arrest, when they were held in the Kamsack RCMP detachment for five days despite a judge's order that they be taken to a detention centre.
RCMP officers claimed Odelia and Neressa confessed over five days of questioning.
"We've got new information about that period … that we think compels an entire rethinking about the case and a complete rethinking about the reliability of their confessions," Lockyer said.
"In essence, we're alleging that the confessions that were put before the court were false confessions."
Deanna Harris is the southeast regional director for Saskatchewan Legal Aid, which helped to fund the review application.
She said a lot has changed in the criminal justice system over the last 30 years, in regards to the understanding of the treatment of Indigenous people.
"One thing that we face so often in Canadian society is that historical injustices, we can't do very much about them other than apologize," she said.
But in this case, there's actually something that can be done to right the wrong, Harris said.
"They are still with us. They are still alive, and we can actually work to acknowledge that there was a miscarriage of justice in their case, and that can be remedied at this point in time."
New bail application expected
The justice minister's decision sends the case back to the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, where dates will be set to hear the appeal.
But Lockyer said before that happens, he will be making a bail application to the appeal court.
Odelia and Neressa previously applied for release, while the federal review was pending, and were conditionally released from custody in March 2023 after a hearing in Yorkton Court of King's Bench.
However, Neressa allegedly breached her curfew condition and is being held in a federal institution in B.C., while Odelia was charged this summer with impaired driving and is in a provincial jail.
Lockyer said it's been "very difficult" for them to readjust to life in the community after spending more than 30 years in jail.
"The bottom line is, why are two Indigenous women still serving life sentences 33 years after their convictions, when at their trial, the judge ordered that they be eligible for parole after 10 years?" Lockyer said.
"It's an indictment of our parole system as well, that they're still in prison 23 years after they became eligible for parole."

Senator shreds Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ with edgy two-word retort to his AI rebrand
Trump’s attempts to rebrand AI are drawing mockery and concern, Eric Garcia writes. It’s a preview of how the issue will be debated on Congress depending how the midterms shakeout

President Donald Trump’s attempts to rebrand AI as “super intelligence” landed with a thud among Democrats on Capitol Hill on Wednesday. It’s a sign that the president might not have carte blanche authority on AI should they take back the majority next year.
The president is attempting to rebrand artificial intelligence under a new name as he has called the alarmism about the dangers around AI a “hoax.” Trump has also said “the only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades.”
But Democrats brushed off attempts by the president to write off the concerns Americans have around AI.
Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona and a number of Democrats are talking about putting in place guardrails as many in the AI industry have begun to blow the whistle about the need to rein in the industry. Earlier this month, Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher, announced he had resigned from Anthropic, saying “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Republicans in the House and Senate writ large, including House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), have dismissed fears about AI and Washington’s capacity for oversight.
“F***ing stupid,” Gallego told The Independent. “Next question.”
But the deference Trump receives around AI might change should Democrats win back control of both chambers of Congress. Polling shows Trump’s approval rating nosediving and Democrats have to flip only four Senate seats to win back control of the upper chamber.
Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, told The Independent that there would be investigations around AI should his party win back control of the Senate.
“He is just flailing trying to find wins for the election, so put me down as dubious to what he’s talking about,” Wyden said about Trump.
Democrats have been drawing up legislation on AI or releasing reports on the subject since at least 2024, when a bipartisan group of senators led by Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer of New York put out a report on the subject. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) took part in a summit about AI last week with former Trump adviser Steve Bannon in response to concerns about the subject.
“I don't spend a lot of time trying to understand President Trump,” Sanders told The Independent. “I think he is mentally unbalanced. I think he has not a clue about the problems associated with uncontrolled AI.”
There is potential for collaboration going into the next Congress. Reps. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jim Obernolte (R-Calif.) have legislation that would create a tiered system of regulation for AI and require independent audits of AI firms.
And polling shows the president out of step with many voters. A Politico survey released last week showed even 61 percent of people who voted for Trump think there is a moderate or significant risk with AI.
“President Trump puts the safety and security of our nation and our families at risk,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) told The Independent. On Wednesday, she and Schumer held a press conference urging Trump to keep AI tools out of China’s hands ahead of the president’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
But even some Republicans rolled their eyes at the president’s words.
“You can call it different names, it still is going to present great opportunity and great challenges and potential threats,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) told The Independent.

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s presidential campaign has accused Donald Trump of wanting to “colonise” Brazil in order to capture its natural resources by meddling in next month’s presidential election.
The accusation came in a televised campaign advert that was broadcast on Thursday by Lula’s team amid growing fears over the impact alleged US interference could have on the vote.
The TV spot claimed the US president was trying to sway the election in favour of Lula’s far-right adversary in the election, Flávio Bolsonaro, in order to advance Trump’s interests in the South American nation.
“Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonise Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” the female narrator tells viewers in the minute-long video.
The state department has denied claims the US is meddling in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” it said last month in a statement.
Writing on X, Lula accused Bolsonaro of wanting to “hand our natural resources over to the United States”.
“If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again,” the incumbent leftwing president added.
With just over a week to go until the 4 October first round vote, Lula and Bolsonaro are neck and neck in the polls. A second round run-off will be held on 25 October if no candidate secures more than half of the votes.
In recent weeks, there has been growing alarm – both in Brazil and overseas – about Washington’s apparent attempts to influence the result, with a campaign of diplomatic and economic pressure, including 25% tariffs on Brazilian imports.
Speaking at the UN general assembly in New York this week, Lula indirectly criticised the US’ perceived meddling, telling delegates: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy – internal or external – to attack the will of the people. Brazilian democracy belongs to the Brazilians.”
Earlier this week, dozens of Democratic party congresspeople wrote to secretary of state, Marco Rubio, to denounce the Trump administration’s “apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections through what they called a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilisation in Brazil”.
The narrator of Lula’s campaign ad cited a series of recent media stories relating to alleged acts of US meddling.
They include reports about the alleged interference of Big Tech companies as well as a confidential document sent to electoral authorities by Brazil’s intelligence agency warning of a “critical level” of risk of US interference. The campaign video also highlighted recent claims about links between Bolsonaro’s campaign and the conservative donor network Rockbridge, which was co-founded by Trump’s vice-president JD Vance.
Éden Valadares, the communications secretary for Lula’s Worker’s party (PT), said the campaign ad was part of efforts to “alert the Brazilian people” to the ideologically-driven US campaign. “We don’t believe it will work but nor will we sit back and do nothing,” Valadares said.
“President Lula has instructed us … to mobilise Brazilian society … [and] to react in the streets,” added Valadares, who said a nationwide series of events were being planned for this Sunday.
Fears over US meddling are not confined to the Brazilian left. This week, another of the right-wing candidates in Brazil’s election, Renan Santos, also denounced Trump’s behaviour and said he did not want Brazil to become a US vassal state. “They want to interfere in Brazil’s elections to secure satisfactory contracts involving rare earths,” Santos claimed in a social media video.
Recalling the US invasion of Venezuela in January, Santos added: “I don’t want to see Latin America become an American protectorate.”
In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US was “acting as an agent of interference and destabilisation – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.
They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October. The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

Google is taking its first step toward making Project Suncatcher a reality. Announced last year, Suncatcher is Google’s “moonshot” effort to design orbital AI data centers, which AI boosters like Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos have pitched as an alternative to divisive terrestrial data centers. Google’s first experimental satellite will launch on October 1 with the aim of validating Google’s vision for a constellation of AI satellites.
The satellite, dubbed MVP, is about the size of a refrigerator. Inside, it has four of Google’s custom TPU AI accelerators, which are used to train AI models and run inference to generate tokens for AI workloads. On Earth, a data center will run thousands of these chips, which consume massive amounts of power—one of the reasons putting solar-powered AI hardware in space is so attractive.
MVP is starting small, with solar panels that supply only about one kilowatt of power, The New York Times reports. That’s enough to power a microwave or a hair dryer. Google did not build the satellite from scratch. While the AI hardware inside is Google’s, the spacecraft comes from a satellite imagery firm called Planet Labs. The initial plan was to launch two custom satellites in 2027, but Google wanted to accelerate its efforts. So the company opted to integrate its chips into a satellite that Planet Labs had already built for an early test.
Google’s AI test will launch as part of the upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Eventually, Google wants to have networks of orbiting satellites that communicate over high-speed laser connections, probably requiring expensive dedicated launches. This lone satellite will serve as a test of several technologies and will operate for just a few months.

As US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping prepare to meet in Washington for a state dinner at the White House on Thursday, AI has become a top priority. Tech executives from OpenAI and Nvidia have confirmed their attendance at the dinner, as a number of key agenda items are on the table.
Chief among them is a US proposal to establish an AI notification system with China, akin to the Cold War hotline with Moscow, which would allow each country to alert the other about national security issues related to AI. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent first announced the notification system on Sunday with Chinese vice premier He Lifeng.
But for all the high-level progress, Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they expect it to still take a number of weeks to finalize an agreement, even if they are optimistic that the hotline could be in place before the year’s end.
There are several parts that need to be formalized in more detail, including establishing benchmarks on what kind of incident rises to the level of a national security issue, which remains unclear, as well as explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.
Trump officials tell Inner Loop they are essentially targeting a framework for the system to be functional—and, crucially, agreed to by Trump—by the time Bessent next meets with Lifeng in follow-up talks in two months' time in Shenzhen, China.
The discussions around such a mechanism underscore the growing concern around the rapidly developing capabilities of frontier AI models as the US and China race to become the dominant power in the industry.
Trump officials have internally discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.
But with the US expected to extend a trade truce and Trump reluctant to stop exports of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, developing a framework that has enforcement measures with teeth could take time to get White House approval, sources say.
The administration has granted a limited number of licenses this year for Nvidia to sell its H200 chip to China, a critical component for AI labs to increase compute power to train their models. Nvidia’s supporters have argued that not selling the chips incentivizes Chinese companies like Huawei to develop their own chip technology, though according to recent reports, the company has already achieved that milestone with its commercially available AI chips.
Some Trump officials have also suggested the notification system may also be delayed while Trump decides on who to appoint as his next "AI czar” to lead a so-called "AI Force," which is being envisioned as a role in charge of interagency coordination.
Bessent has been one of the names floated as the AI czar, but it is not clear if he’s the standout. Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House AI officials Michael Kratsios and Sean Cairncross are also in the mix, two sources tell Inner Loop.
It remains unclear if Trump will choose someone who will be wearing two hats or is departing their current role to take the position. The previous AI czar, David Sacks, was in the position as a special government employee. Sacks is not considered to be in the mix to return, the sources say.
The push for Bessent has come in part because the AI notification system is seen as something akin to the US-China dialogue between former Treasury secretary Hank Paulson and former Chinese vice premier of finance Wang Qishan. During the 2008 financial crisis, Paulson credited the hotline as helping to stave off China from dumping a large portion of US government sponsored debt issued by Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae.
Meanwhile, while some Trump officials have chafed at the idea of giving more AI power to Lutnick, he remains in contention insofar as he oversees the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which successfully navigated crises with frontier AI model companies this summer.

President Droupadi Murmu on Tuesday (September 22, 2026) urged popular film artists not to endorse products harmful to people's health, saying a “true star” spreads light, not darkness, highlighting the impact of words and actions of celebrities on young minds.
Ms. Murmu distributed the 72nd National Film Awards for 2024 in various categories of cinema at Ekta Nagar (Kevadia), near the Statue of Unity, in a glittering ceremony attended by top talents of the film industry.

Government hospitals across Tamil Nadu are facing a shortage of surfactant medicines, a critical and life-saving medicine for pre-term babies.
The shortage has been persisting for the past few months, and several Special Newborn Care Units (SNCUs) at government hospitals have been flagging it up for the Health Department.
Doctors said surfactant medicines are essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies in need of the therapy. They utilised external bovine or porcine surfactants (intratracheal) in pre-term babies. These surfactants were part of the speciality drug rate contract purchases of the Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation (TNMSC).
Inquiries with a number of hospitals and doctors revealed that a number of centres were facing short supply of surfactants in the past few months. Official sources confirmed that government hospitals, among them medical college hospitals in Theni, Dharmapuri, Tiruppur, Cuddalore, Tiruvannamalai, Vellore and Karur districts and in Chennai, reported surfactant vial shortage, while some hospitals said they had uninterrupted supply.
A doctor, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the shortage prevailed in the past three to four months owing to a number of factors. “First, we got no allotment. Secondly, some centres miscalculated their requirement, which is based on the average number of pre-term babies delivered, and thirdly, there was higher utilisation. This is a life-saving medicine essential to inflate the lungs of pre-term babies who are otherwise solid,” he said.
A doctor at another hospital said continuous supply was not assured, and shortage occurred frequently. “Currently, we are borrowing from other sub-centres which are referring babies to us. It is very difficult for us to manage newborn units without surfactants. Sometimes, we purchase them privately using SNCU funds to save the babies,” another doctor said.
A senior paediatrician said that after 34 weeks of gestation, the foetal lungs are generally mature enough to support exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide after birth. “However, in very pre-term babies, the alveoli, which are the tiny air sacs in the lungs, may not be sufficiently mature to function effectively on their own. Surfactant, a substance produced in the lungs, helps keep the alveoli open. But in babies born very prematurely, not enough surfactant may be produced, making it difficult for them to maintain adequate oxygen levels. Depending on the baby’s condition, doctors may use respiratory support such as CPAP or a mechanical ventilator. Surfactant is delivered directly into the lungs through the endotracheal tube to prevent hyaline membrane disease.”
Lung maturity in a newborn is critical as decreased oxygen could cause hypoxia and conditions such as retinopathy of prematurity and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, he said.
A Health Department source denied that there was any shortage. “There was no procurement delay. Some centres may have miscalculated their requirement, resulting in shortage, or may have utilised more vials. In such circumstances, they have obtained the required supply from neighbouring facilities. A six-month purchase order, worth nearly ₹9 crore, has been issued. Additionally, operational costs are provided for paediatricians to make local purchases whenever required,” he said.
Another official said the TNMSC has issued purchase orders and it will be supplied within two days. Officials said Cuddalore faced shortage and arrangements were made to send supplies from Coimbatore. The situation was being closely monitored, they said.

Education, Barcelona & Basque culture - why Spain are dominating football
- Published
World champions. European champions. Olympic champions. Undefeated in two and a half years. Spain are the dominant force in men's world football.
Of the past 10 major international tournaments, they have won five.
Going into Saturday's Nations League meeting with England at Wembley (19:45 BST), they are on an international record 38-match unbeaten run. They have not lost since a 1-0 defeat by Colombia in a 2024 friendly.
And the success does not stop with the senior men's team. During that time, Spain have also won:
- Six Under-19 European Championships
- Three Under-21 European Championships
- The Women's World Cup in 2023
At club level, Spanish teams have won half of all available Champions League and Europa League titles since 2009.
Spain football expert Guillem Balague told BBC Radio 5 Live there are "three pillars" that explain Spain's coaching culture and its unprecedented success.
"The first one was university, and in particular something called the National Institute of Physical Education," he said. "University entered physical education in Spain a long time ago, in the 1990s, and they created physical coaches and football coaches with a deep understanding of learning and training processes.
"Some of those fitness coaches became really big managers, like Rafa Benitez or Marcelino Garcia Toral. They came from learning and studying what football was about ahead of anybody else.
"The second pillar is the Basque culture. The Basque Country represents historically a special reference within Spanish football because they relate to work ethic, massive work ethic, daily effort.
"And the third pillar is what everybody knows: the Barcelona influence, Johan Cruyff and the tactical revolution that followed through him."
The Barcelona influence
Eight players from Barcelona's La Masia academy were in the Spain squad who won the 2010 World Cup under Vicente del Bosque, and another eight were in Luis de la Fuente's group as they lifted the trophy again this summer.
Barcelona won their first European Cup in 1992 under Cruyff playing total football - a style pioneered by the Netherlands team of the 1970s in which he played, and later mirrored at the Nou Camp under Pep Guardiola's management between 2008 and 2012.
That was a period where Barcelona won three consecutive La Liga titles, while Spain won back-to-back European Championships in 2008 and 2012 either side of their 2010 World Cup triumph.
Xavi, Andres Iniesta and Sergio Busquets were brought through in a system where players learn the art of ball possession and positional play in its purest form.
Jordi Gratacos, Barcelona's international director of academies from 2009 to 2011, and then from 2016 to 2020, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The number one thing is to understand the tactical meaning of the technical action. What I mean is to create intelligent players [who are] very good in technical aspects.
"In this level, all players are very good in the technical aspects. The most important are these players who always decide the best option inside the field and make others better.
"The main objective is to prepare the players to take the position. It's an open education when you create some scenarios, context and ecosystem where the player needs to decide, and the coach needs also to say: 'This was the best option - next time, take the other option.'
"The most important thing is that they need to decide inside the game."
In his first two seasons as Barcelona manager, Hansi Flick is repeating what Guardiola did - not only in the sense that he has won two La Liga titles in a row and chasing a third.
Academy products form the engine of his project, with Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo and Pau Cubarsi forming key components of success at both club and international level - just as the generation of 2008-12 did.
Spain have found the formula to repeat success, and Barcelona are at the heart of it.
The Basque Country
If Barcelona and Catalonia represents the artistry of Spanish football, the Basque Country represents its character.
Five players in the 2026 World Cup squad were from the region and came through at either Athletic Bilbao or Real Sociedad - clubs where eight players were playing at the time Spain won Euro 2024.
Then there is Mikel Merino, who scored a quarter-final winner against Germany at Euro 2024, before going on to score six goals in six games in World Cup qualifying, and late winners against Portugal and Belgium over the summer.
Although not Basque, Merino is from Pamplona in the autonomous community of Navarre - a region that has a significant influence of both Spanish and Basque culture.
Just five kilometres away from Pamplona is Zizur Mayor - the town where former Chelsea captain and Spain international Cesar Azpilicueta grew up.
When asked to describe Basque culture, Azpilicueta told BBC Radio 5 Live: "The discipline, the culture of working hard, of not giving up or being resilient, not very flashy.
"Normally, people want to display this culture of fight, being tough - like English football - more duels, more physical, less technical.
"But also in terms of tactical approach, more compact, great knowledge of knowing where to go, and with the ball keep it simple and try to go forward as quick as possible."
The five Basque players from the 2026 squad have formed an important part of Spain's recent success and are an embodiment of what Cruyff thought of players from that region.
Cruyff once said: "The first thing I did as a coach, was to sign four players from the Basque region. They are not afraid of anything."
For current Spain boss De la Fuente in 2026, Unai Simon played in goal, with former Manchester City defender Aymeric Laporte a key cornerstone of a defence that conceded just one goal in eight matches all tournament.
Nico Williams assisted the winning goal for Ferran Torres in the final against Argentina, Martin Zubimendi made a positive impact from the bench in both the Euro 2024 and World Cup finals, while Mikel Oyarzabal has scored 18 goals in his past 20 Spain appearances.
This influence stretches beyond the pitch as Basque coaches are in charge at four of England's biggest clubs - Mikel Arteta at Arsenal, Unai Emery at Aston Villa, Xabi Alonso at Chelsea and Andoni Iraola at Liverpool.
Education of the coaches
On to the final pillar - education.
Former Liverpool boss Rafael Benitez explained: "We were creating in Spain a group of fitness coaches who knew about football.
"I went to Liverpool John Moores University to see the programme of the sports scientists and they didn't have the knowledge in football that we had.
"They were really good in fitness, but with the ball and on the pitch, they didn't know how to manage. So you didn't have in England, this professional, this specialist in football, sports medicine and everything that we were studying in university.
"That was a crucial part of the formation of why Spain was improving and has been improving since then."

A video showing a group of people removing and breaking metal barricades near a water body is being widely shared with a claim that it shows people in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: A video shows devotees in Karnataka vandalising barricades after authorities restricted Ganesh idol immersion.
Fact: The video is from Hyderabad. It shows members of the Bhagyanagar Ganesh Utsav Samithi removing barricades at Tank Bund while protesting restrictions on Ganesh idol immersion. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an Instagram post by South Matters featuring the same visuals.
