Why Americans are warming to China
More than half of Americans still say they view China negatively. But that percentage is dropping.
President Donald Trump rolled out the literal red carpet for Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday afternoon, greeting his plane with a military band and a jet flyover at Maryland’s Joint Base Andrews.
It’s a very warm welcome for the man Trump once dubbed his “enemy,” and it reflects a fascinating, dramatic shift in his tone toward China — a country that Americans have also come to view more favorably over the past five years. (More on that about-face in just a minute.)
Trump and Xi have lots to discuss during this week’s state visit. On Wednesday, the two countries agreed to extend the current pause in their on-again, off-again trade war — but that kicks several pressing issues, like technology restrictions and access to critical minerals, further down the road.
AI safety advocates are also hoping the two leaders can reach some kind of agreement to slow down or safeguard AI development, following calls from a chorus of American tech executives.
Several of those execs are expected to attend a state dinner at the White House this evening, though the prospects of any substantive AI accord still seem pretty slim. This is more a sip-sparkling-wine-and-see-the-Archives kind of meeting than a signing-big-deals visit.
Go a little deeper
Trump isn’t the only one reassessing China these days. A trio of recent polls found that Americans also feel markedly more positive about China than they did five years ago, with the largest gains among young people. On average, American sentiment toward China is about the same today as it was 10 years ago — before Trump launched his first trade war.
What changed Americans’ minds about China? There is undoubtedly no one cause. It probably helps that Trump himself has changed his tune, no longer portraying the relationship between the US and China as an existential rivalry between so-called great powers.
Americans’ views on China have also recovered steadily since the Covid-19 pandemic, as memories of that period fade into the rearview. And foreign-policy issues — like, say, the status of Taiwan — generally aren’t top of mind for the average American voter.
But there’s also a cultural component here, particularly for young Americans. “Younger Americans are less wedded to notions of American primacy and more comfortable with coexistence,” Ryan Hass, a China scholar at the Brookings Institute, posted on X.
Many young Americans have, in fact, grown up embracing aspects of Chinese culture, from TikTok to Labubu. And there’s a pervasive sense, in some corners, that Western-style capitalism hasn’t precisely delivered the goods.
But let’s not kid ourselves here — China has plenty of problems, too. Like an economic slowdown, a mounting demographic crisis, and a culture of widespread political repression, to name just a few. For now, at least, an increasingly hostile US isn’t one of them.

To gauge if something’s actually healthy, check its nutrition label. And likewise, don’t make the mistake of assuming a food’s good for you just because it claims to be minimally processed.

Beau Lamarre-Condon asked a friend, “What would you do if I told you I killed somebody?” nine months before allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a Sydney court has heard.
The New South Wales police officer then assured the friend he hadn’t killed anyone, before admitting he had entered Baird’s house while he was away, before stealing a Polaroid camera and eating an Easter egg.
Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Baird, 26, and his partner, Davies, 29, with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Georgia Cook, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the NSW supreme court on Friday that the policeman had become “infatuated” with Baird during their brief relationship.
When the relationship ended in April 2023, Cook said Lamarre-Condon continued to speak about Baird.
He asked her a concerning question when they went to dinner a month later, Cook told the jury.
“One of the first things he said was, ‘What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?’” she told the jury.
Cook told Lamarre-Condon she wouldn’t help as she didn’t want a ghost haunting her, the court was told.
Lamarre-Condon laughed it off and said: “Don’t worry I didn’t do that, but I did do something crazy.”
Cook told the court the policeman said he had been watching Baird from outside his home, including on one occasion when he had friends over.
Lamarre-Condon saw Baird and his friends take photos using a Polaroid camera the officer had given him as a gift, Cook said.
When the group left Baird’s home, Lamarre-Condon had seen where the house key had been placed, Cook said.
“He had got the key, unlocked the door, stole the Polaroid camera and ate Jesse’s Easter egg,” she said on Friday.
Lamarre-Condon would travel to Baird’s home in his mother’s car and wear a black hoodie so he wouldn’t be recognised, the court was told.
The policeman and Baird began seeing each other again briefly a few months later.
But Baird ended the relationship in November 2023 after the accused went through his phone and deleted messages from other men. Lamarre-Condon was “really upset”, according to another one of the officer’s friends, Shae Davison.
Lamarre-Condon asked to stay at her house because he did not want to be alone, Davison told the jury.
The police officer arrived at her home with a backpack the next day and asked to send a message from her Instagram to Baird as “one last try to win Jesse back”, she told the court.
But Lamarre-Condon did not want her to read the message, claiming there were medical details he did not want her to know.
She didn’t want to do it initially but said: “He put a lot of pressure on me, he said he never asked anything of me, he’s so upset, can I help.”
“He wore me down,” Davison said on Friday. “It felt like guilt-tripping to me and using my friendship to get what he wanted.”
She agreed, on the condition Lamarre-Condon read out the text to her, while leaving out the medical details.
When he read out the message, she asked him to delete parts that weren’t true, and it looked like he was typing and actioning her edits, she told the court.
He then sent the note in a series of messages, and told her she was allowed to read it after 4 December 2023, when he told her he was set to undergo surgery. He left her home about an hour after he arrived.
The 1,600-word Instagram note claimed Davison had gone to Westmead hospital with Lamarre-Condon.
“He was told he had a cancerous tumour growing in his left shoulder joint/ligament area,” the text read out in court stated.
“Worst-case scenario, it could result in … possibly having his arm amputated.
“He was then immediately subscribed [sic] numerous medications … everyone knows these medications are some of the strongest you can be subscribed, which throw off your hormones massively, which throws off how a person can act in their day to day life.”
The friend told the jury she had not attended the hospital with Lamarre-Condon, nor did he clear this part of the text with her.
The messages tried to justify the officer going through Baird’s phone and stated “this is very out of character for him”.
“There is real love there, trust can be built back on that,” the note purportedly from Davison stated. “Even if you guys never hang out again, I know Beau wants to make things right.”
The friend was unsure if Baird read the messages but said it was possible he had seen them through Instagram’s preview function. Lamarre-Condon later asked her to unsend the messages.
She obliged and tried to ask him about the content of the messages but he did not want to talk about them.
“He was quite annoyed, I could tell in his voice he was frustrated that I had [read them],” she said.
It’s alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.
The defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

To address India’s alarming mental healthcare gap, NIMHANS in collaboration with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur, and the Lokopriya Gopinath Bordoloi Regional Institute of Mental Health (LGBRIMH), Tezpur, will formally launch a collaborative project titled ‘HEADS’ (Human-in-the-loop Evaluation of Assisted Depression Screening) on Thursday.
Funded by the Wellcome Trust, a major international charity foundation, the two-year study aims to build and evaluate AI-assisted approaches for the early identification and screening of depression. The initiative places a strong emphasis on Indian regional languages, specifically Kannada, Assamese, Hindi, Bengali, and English, which have historically remained substantially underrepresented in mental health AI research.
Bridging multilingual gap
Lekhansh Shukla, assistant professor of psychiatry at NIMHANS and principal investigator of the project, said India carries one of the world’s largest depression treatment gaps, where only about one in five individuals affected by depression receives timely, appropriate care.
During the project’s hybrid launch event at NIMHANS, experts will highlight the critical limitation of existing digital health innovations. Most mental health AI tools are built using English-language, urban datasets, rendering them ineffective in diverse, non-English clinical settings, he said.
“In our earlier research, we found that even frontier models cannot understand or translate Indian languages, especially when discussion was about feelings and emotions. HEADS instead builds for Indian languages from day one, developing artificial intelligence that understands clinical conversations in Kannada, Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, and English,” Dr. Shukla told The Hindu.
‘Human-in-the-loop’
A central principle of the project is a strict ‘human-in-the-loop’ framework, ensuring that AI tools serve purely as supportive clinical decision-aids to help clinicians recognise symptoms earlier without ever replacing professional clinical judgment.
In a pioneering effort for Indian mental health research, the study has embedded a 15-member panel of Lived Experience Experts - individuals who have survived depression, anxiety, or substance use disorders - across every phase of the project. This panel has actively shaped the study’s design and informed consent protocols. They will also participate in language-evaluation groups across all targeted Indian languages, audit AI algorithms for hidden bias and stigmatising language, and stress-test systems before deployment, the doctor said.
Two-year evaluation
Over its 24-month duration, the HEADS project will record and analyse approximately 4,500 clinical interviews across healthcare sites at NIMHANS and LGBRIMH. Meanwhile, IIT Kharagpur will lead the core engineering, system development, and AI-safety work to ensure responsible deployment. Senior leadership, investigators, and project team members across all partner institutions attended the hybrid launch, marking a landmark step toward equitable digital mental healthcare in India.

Kashmir’s apple growers remain without crop insurance, with the Jammu and Kashmir government telling the Legislative Assembly on Tuesday that the Restructured Weather Based Crop Insurance Scheme (RWBCIS) has yet to be implemented for horticultural crops in the Union Territory.
The Agriculture Production Department will invite fresh bids after the Centre finalises revised operational guidelines for the scheme, the government said in response to a question by CPI(M) MLA Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami.
“The department had earlier invited bids from empanelled insurance companies for horticultural and commercial crops. Four bids were received for traditional and high-density apple and saffron in Kashmir, and five for mango, litchi and saffron in Jammu,” it said.
The government informed that the Agriculture Insurance Company of India (AIC) emerged as the lowest bidder for Kashmir, while Tata AIG was the lowest bidder for Jammu. AIC quoted premiums ranging from 10% to 39% in Kashmir, compared with 26.41% to 41% in Jammu.
“For traditional apple in Budgam, Bandipora, Baramulla and Kupwara, the quoted premium was 34%. Saffron premiums in some districts ranged from 37% to 39%, above the 30% threshold,” it said.
According to the government the 2025-26 bid block, involved a proposed sum insured of Rs 6,594.93 crore against a premium of Rs 1,280.87 crore.
Farmers’ share was estimated at Rs 329.75 crore, while the government contribution was Rs 950.93 crore.
“J&K’s share was Rs 182.35 crore, including Rs 85.39 crore towards premiums within the 30% threshold and Rs 96.96 crore towards the amount above it. The Centre’s 90% share of the subsidised premium was estimated at Rs 768.57 crore,” it said.
The J&K Finance Department, in a March 16, 2026, communication, advised the Agriculture Production Department to issue a fresh tender covering all 20 districts for “administrative synchronisation, uniformity in implementation and alignment with national policy decisions.”
The Centre had issued similar advice on February 4, asking J&K to prepare a fresh tender for all 20 districts in view of proposed changes to the operational guidelines of the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana and RWBCIS.
The revised framework was envisaged for implementation from Kharif 2026.
A Centre-appointed subcommittee constituted in September 2025 has been working to standardise insurance term sheets for apple, banana, grape, mango and pomegranate under RWBCIS.
J&K held discussions with the Centre and the subcommittee on June 13 and July 29 to finalise the apple terms.
The department said both apple term sheets have now been finalised.
The subcommittee is completing its work, after which the revised guidelines will be followed by fresh bidding in Jammu and Kashmir.
The government has not specified when the contracts will be awarded or insurance coverage will begin.
The delay leaves Kashmir’s apple growers without formal weather-based cover against recurring losses from hailstorms, frost, heavy snowfall, flash floods, cloudbursts and other weather-related events.

Edmonton Police Service asks court to order homeless man to pay $8,400 before proceeding with lawsuit
Dwayne Cardinal is suing the city and EPS over encampment cleanup
A man experiencing homelessness who is suing the Edmonton Police Service (EPS) is facing a new hurdle after the police department applied for an order requiring him to pay $8,400 in security for costs.
Dwayne Cardinal is suing EPS over an encampment cleanup on July 15, 2024, alleging misconduct by officers. He alleges excessive force was used during his arrest.
The allegations have not been tested in court.
Security for costs can be ordered as a financial guarantee to cover a defendant's estimated legal expenses if the plaintiff loses the lawsuit.
A bill of costs for the EPS chief, included in an affidavit filed with the application, outlines estimated legal expenses, including fees related to questioning both Cardinal and the defendants.
In its arguments, EPS points to Cardinal’s statements saying he has been homeless for 10 years and receives less than $600 a month from income support. EPS argues it is unlikely that he has assets to satisfy a cost award if he loses.
EPS declined to comment on the order, stating the issue is before the courts.
The lawsuit names former Edmonton police chief Dale McFee and constables Mathew Bruno and Levi Clarke. Cardinal alleges battery, false arrest, false imprisonment, negligence and violations of his Charter rights during his arrest.
‘Diabolical’
Cardinal's lawyer, Chris Wiebe, said he believes it was "diabolical” for EPS to ask the court for an order that his client pay $8,400 before he can continue his lawsuit against the police department.
“My client receives less than $600 a month from income support. The EPS has an annual budget of over a half-billion dollars. If the EPS are successful, it would set a horrible precedent," Wiebe said in a statement.
In Cardinal's civil lawsuit and related police complaint, he says Edmonton police used a Taser on him, leaving eight probe and stun wounds. He also alleges that officers kicked him in the back between his shoulder blades and dragged him across the ground to a police vehicle.
It is not contested by the parties that a Taser was used.
Cardinal alleges he was unlawfully detained after officers ordered him to stop packing his tent and stand aside without explaining why he was being detained. He says he was arrested despite complying with officers and packing up his belongings to leave the site.
He also alleges officers violated his Charter rights by failing to promptly tell him why he was being arrested and detained before using physical force. An EPS court application currently seeks to have those Charter claims struck from the lawsuit.
Const. Bruno’s notes state that he read Cardinal his Charter rights after his arrest.
Cardinal says police failed to prevent City of Edmonton workers from seizing and disposing of his tent and personal belongings while he was detained, and that officers dropped him off near a shelter rather than ensuring he received prompt medical treatment for his injuries.
In the affidavit, the EPS argues the officers were lawfully clearing an illegal encampment on private property and allege Cardinal was aggressive and unco-operative. The EPS says Cardinal swore at officers and refused to identify himself, and pushed a tent toward an officer, which prompted his arrest.
EPS says Cardinal physically fought arrest and that medical services attended the scene, determined the Taser probes did not penetrate Cardinal's skin and cleared him as requiring no medical care.
EPS says its role was securing officer and worker safety, while property disposal was at the discretion of city workers.
Cardinal’s lawsuit also names the City of Edmonton. He’s asking a judge to find the city liable for seizing and disposing of his personal belongings during the cleanup.
The city has disputed his claim, arguing its workers were authorized to remove the property under Alberta’s Municipal Government Act and that the items posed health and safety risks.
Arguments against the city were heard last month and the judge has yet to make a decision on that application.
The hearing for EPS’ application, which covers both the security for costs request and the striking of Charter claims, is scheduled to take place on Oct. 14 at the Edmonton Court of King’s Bench.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

In a remarkable example of the human brain’s adaptability to sensory loss, scientists have found that people with deafness develop superior peripheral vision, which is vision outside the eyes’ central focus.
Researchers from the Universities of York and Sheffield used MRI scans along with visual stimuli among 16 hearing adults and 16 deaf adults and compared them. They found that the latter group responded to objects and movements even in the far-reaches of their eyesight, granting them an extra advantage in sensing their environment and detecting danger.
How this happens
The brain is rewired, with a redistribution of neural resources: among the deaf, there was a greater neural weightage given to far-peripheral vision in the primary visual cortex (the part of the brain responsible for deconstructing visual input) and the lateral geniculate nucleus (a visual relay centre situated deep within the brain).
“The brain does a really clever thing, in that it doesn’t expand overall visual capacity, but does a type of trade-off that redistributes its existing resources,” Heidi Baseler, co-author from the University of York’s Department of Psychology and the Hull York Medical School, explained in a release.
The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
In people with deafness, this adjustment is particularly important as it enables them to better catch “unexpected events that might happen just out of the central line of sight, that those of able hearing would be aware of more acutely through the sound that they might make,” and therefore could avoid, say, a car collision, for instance, Dr. Baseler said.
Interestingly, the brain does not entirely expand its visual processing capacity, but provides more power to peripheral vision and a little less to the central visual field to people with deafness. This finding could help better understand of how the brain adapts to sensory loss.
The compensation effect
It has, in fact, been a long-held belief that those with a sensory deficit develop a stronger ability with other senses as compensation, also known as the ‘compensation effect’.
And this has been scientifically proven in several instances. For instance, 20 years ago, researchers studied the major sensory differences between the visually impaired and sighted persons, and found that the average pure tone hearing (the quietest sounds a person can hear) threshold of people with blindness was significantly higher than that of sighted ones. The paper was published in the International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics.
This research result could help future designers “incorporate human factors in product design,” particularly with respect to visually disabled users, said the paper.

Ominousness permeates Darkling. In Titas Halder’s dramatic monologue, we witness a young girl’s coming of age set against the backdrop of the 1984 toxic gas leak in the Indian city of Bhopal, an environmental catastrophe that remains one of the worst industrial disasters in global history, leading to thousands of deaths.
Actor Linnea Berthelsen – best known for her role as Kali in Netflix series Stranger Things – makes her UK stage debut and gamely takes on the singular role in a tightly wound, physical performance. Leaping across Simon Kenny’s artful, soil-filled set, Berthelsen embodies childlike wonder as she recounts her early years playing in the rain, savouring bowlfuls of plain rice and idolising her older sister.
So far so good. Except, alongside her emotional growth, the silhouette of a new factory rises in the background – effectively portrayed by lighting designer Rajiv Pattani’s projection – foreshadowing the calamity to come. When it eventually arrives, we hear of the horrors she witnesses, stepping over maimed bodies, facing blinded relatives and breathing in toxic fumes, all relayed through increasingly frenzied description.
Herein lies the main issue with Darkling. By using a monologue format – especially one where our narrator is never dramatically questioned – all the audience receives are streams of poetic description, a barrage of words that never feel emphatic or adequate enough to match the gruesome scale of such a tragedy. Coupled with Halder’s uneven pacing, which lingers in childhood for too long before alighting on trauma and then descending into a hectoring denouement that places the blame for the disaster on individual shoulders, Berthelsen is faced with a gargantuan task to maintain a sense of dramatic tension.
As Matthew Xia’s production draws to a close, with a strangely repeated narrative beat that equates female worth to motherhood, you are ultimately left feeling that this is a tragedy told without the requisite horror. Darkling is a worthy reminder of an often-overlooked disaster – but one that may well fail to take root in the mind.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his government is investigating a June incident in which an OpenAI agent accessed “non-public files” from the country’s online Medicare statistics portal. OpenAI said in a statement that “our models took actions we did not intend” in causing the breach, which it only recently disclosed to the Australian government.
Speaking in New York on Wednesday, Albanese said three other public health statistics systems also “may have been impacted” across Australian federal and state governments. He added that these portals “contain non-sensitive Medicare information” such as aggregate statistics and that early indications suggest “no personal information is believed to have been accessed.”
That said, Albanese stressed that the “situation is obviously unacceptable” and that he has expressed his “extreme concern” over how the incident was handled to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
Much like the now-infamous Hugging Face hacking incident, Albanese said this system breach stemmed from OpenAI’s own testing of an internal model, this time to conduct “Internet based research into public medicine spending.” When the company’s AI agent encountered “repeated blocks” in its search for specific information, Albanese said, it “attempted alternative ways to obtain the info” and “found a way around those blocks.”
“[It] didn’t accept no for an answer, if you like,” Albanese said. “There is no suggestion of foreign actors here. This is a research project that has got into areas that it shouldn’t have.”
In a statement provided to multiple outlets, OpenAI said it had “identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation.”

Was this award-winning book written by AI? Scandal deepens skepticism in literary world
Thélyson Orélien's debut novel shortlisted for prestigious prizes. Then the allegations started pouring in
A Quebec-based author is at the centre of an artificial intelligence scandal shaking the French literary world and raising questions around how the industry should be using AI — and its detection tools.
Breakthrough star Thélyson Orélien, a Canadian-Haitian poet and author, has been accused of writing his debut novel using generative AI, which he vehemently denies. The scandal comes as C’était ça ou mourir is being considered for various prestigious awards.
The allegation first surfaced Monday – the same day Orélien won the Prix du roman Fnac – on the anonymous X account "Balance ton Claude," which claims to expose AI slop.
The account claims to have analyzed several excerpts from the book using the AI-detector tool Pangram, which found the text was “100 per cent” AI.
CBC News replicated the Pangram experiment with different excerpts of the book, which led to the same result.
Speaking to franceinfo Wednesday, the president of the Académie Goncourt, which shortlisted Orélien for an award, said the latter wouldn’t be disqualified unless “irrefutable evidence” were to surface.
“The academy is taking the time to consider the various factors involved in this case before making a decision that will preserve both the integrity of the prize it awards and that of its work,” Claudel Philippe told CBC in a statement Thursday.
The executive director of Writers’ Trust of Canada, David Leonard, says the question of how trustworthy these AI-detection tools are is an issue the entire industry is grappling with. For now, the organization, which recognizes local writers, relies on self-declarations made by the authors.
But it’s exploring its options, he says.
“It's a very fast-moving issue,” Leonard said. “We don't want to be in a situation where we're getting false positives, nor do we want to be in a situation where we're using a tool that is not effective.”
On Thursday afternoon, Orélien's Montreal-based publishing house, Éditions du Boréal, announced it was suspending its press tour for the author, who is currently in France gearing up for award season.
"We unreservedly condemn the hateful messages and personal attacks of recent days and call on everyone to exercise restraint," it wrote in a statement.
It adds that its decision is to preserve Orélien's well-being and that the book, which was published in the spring, remains available.
What happened?
C'était ça ou mourir, which translates to "It was either that or die" tells the story of a man who undertakes a perilous journey across the Americas to escape gang violence in Haiti’s Port-au-Prince.
Orélien has previously said his own experience of leaving Haiti following the 2010 earthquake and stories of other migrants he met in Montreal helped shape the novel.
In a statement Tuesday evening, he attempted to soothe the scrutiny of his heavy use of metaphors and similes in the book, which many have pointed to as tells that AI was involved in the writing process.
"I come from a Haitian and Caribbean literary tradition in which poetry, imagery, repetition, and rhythm carry a living voice," Orélien said in the statement written in French and released by Éditions du Boréal.
"One might debate my style, but treating its techniques as evidence of artificial intelligence has nothing to do with literary criticism," he said.
In the same statement, Éditions du Boréal affirmed its support for the author, saying Orélien's manuscript was drafted several years ago and evolved over multiple exchanges with his editor.
However, new allegations have cast doubt on Orélien's credibility beyond the fiction-writing sphere.
Allegations of plagiarism
On Wednesday, the Quebec newspaper La Presse uncovered multiple instances of possible plagiarism in Orélion’s columns across different publications dating back to 2012. Radio-Canada's Décrypteurs has since verified those findings.
Orélien has not addressed the compounding scandal.
Speaking to Radio-Canada’s Tout un matin Thursday morning, La Presse’s vice-president of information, François Cardinal said he read the book – stopping short of calling it “incredible” – and at no point suspected the involvement of AI.
“We’ll never have a definitive answer on AI one way or the other. We can’t prove beyond all doubt that AI was used. And we can’t prove that AI wasn’t used,” he said.
But given the plagiarism allegations, he said the publication will likely not consider Orélien for future columns.
In an update Thursday morning, Éditions du Boréal said it was taking stock of the newest and "very serious" plagiarism allegations.
Thursday afternoon, the literary festival Salon du livre in the Eastern Townships announced it was dropping Orélien as its guest of honour.
A few hours later, Éditions du Boréal announced its suspension of Orélien's press tour.
In its latest statement, it continued to defend its editorial process, adding that despite its best efforts to produce a "definitive answer" as to whether the book was written by AI, the publishing house says it is simply "impossible at this stage to confirm or deny the allegations."
"The fact remains that the novel has reached tens of thousands of readers across the French-speaking world, as well as numerous international publishers," reads the statement. "In the absence of serious, tangible evidence, it is not for us to decide whether it has the right to exist."
Tools detect AI, not ideas
For Florent Michelot, a Concordia professor who researches AI in education, Orélien’s ordeal raises a key question: Have we entered an era where the final product is no longer enough when judging someone’s work?
“I didn’t read the book, but maybe [Orélien] developed very complex personalities for his characters, maybe he developed a wonderful atmosphere … and the AI only helped to write the sentences,” he said.
Michelot says he's personally tested Pangram, the AI-detector tool, and like many other experts who have spoken out since the controversy broke, he says the tool is "amazing."
Basically, the tool identifies patterns based on probability, he explains. If every word in an excerpt is statistically the most likely word to follow the one before it, then AI was most likely involved in the writing, according to the tool.
So, as more people lean on AI for things like research, spellcheck and translations, Michelot wonders if the creative process will begin to gain more value over the finished product.
Humans reading humans
For French literature professor Emeline Pierre, who teaches at the Université de Montréal, the controversy has created a sense of unease, she says. The questions of why Orélien was targeted and why now are central to how she's digesting the situation.
Regardless, she puts in doubt the reliability of AI-detecting tools. As for the repetitions and metaphors in Orélien's text, she says they are characteristic of writing styles in the Caribbean.
"Once again, we see the journey of a Black person who makes their mark. And when that person perhaps goes too far — garners too much recognition — it seems to me that they eventually become a source of discomfort," she said.
She says the attention the controversy has garnered harkens back to the case of Jason Arday, a Cambridge professor who gained prominence after becoming the university's youngest professor in 2023 at age 37.
He was found dead inside his apartment after becoming the focus of a plagiarism scandal.
Pierre worries about the effect the Orélien story will have on emerging young Black writers, adding that the speed with which scandals seem to close in on their subject when they’re Black is worrisome.
The executive director of the Writers' Trust of Canada says despite the controversy and AI’s seemingly growing writing proficiency, it’s not the future of literature itself he’s worried about, but the viability of writing as a career.
He says many authors support themselves by taking on other types of writing jobs and those are being eliminated by AI.
“So these tools are making it much more difficult for writers to make a living,” he said.
“We'll continue to write literature, and people wanting to read human-authored works will continue to want to read human-authored works.”

Residents eating garden weeds in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
- Published
"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.
She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.
Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.
They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.
They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.
Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.
Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.
Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.
It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakova Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.
Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.
Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.
Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.
Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive.
"There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May.
"I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."
Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.
Which weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.
No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.
While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.
Warning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below.
Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east.
Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.
Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.
She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information.
"I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."
While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.
Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety.
"They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.

  - Published3 days ago
Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.
They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana.
Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky.
Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".
Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".
That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish.
"This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine.
"If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Australia is investigating whether OpenAI broke the law after an agent hacked into its health statistics portal in the first widely known incident of an AI agent hacking a government website.
The Australian government is reviewing whether it should involve the federal police after the agent accessed non-public files from the social and health services agency, Services Australia, in June.
Australia only found out about the incident when OpenAI alerted the government on September 10—almost three months after the hack—by sending an email to a public mailbox. Sam Altman had reportedly not mentioned the incident when he met Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, earlier this month, even though OpenAI had been aware since August. The company took “way too long” and the notification should not have just gone through a public inbox, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a press conference in New York on Wednesday. There will also be an inquiry into why Services Australia then took five days to escalate the email to Australia’s Cyber Security Centre.
OpenAI’s agent had been conducting internet based research into health statistics in a development project by an internal OpenAI research team. When it could not access certain information, the agent attempted alternative ways until it found a work around and gained unauthorized access. It also wrote files to the internal server, which the government is waiting on OpenAI for more technical information on. The government is also investigating whether the agent gained unauthorised access to three additional government websites it interacted with.
“There will obviously be legal consequences on it,” Albanese said as he disclosed the “unacceptable” incident. He said he had spoken with Altman over the phone earlier that day about his “extreme concern” about the incident and “disappointment” with the nature and length of time the company took to inform the government. While Albanese did not answer whether he had apologised, Altman “clearly accepted that the company had not done good enough,” he said.
The Australian government currently believes no one’s personal data was accessed, though investigations are ongoing. The website in question is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics such as spending. It was therefore behind much lower levels of security than personal data would have been, Marles said in Sydney. “The impact of the incident is actually relatively minor, but this is a serious incident, obviously, and one that is completely unacceptable,” he cautioned.
A number of incidents over the summer, including OpenAI agents’ hacking of HuggingFace—highlighting the threat of frontier model agents acting rogue—were raised at the United Nations General Assembly this week, with Secretary General António Guterres welcoming calls to control AI. Altman himself had warned the United Nations Security Council earlier on Wednesday about his concern that humans could lose control of these systems.
“It was a shock that it occurred, because it was real and serious,” Albanese said about the incident. “But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves.”
Australia is establishing a task force to look at the incident and emerging AI cyber threats. It will consider possible law enforcement and legislative responses to ensure that incidents like this don’t happen again.

Trump’s aide Natalie Harp who has come under scrutiny for her influence dishes on life in the White House
Describing Washington as lacking a sense of urgency, the executive assistant said the capital ‘does not work at the speed of TRUMP!’

Newly released candid responses from Natalie Harp, the 35-year-old White House aide widely reported as a key figure managing President Donald Trump’s social media presence, offer a rare glimpse into her daily routine and working relationship with the president.
The full, unedited comments were recently published online by Washingtonian magazine after brief excerpts were originally selected to accompany its October profile feature on the region’s 300 Most Powerful Women.
According to the outlet, the written answers were provided by White House Communications Director Steven Cheung on Harp’s behalf on August 18 — a period marked by heightened public scrutiny following her inclusion on a secret flight out of Turkey with the president and a viral mention in a speech by Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff.
Addressing the demands of her job as Special and Executive Assistant to the president, Harp pointed to her upbringing and early academic trajectory as preparation for the high-pressure environment. She noted that she completed her undergraduate degree in three years before earning an MBA with a 4.0 GPA.
“I was blessed with parents who showed me, by example, that ‘work’ is not a place you go to 8 to 5, but something you do until everyone, and everything, you are responsible for is taken care of, to the best of your ability,” Harp said. “Living by this maxim means being ‘on call’ for the Administration, Congress, and the Citizens we serve, around the clock.”
Harp, whose written style and emphatic use of capitalization mirror the distinctive tone of Trump’s posts on Truth Social, expressed frustration with the pace of the nation’s capital when describing the main difficulties of her post.
“Washington, D.C., does not work at the speed of ‘TRUMP!’” Harp said. “We have only four years to, MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN, and that sense of urgency is absent from too many, while the Radical Left tries to stop, or slow down, the momentum the President is building for the Golden Age of America.”
When asked how she manages the daily stress of travel and long hours, Harp explained that she turns to her faith each morning rather than conventional routines.
“Since the epicenter of ‘power’ is not Washington, D.C., but Heaven, every morning I listen to a few chapters of the Bible on audiobook, and pray for God’s wisdom and strength in whatever situations may arise,” she told Washingtonian.
Dismissing questions regarding whether her age has presented challenges in a high-level political role, Harp praised Trump’s approach to staff selection and talent evaluation.
“Age is just a number. Years count how long you have been doing something, not necessarily how good you are at it,” she said, adding that the president “has the rare gift of seeing something in people that perhaps they don’t see in themselves, male or female, young or old.”
Harp also cited White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and author Joni Eareckson Tada as primary role models, crediting their resilience under difficult personal circumstances.
“Fighting cancer while serving as Chief of Staff for the Most Consequential President in History, Susie Wiles is an example to all of what can be accomplished when one has the strength and resolve to do so,” Harp wrote, adding a quote she attributed to the president: “You can’t prove your merit on quiet waters.”
